subject: Voice AI Investment Surges as Enterprise Applications Gain Traction
body:
# Voice AI Investment Surges as Enterprise Applications Gain Traction

[![Founder and CEO of Abridge, Shiv Rao speaks during the Live Keynote Pregame during the Nvidia GTC (GPU Technology Conference) in Washington, DC, on October 28, 2025. (Photo by Jim WATSON / AFP) (Photo by JIM WATSON/AFP via Getty Images)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!QJFL!,w_1100,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F9fa52d53-6f91-40d2-b0f4-a9c56516f664_5392x3592.jpeg "Founder and CEO of Abridge, Shiv Rao speaks during the Live Keynote Pregame during the Nvidia GTC (GPU Technology Conference) in Washington, DC, on October 28, 2025. (Photo by Jim WATSON / AFP) (Photo by JIM WATSON/AFP via Getty Images)")](https://substack.com/redirect/3d98177d-38cd-4b76-8316-febb26a0349e?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ)

Venture investors poured over $7 billion into voice AI startups in the first quarter of this year, far more than in any previous period, as products based on vastly improved voice recognition technology proliferate in the workplace.

ElevenLabs, Synthesia, and Runway (which is known for its video models but handles large amounts of voice generation) have all raised sizable new rounds since the start of the year. The global market for voice recognition technology, expected to be worth [$22 billion](https://substack.com/redirect/8a914e3e-8147-4832-9631-7fcb23fe2f11?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ) in 2026, is projected to nearly triple in size over the next five years.

Global Voice AI Deal Value (Excluding OpenAI & Anthropic)Quarterly totals ($B) raised for venture-backed voice AI startups from Q1 2022 to Q1 2026

[![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!K5-0!,w_640,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fef29263c-abce-4ea0-8b20-3c40c2f9a38d_1220x780.png)](https://substack.com/redirect/cd2e0d3a-b575-44b8-a716-5783c9a7d5a8?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ)

We’re taking a look at how the tools are being deployed in a few key enterprise verticals. We have the stories of how Abridge launched across care centers in the Phoenix area, DeepL’s integration with Aramark, and more.

#### But first: talk about voice with us at our summit on Wednesday

Given the rush of interest in voice, we’re excited to be hosting the first-ever **[Cerebral Valley Voice Summit](https://substack.com/redirect/9b8f16eb-c8c6-4945-ae4b-6b6b238784bf?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ)** this Wednesday, May 6, in San Francisco.

We’ll take the themes of this story — like healthcare, customer service, and personal note-taking — and discuss them live and in-depth with the CEOs of Sierra, Abridge, Deepgram, Wispr Flow, and more.

Come contribute to the conversation. Applications to this invite-only summit are closing soon. You can apply [here](https://substack.com/redirect/54606906-f2a6-488b-9c0a-123082d4f1bc?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ).

Now, back to the story.

## Ambient AI in the Doctor’s Office

**Dr. Craig Norquist** remembers when ambient AI scribes first hit the market a decade ago. As Chief Medical Information Officer for HonorHealth — a Phoenix-area network of 200 care centers and 17,000 staff — he watched doctors try the technology, shrug, and walk away.

But the post-ChatGPT development of voice AI has changed everything. Generative AI supercharged the venerable but slow-developing voice recognition sector, and two years ago HonorHealth was in serious talks with Abridge, the AI note-taking platform built for physicians (CEO **Shiv Rao** pictured).

In February, Abridge launched at HonorHealth with 500 licenses for around 3,000 physicians and PAs, who are using Abridge in the background to record and take notes as they meet with patients.

# Karim

**Welcome back to Flow State,** the instrumental music newsletter. You’re on the free tier – to unlock our daily playlists, weekly mixes, and support our work, upgrade today:

[Upgrade to paid](https://substack..xkJW7Hj_I7SLQptPxoWtFk_zOOJplBbo9ePArhe8dNs?&utm_medium=email&utm_source=subscribe-widget&utm_content=198802877)

---

**It’s Friday so we’re listening to something more upbeat. Today we’re listening to Karim, a Moroccan electronic musician based in Casablanca. Shout out to [Shawn Reynaldo](https://open.substack.com/users/2580013-shawn-reynaldo?utm_source=mentions)’s [First Floor newsletter](https://substack.com/redirect/4c9b83de-77e2-4a31-9ec2-e2f1d28ba557?j=eyJ1IjoiZnZlciJ9.8N73-dqQlrWLx3o5gPfyirClhk7-cxP_NqOwOQYAApk) for putting us on. In 2014, Karim founded Tikita Records, which spotlights artists from around the globe with a focus on hypnotic sounds – minimalist, techno, and ambient. He just released his own debut LP,** ***Lila*****, which channels Moroccan traditional styles via modular synthesizers. Specifically, he drew from the Gnawa, “a religious-spiritual musical tradition descended from West African peoples brought to Morocco as slaves hundreds of years ago.”¹** ***Lila*****’s entrancing repetition draws a connection between Gnawa nighttime healing rituals and contemporary raves. We’re also listening to** ***Sqala*****, his 2021 collaboration with French producer Amandra, which has two versions of the title track and four remixes of them, including one by [Donato Dozzy](https://substack.com/redirect/fd8b9c1c-c282-47ad-a6fe-00bb715d4c97?j=eyJ1IjoiZnZlciJ9.8N73-dqQlrWLx3o5gPfyirClhk7-cxP_NqOwOQYAApk).**

# How to make your AI brand stand out (when everything else feels the same)

[![](https://review.firstround.com/content/images/size/w1600/2026/05/AI-Powered_Hero-v2-1.png)](https://email2.firstround.com/c/eJxUj01u6zAMBk8j7RyQFEUqCy0e8OB76IdOjDp14Tju9QsH3XT5fRhgMD3XisLeMqom1aCUvD3KvAxzz1Igmqm1ScQYALBNQDD5e9Zr4irSSTkU4pKoaGe51spUC1Y_ZwISiMgYOXG6pAINA1OT1hCKOYZp3p77tr4--6WtD7_k-75_PV3452h0NG52zPZ9-Uudv6OxlqgdhVwYHy78j52NxGBArWlgm3ioV4yDCnSMmAJD91veymHTui3zcepvZ-fbvOf6Wj6Gd7jf8-2-PvffdWT6CQAA___NZ1cG)

In the first couple years after the ChatGPT moment, slapping “AI” on your product was good enough to get buyers to pay attention. It’s not anymore.

“AI powered” worked as a differentiator when it felt new. But that stops being a position when five other credible “AI-powered X” companies are out there. And now there are — because models are shared, infrastructure is abstracted and products that once required months of engineering can launch in days or hours. Worse, all these companies use the same gradients, sterile screenshots and LLM-smoothed copy, making it impossible for customers to tell them apart.

**Arielle Jackson** has spent over a decade working with First Round founders on positioning, brand identity and launch communications. Her advice has shifted a lot over the last two years. The new problem she sees founders faced with: AI accelerates sameness.

In her new piece on The Review, Jackson lays out what founders need to do instead:

1. Start with an opinionated point of view that actually repels some people (intentionally)
2. Create positioning that you revisit every few months as the terrain moves
3. Develop a visual and verbal identity distinctive enough that a competitor copying it would look like a parody

She walks through how Cursor had to reframe its positioning twice in under two years, why Clay’s recent out-of-home campaign is the cleanest expression she’s seen in the category and what Anthropic’s Department of War standoff actually did for Claude’s App Store ranking.

Thanks, as always, for reading and sharing!  

*-The Review Editors*

# Never seen a data quality issue that wasn’t actually an ownership problem | John Wernfeldt

#### About Our Contributing Expert

### John Wernfeldt | Managing Director: Data, Analytics & AI

[![John Wernfeldt featured on Modern Data 101](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!Xfij!,w_1100,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fa9b522a4-b081-4a35-b935-aa445d9d0b44_1600x900.png "John Wernfeldt featured on Modern Data 101")](https://substack.com/redirect/a63030c3-c785-44fd-aedd-79572d8b7c0a?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ)

[John Wernfeldt](https://substack.com/redirect/15a0d3bb-61b1-47ba-a401-20dbe67c5f1c?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ) works with CDOs and senior data leaders who are under pressure to “be AI-ready” while still struggling with trust, ownership, and decision clarity in their data. His focus is practical data governance and foundations, the kind that reduce rework, end metric debates, and give executives confidence to act.

Based in Stockholm, John is Managing Director at Northridge Analytics, where he helps organisations turn data and analytics into tangible business value, and President of DAMA Sweden. His background spans data strategy, governance, architecture, and analytics leadership roles at Gartner, Capgemini Invent, and KPMG.

Known for cutting through hype, John emphasises clear decision rights, fit-for-purpose quality, and governance embedded into delivery. His work helps organisations move from fragmented, fragile data to trusted foundations that scale with analytics and AI. We’re thrilled to feature his unique insights on [Modern Data 101](https://substack.com/redirect/1e48bf87-65d3-40c8-bc2c-a9be0d2a05d3?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ)!

> *We actively collaborate with data experts to bring the best resources to a [15,000+ strong community](https://substack.com/redirect/f1d7c58a-01d8-46e6-b84c-63fff3fbee7c?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ) of data leaders and practitioners. If you have something to share, reach out!  
> 🫴🏻 Share your ideas and work: [community@moderndata101.com](https://substack.com/redirect/d6bdc2d7-a99f-485b-beb3-ca9392dd9a69?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ)*

###### **\*Note: Opinions expressed in contributions are not our own and are only curated by us for broader access and discussion. All submissions are vetted for quality & relevance. We keep it information-first and do not support any promotions, paid or otherwise.**

---

### Let’s Dive In

I’ve never seen a “data quality issue” that wasn’t, at its core, an ownership problem. I’ve seen this play out more times than I can count.

A number looks off, someone flags it, everyone agrees it’s “important.” And then the questions begin. Sales uses it in forecasts, finance uses it in reporting, marketing uses it in KPIs, analytics builds dashboards on top, and IT moves the data and gets asked to fix it.

**Everyone touches the metric, yet no one owns it.**

## When a metric breaks, the same explanations always show up

When the number is questioned, the conversation goes in predictable directions.

A [recent survey on the state of data and AI in enterprises](https://substack.com/redirect/54a28f6a-aeb9-45a4-90d0-8315705541f5?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ) conclusively suggests how the same metric gets corrupted as it changes hands. Because no one in particular owns the health of the metric. Many of us touch the same metric, and we end up seeing different versions.

[![9 in 10 experience conflicting versions of the same metric | Excerpt from the Modern Data Report 2026](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!k9HO!,w_1100,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fd404c92a-b974-4cc3-8

# Why Leaders Can't Delegate Judgment to Systems: Where Accountability Exists

#### About Our Contributing Expert

### Arun Gamidi | Enterprise Data & Analytics Leader

[![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!j0uD!,w_1100,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F2121ff40-c33e-4780-8a61-9da11c672dd7_1600x900.png)](https://substack.com/redirect/bc18154f-059a-4ec5-b75e-b02cc5f66aed?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ)

[Arun Gamidi](https://substack.com/redirect/ccf65bb8-a299-4e47-b1c1-c268327f337b?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ) believes most data initiatives fail not because of bad technology, but because they never connect to the decisions that actually matter. A data and analytics leader with deep experience in financial services, Arun has spent his career building and scaling data ecosystems in high-stakes enterprise environments where the cost of unclear decisions is real.

His work is grounded in a decision-first philosophy: data and AI create value only when they clarify the choices leaders must make. His framework, DATA by Design (Direction, Alignment, Trust, and Activation), gives organisations a repeatable path to align data initiatives with business goals, build trust in their information, and ensure insights reach the moment of decision.

Arun currently leads Enterprise Data & Analytics at MGIC. Through that work and his weekly Leadergence newsletter, his focus is on equipping data leaders to operate with confidence, not just access, in an AI-accelerated world. Readers can follow his ongoing thinking at [Leadergence](https://substack.com/redirect/206267df-d32c-4875-953e-7c1ce15741a5?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ) on LinkedIn. We're thrilled to feature his insights on [Modern Data 101](https://substack.com/redirect/260901d8-43ad-411e-a3e1-d36405235f51?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ)!

> *We actively collaborate with data experts to bring the best resources to a [20,000+ strong community](https://substack.com/redirect/8c3081f7-56c8-4c2c-9114-0839ae0cb77a?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ) of data leaders and practitioners. If you have something to share, reach out!  
> 🫴🏻 Share your ideas and work: [community@moderndata101.com](https://substack.com/redirect/70bb27c0-ee52-4faf-9ca4-6bfc3922de2a?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ)*

###### **\*Note: Opinions expressed in contributions are not our own and are only curated by us for broader access and discussion. All submissions are vetted for quality & relevance. We keep it information-first and do not support any promotions, paid or otherwise.**

---

### Let’s Dive In

Every decision has a consequence. And every consequence has an owner. But systems do not experience consequences. Neither can they own “consequences.”

They do not carry the weight of a wrong call or the satisfaction of a right one. That capacity belongs entirely to people. This is not a limitation of current technology, but a structural reality that more advanced systems will not change.

When something goes wrong, no one asks the model what it would do differently. They ask the leader responsible for the project or the model owner running the algorithm. That question has always pointed in the same direction, and it always will.

---

## The Problem: Accountability Drift

No leader decides one morning to stop being accountable. It happens gradually in the space between a recommendation arriving and a decision being made.

Systems are fast, and they are confident. They surface answers before the question has fully formed. That speed creates a pull, and most leaders do not notice they are following it.

The question shifts. It moves from “*What am I responsible for deciding?*” to “*What does the data say?*” That may look like diligence

subject: Do Less.
body:
# Do Less.

[![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!BwTO!,w_1100,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F6e126038-9785-4859-85de-fb479374d298_1024x1024.png)](https://substack.com/redirect/7b24934b-4456-4a3b-b425-0d4e76b43a69?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ)

On my left ribs, I have a too-big tattoo of text from my favorite book, Cat’s Cradle by Kurt Vonnegut: “busy, busy, busy.” In the book, the quote continues: “... is what … we whisper whenever we think of how complicated and unpredictable the machinery of life really is.” The lesson is: Don’t be so sure you know how any of this works.

At the auspicious age of 42, life keeps surprising me by revealing that my most basic beliefs are wrong. Like: *distance = rate x time*. It turns out that more time *doing* does [not necessarily lead to better results](https://substack.com/redirect/370f8357-c3da-42c9-a71d-4e74b854f046?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ).

I’ve slowly gotten better at recognizing this faulty logic in certain domains, but the pattern repeats across time scales and activities. More isn’t more. More is actually less.

When I went on sabbatical toward the end of last year, I was excited by the prospect of finally getting time to “work on myself.” Writing a lot alongside an intense job had left little time for anything else in 2025, and as a result I had a sense that I was failing to progress in some critical dimension. At long last, I would have the chance to catch up to the person I wanted to be!

I’d been running a longform reading debt all year, so I set about attacking it. Audiobooks on 2x speed. Two books a week. Podcasts crammed into the gaps. I downloaded one of those speed-reading apps that shows you a blur of individual words to plow through my Substack backlog.

It sort of worked, in the sense that the pile got shorter, and the scratchy strain of looking at certain folders on my computer diminished. But behind it I had a nagging sense that I wasn’t actually *getting* anywhere. There are always more books. The list refills twice as fast as I can empty it. And I wasn’t absorbing a whole lot of what I was reading — I’d finish a book and, a week later, struggle to articulate what it was about beyond a sentence or two. I was processing so many words per week — how could it be that I was hardly learning anything at all?

Slowly, I realized I was working with the wrong mental metaphor. I’d been treating my brain like a hard drive: Transfer the file, and it’s there. But that’s not how it works at all, not even close. Learning is more like digestion. You don’t absorb more nutrition by eating faster. Past a certain rate, you just stop digesting, and the food you’re cramming in isn’t feeding you, it’s just passing through. The real nutritive work — the part that actually makes you stronger — happens after you stop eating, over hours, invisibly. And you can’t speed it up by eating more.

Ideas work the same way. They have to be broken down, recombined with things you already know, connected to something you’ve experienced. That process runs on downtime — walks, showers, sleep, staring out windows. Cramming more in doesn’t help. It’s eating another meal before you’ve digested the last one.

I think I can count on two hands the number of important ideas I’ve discovered via podcasts, spread across hundreds of hours of listening. The ROI is terrible. Meanwhile, when I’m short on ideas for posts, the thing that always works is a hot yoga class. Ninety minutes in a room with no phone. I can’t *stop* myself from having ideas in that environment, and not being able to write them down means I’m automatically selecting for the two or three good enough to remember afterward. The rest evaporate, which is fine — distance gives you perspective on which ideas are worth keeping.

The bottleneck, it turns out, was never how fast I could t

More soon,

# The Org Chart Math Behind AI-Native Speed

Tomasz Tunguz

Venture Capitalist at [Theory Ventures](https://6a50e11d.click.kit-mail3.com/92uem3eq2kunh6w2xdzt9hzd7wkg3bwh972mn/9qhzhnhd08kk9dt9/aHR0cHM6Ly90aGVvcnkudmVudHVyZXM=)

> “Since last November, 100% of my code has been written by Claude Code. I have not manually edited a single line, shipping 10 to 30 PRs per day.”

Boris Cherny, creator of Claude Code, ships 20-30 pull requests per day. Major code changes, not typo fixes. He runs five parallel AI instances, each on a separate branch.[1](#fn:1)

Compare that to a traditional engineer : 3 PRs per week.[2](#fn:2) Cherny isn’t 10% more productive. He’s 30x more productive.

That productivity gap compounds at the company level. Anthropic generates ~$5 million per employee.[3](#fn:3) Cursor, $3.3 million. Midjourney, $2 million.[4](#fn:4) Traditional SaaS considers $200-300k strong. A 10-20x difference.

One explanation : communication overhead. The math follows Metcalfe’s Law.[5](#fn:5) Each new team member adds n-1 new connections. Coordination drag doesn’t grow linearly. It explodes.

Now consider what AI does to this equation.

A traditional 150-person organization runs four layers deep. The org chart creates 11,175 potential communication channels. Meetings multiply. Alignment decays.

An AI-enabled team producing equivalent output might need 30 people. Communication channels drop to 435. A 96% reduction.

[![Communication channels in 150-person org vs 30-person AI-enabled org](https://res.cloudinary.com/dzawgnnlr/image/upload/w_1512,h_1054,c_fill,g_auto,q_auto,f_auto/s0pmjkgfnwo7ktgkvknh)](https://6a50e11d.click.kit-mail3.com/92uem3eq2kunh6w2xdzt9hzd7wkg3bwh972mn/p8heh9h4mekk83bq/aHR0cHM6Ly9yZXMuY2xvdWRpbmFyeS5jb20vZHphd2dubmxyL2ltYWdlL3VwbG9hZC9xX2F1dG8sZl9hdXRvL3MwcG1qa2dmbndvN2t0Z2t2a25o)

This is one reason AI-native startups are pulling ahead, and why building AI companies feels fun. The advantage comes from organizational structure. Fewer humans, fewer channels, faster iteration, compounding speed.[6](#fn:6)

R&D adopts this fastest. AI writes the code. Human communication becomes the bottleneck. The span of control debate shifts from “how many people can one manager oversee?” to “[how many AI agents can one human orchestrate?](https://6a50e11d.click.kit-mail3.com/92uem3eq2kunh6w2xdzt9hzd7wkg3bwh972mn/6qheh8hlz4vv0wfo/aHR0cHM6Ly90b210dW5ndXouY29tL2hvdy1tYW55LWFnZW50cy1jYW4teW91LW1hbmFnZS8=)”

Small teams have always paid less coordination tax. AI cuts it further.

---

1. Cherny, Boris. [Claude Code creator landed 259 PRs in 30 days](https://6a50e11d.click.kit-mail3.com/92uem3eq2kunh6w2xdzt9hzd7wkg3bwh972mn/kkhmh6hnrpgg42al/aHR0cHM6Ly9uZXdzLnljb21iaW5hdG9yLmNvbS9pdGVtP2lkPTQ2NDA3OTY3), Hacker News, 2025. [↩︎](#fnref:1)
2. Seporaitis, Julius. [What Can 75,000 Pull Requests Tell?](https://6a50e11d.click.kit-mail3.com/92uem3eq2kunh6w2xdzt9hzd7wkg3bwh972mn/3ohphkh30866v4ur/aHR0cHM6Ly93d3cuc2Vwb3JhaXRpcy5uZXQvcG9zdHMvMjAyMS8wNy8xOS93aGF0LWNhbi03NTAwMC1wdWxsLXJlcXVlc3RzLXRlbGwv), 2021. Estimated from [Anthropic’s ~$20B revenue run rate](https://6a50e11d.click.kit-mail3.com/92uem3eq2kunh6w2xdzt9hzd7wkg3bwh972mn/8ghqhohoz8eeknak/aHR0cHM6Ly93d3cuYmxvb21iZXJnLmNvbS9uZXdzL2FydGljbGVzLzIwMjYtMDMtMDMvYW50aHJvcGljLW5lYXJzLTIwLWJpbGxpb24tcmV2ZW51ZS1ydW4tcmF0ZS1hbWlkLXBlbnRhZ29uLWZldWQ=) (Bloomberg, March 2026) divided by ~4,300 employees (LinkedIn). [↩︎](#fnref:3)

# Smart tech is making war a dumber choice

[![The Economist](https://image.e.economist.com/lib/fe8d13727c650c7976/m/1/d2979654-fae4-451b-bdca-c79bb5522f6b.png;)](https://click.e.economist.com/u/?qs=ABB7InYiOjEsImQiOjQ4OTB9AAcAAAAAAfyUn7rFE9nmi3o3o2wRGTCoeiK6yxv_eZpIf4SUlVL7Ls4C_EbSCuA6urdgyfuN-FblfvQ4RUt7JKlnISfFNcEDaqbtEMQHbT2McT28urFb3Q)

May 28th 2026

![Highlights from the latest issue](https://image.e.economist.com/lib/fe8d13727c650c7976/m/1/1bd2eba9-7c72-4142-ba9c-3c1bffdeefe6.png)

Highlights from the latest issue

[![desktop](https://pas.economist.com/view/2/56924/9f13522fa690c061086a3872c30323fa/2190611?ad_region=Latin America&ad_country=Belize&send_date=28/05/2026&segment=4-BZ)](https://click.e.economist.com/u/?qs=ABB7InYiOjEsImQiOjQ4OTB9AAcAAAAAAfyUn7rGCduOGL9pfJKQu5daZjmTIu3I_yEQb0Ytf7jk0C3Jl1XDzGJk-z5rLoSgzA_8T9vHFsIAPfRWIeuS6x72XxtbRBDQ5Uub9tHKaAIH3w) [![](https://image.e.economist.com/lib/fe8d13727c650c7976/m/1/6fd080a2-d6e9-4dce-98f1-0f50c2ad84fb.png)](https://click.e.economist.com/?qs=ABB7InYiOjEsImQiOjQ4OTB9AAcAAAAAAfyUn7rIDn9WObAw4N-rUpi6QN-4-Xel9PITLSJz-uS-za-WR2T-mmBzy9RLmG00FosiVInSEeEcnTNp2amH-AsDvaMXfRK8zRCXk53R "") ![](https://image.e.economist.com/lib/fe8d13727c650c7976/m/1/8ae94367-2bde-424d-b6c2-36d6b9fe77f1.jpg)

Robert Guest

*Deputy editor*

One afternoon nearly 30 years ago, I stood on a hilltop watching a city burn. It was the day after South Africa had sent troops into its neighbour, Lesotho, to “restore order” after an army mutiny. It was supposed to be easy. South Africa is the big regional power. Lesotho is tiny. The distance from the border to the centre of Lesotho’s capital, Maseru, is only a few hundred metres. Yet somehow the South Africans messed it up, unleashing utter mayhem that ended with scores dead and mobs burning shops and factories to the ground.  

This forgotten calamity illustrates two truths about war. First, the leaders who order troops into battle are rarely as smart as they think they are. They overestimate their own strength; they fail to understand the other side. Second, when people see foreign forces marching into their country, they tend to respond ferociously. Both are reasons to be wary of starting wars of choice. This week’s cover story adds a third.  

[An essay](https://click.e.economist.com/?qs=ABB7InYiOjEsImQiOjQ4OTB9AAcAAAAAAfyUn7rJJVusLnlndV2qoJg9LZejGRxZ9ADXqnyYs1T7UjVFrl3CI9uZ7-6qt7trMEQbooznoABRaoTtQfm-ktIV6ucewEZ_zLUdyEes "An essay") by our outgoing defence editor, Shashank Joshi, describes how technology has made it cheaper and easier for weaker powers to resist stronger ones. Think of the swarms of Ukrainian drones that [obliterate Russian invaders](https://click.e.economist.com/?qs=ABB7InYiOjEsImQiOjQ4OTB9AAcAAAAAAfyUn7rKa-Zu8SDAP5npiK93xvn7LfdNA8PUB0P4Ga_PlI0dUBJ4l6FSJhcRDswM1EdtC0NQE6Qn-jYQz8bxKHzNXFjOP1_lMe26OLFt "obliterate Russian invaders") every time they try to advance. Or the low-cost Iranian munitions that have closed the Strait of Hormuz, hobbled the global economy and humiliated an American president. [In a leader](https://click.e.economist.com/?qs=ABB7InYiOjEsImQiOjQ4OTB9AAcAAAAAAfyUn7rLAkBRvUXESm4aI7nIyLajLvmkEbEArlTK7_yk19dFeAV9nN5vsoutHXuKWRa73meCifTPY6WSvEqX0zUCy9rJGID3PX5xCjMf "In a leader"),
 Shashank explains how these and other developments have changed the calculus of war. Attacking another country was always a gamble. As technology gets smarter, the odds for aggressors have got worse: wars of choice are more likely to end in ignominious failure. Xi Jinping might do well to read Shashank’s essay.  

This week’s edition of The Insider will dig deeper into all of this. Shashank will be joined by Adam Roberts, our foreign editor, and a panel of our correspondents. Subscribers can [watch the episode now](https://click.e.economist.com/?qs=ABB7InYiOjEsImQiOjQ4OTB9AAcAAAAAAfyUn7rMZH7f6deZeZBUCyV6itkEeKuy7Dh2zIAAIKpMNXMp2Dh8YLTD7anSwvUh9fbN4UMx2cmc_cZtgmBLHlkrzbYG41nMQtf9xOjo "watch the episode now").

IT'S 2026! ==> People always ask me for what I read and where I get my info. Lucky for you I've quietly started a newsletter for everything startups -- get on it here ===> https://www.GreatStartups.com/newsletter/?utm_source=ghi&utm_medium=nl&utm_campaign=gs

Grasshopper's conversions increased when they published their entrepreneur story on the homepage.

After 12 years [Grasshopper](http://www.grasshopper.com/) had **$30M+ in revenue**, over 150,000 customers and was bought by [Citrix](http://grasshopper.com/citrix-acquires-grasshopper/).  

David, CEO of Grasshopper, shared one of his most memorable growth hacking tricks.  

One of the guys that was doing A/B testing for them offered to put founder’s photos on the homepage and tell the **entrepreneur story**, how they started, why, struggles, etc."  

They did it and, all of a sudden, conversions increased.  

![](http://e.growthhackingidea.com/files/e.growthhackingidea.com/general/avatar.png)Cheers,  
Charlie Patel ;)

subject: What Would AI Email Cost?
body:
# What Would AI Email Cost?

Tomasz Tunguz

Venture Capitalist at [Theory Ventures](https://6a50e11d.click.kit-mail3.com/v8uxq0x97durhv7ln08sghvkvvr98s9hkvrz0/08hwh9h2r83gmecl/aHR0cHM6Ly90aGVvcnkudmVudHVyZXM=)

In yesterday’s post (which an agent pushed in raw outline form via email!), I wrote about the future of AI email. What does that future cost?

[![chart_monthly_cost_by_model](https://res.cloudinary.com/dzawgnnlr/image/upload/w_1512,h_850,c_fill,g_auto,q_auto,f_auto/dit9l3qsdydgiuitwqud)](https://6a50e11d.click.kit-mail3.com/v8uxq0x97durhv7ln08sghvkvvr98s9hkvrz0/l2hehmhl7g86omh6/aHR0cHM6Ly9yZXMuY2xvdWRpbmFyeS5jb20vZHphd2dubmxyL2ltYWdlL3VwbG9hZC9xX2F1dG8sZl9hdXRvL2RpdDlsM3FzZHlkZ2l1aXR3cXVk)

If you are using state-of-the-art model ranging, it costs between $22 to $130 per month. Would you pay for that? At work, I imagine, many would. Let’s take the middle case of $26/month raw cost.

A software company seeking 75% gross margin would charge about $350 per year for that product excluding hosting & serving costs. So let’s call it a $500 per year list with a 15% discount at scale.

A Google Enterprise plan is $11-18/month. A fully agentic solution would then cost about twice as much.

[![chart_all_models_comparison](https://res.cloudinary.com/dzawgnnlr/image/upload/w_1512,h_850,c_fill,g_auto,q_auto,f_auto/jzub0jaabu34dj6lh6ci)](https://6a50e11d.click.kit-mail3.com/v8uxq0x97durhv7ln08sghvkvvr98s9hkvrz0/m2h7h5h3zrdmodam/aHR0cHM6Ly9yZXMuY2xvdWRpbmFyeS5jb20vZHphd2dubmxyL2ltYWdlL3VwbG9hZC9xX2F1dG8sZl9hdXRvL2p6dWIwamFhYnUzNGRqNmxoNmNp)

Smaller models help. They cut cost by 10 to 20x, but we can do better.

By running the models locally, when the cost plummets to zero : users’ GPU does the work.

It’s this type of cost optimization that I have done crudely here that I think will define the next 12 to 24 months of AI software : determining which components can be executed deterministically, like the email filters, which are just rules. And the next is matching the model to the workload.

With some basic heuristics and techniques we can drop the overall cost by 100x. Given the tremendous shortage of GPUs, this [segmentation of inference is inevitable.](https://6a50e11d.click.kit-mail3.com/v8uxq0x97durhv7ln08sghvkvvr98s9hkvrz0/7qh7h8h95grw0etz/aHR0cHM6Ly90b210dW5ndXouY29tL2luZmVyZW5jZS1tYXJrZXQtc2VnbWVudGF0aW9uLw==)

subject: Fusion's DeepSeek Moment?
body:
# Fusion's DeepSeek Moment?

*[Caleb Harding](https://substack.com/redirect/b2972d56-bd24-47cc-b359-9adcd0f6fa82?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ) is a Mandarin-speaking BYU CS graduate. He previously interned at the US Embassy in Jakarta and Doublethink Lab in Taiwan. He is currently based in D.C.*

When you think of the biggest technologies of today, the most promising fields for the future, what comes to mind? If your first two thoughts were AI and quantum tech, congratulations — the Chinese Communist Party agrees with you. But what they listed third on the list of “Cutting-edge S&T breakthrough efforts” (前沿科技攻关) in their 15th Five-Year Plan might surprise you: nuclear fusion.

The detailed table entry for nuclear fusion indicates that the CCP is paying close attention to nuclear fusion and is invested in its success. Their goals for the next five years are described as follows:

> “Achieve breakthroughs in key fusion technologies including tritium fuel preparation and recycling, materials irradiation testing, high-performance lasers, and superconducting magnet manufacturing; conduct plasma operation experiments on deuterium-tritium fusion and feasibility verification across multiple technical approaches; advance the engineering development process for nuclear fusion R&D.”

Who will execute on this? A whole network of researchers, national labs, and SOEs is driving ahead on the necessary research and manufacturing developments. But China’s most promising assets may lie outside of that system: a handful of startups that are iterating aggressively to take fusion commercial.

Yang Zhao 杨钊 is the CEO and cofounder of China-based Energy Singularity (能量奇点), one of the key players in this space. After graduating with a PhD in theoretical physics¹ from Stanford in 2017, Yang spent a year drifting before deciding on his mission in life: to accelerate the timeline for commercial fusion.

After getting a grasp of start-up operations at an AI education firm, Yang Zhao and three other friends² founded Energy Singularity in Shanghai in 2021. Their approach is similar to that taken by Commonwealth Fusion Systems (CFS), one of the most well-known US companies in the US. With a new kind of more powerful magnet, both companies intend to make fusion viable by shrinking the scale of reactors and, by extension, their cost.

[![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!exns!,w_1100,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F226a75f2-653a-4b0e-9983-406c523c71bc_1080x533.png)](https://substack.com/redirect/2e935ff1-07db-41cf-ad67-90618281afa0?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ)

Yang Zhao, CEO and cofounder of Energy Singularity. [Source](https://substack.com/redirect/e38e8708-3627-460a-b42f-ce7701ceb9cd?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ)

Energy Singularity has had some significant breakthroughs since then. Last year, they achieved first plasma on Honghuang 70 (HH-70, 洪荒70), the world’s first functioning high-temperature superconducting (HTS) tokamak. Design and construction of that experimental reactor was completed in just two years, at record speed. This year, they created a magnet capable of producing a magnetic field of 21.7 teslas, passing CFS’s previous record of 20 teslas.

CFS may yet beat them to the punch. Energy Singularity built HH70 as a proof-of-concept device for HTS tokamaks — an impressive feat. But it doesn’t achieve a Q value greater than 1. The Q-value is a ratio of energy output to input; Q = 1 is break-even, and achieving Q >= 10 is considered the key milestone to prove the commercial viability of fusion. With significant funding and a few years’ head start, CFS is skipping the proof-of-concept device and already working on their Q >= 10 device, SPARC.

First plasma (systems operational) for SPARC is expected in 2026, with net energy production aimed for 202

# Use your Exoskeleton

[![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!GUaU!,w_1100,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F5b4f9bea-e256-4541-b8f4-6a8826619915_2092x1625.png)](https://substack.com/redirect/b0d447d7-0819-48f3-a2c6-63508b3c6374?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ)

AI speeds up the game. It doesn’t remove the product decisions needed.

*Hi, I’m Greg 👋! I write weekly product [essays](https://substack.com/redirect/06846501-391c-4d59-b058-a6cdac1fb4c3?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ), including system “handshakes”, the expectations for workflow, and the jobs to be done for data. [What is Data Operations?](https://substack.com/redirect/39970754-84c2-4642-b454-1daa10251d72?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ) was the first post in the series.*

This week’s toy: a [new emoji for anyone who likes a fisheye face](https://substack.com/redirect/52d30d91-7128-4830-8862-34fce0747029?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ).

[![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!s1Sk!,w_109,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F698200e2-c92b-47e8-a293-c700b157b8a4_443x405.png)](https://substack.com/redirect/0b92f332-3f97-4249-aff9-e5b61d4a7a17?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ)

Emoji seem like a small thing, but the ones that stick make it to the keyboard of every mobile phone in the world, so the process is pretty interesting in itself. Too-strong zoom on a selfie must be a universally understood image now.

Edition 295 of this newsletter is here - it’s March 9, 2026.

---

Thanks for reading! Let me know if there’s a topic you’d like me to cover.

---

## **The Big Idea**

*A short long-form essay about data things*

### ⚙️ Use your Exoskeleton

[![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!GUaU!,w_1100,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F5b4f9bea-e256-4541-b8f4-6a8826619915_2092x1625.png)](https://substack.com/redirect/b0d447d7-0819-48f3-a2c6-63508b3c6374?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ)

When I was a kid, I wanted laser eyes.

Not metaphorical laser eyes. Actual comic-book-origin-story laser eyes. I read too much X-Men, saw Scott Summers vaporize a problem, and thought: yes, that seems useful.

That same feeling is the closest description I have for what using AI well feels like right now. You can summarize a market in minutes. You can turn a rough product idea into a working prototype by lunch. You can ask a model questions that used to require interrupting an engineer, a designer, or a data person.

The power is real. The confusion is real too.

The mistake is thinking the new superpower is execution. It is not. The real shift is that execution got cheap enough that judgment became the bottleneck.

### The bottleneck moved

Three years ago, I was building API calls into spreadsheets and thought I was discovering fire.

If I had an idea in 2022, one of the first questions was usually: who do I need to ask to make this real?

Now, if I have an idea that needs a scratch implementation, I can ask Claude, Cursor, or another coding agent to produce the first pass. I can get a UI, some glue code, a rough data model, and basic tests without opening the old queue of favors and dependencies.

That sounds like pure upside, and for a while, it feels like it. Then you live with it for a few weeks and realize you can generate more surface area than you can evaluate.

More screens. More branches. More speculative workflows. More “pretty close” solutions that still hide bad assumptions.

AI did not remove the need for product thinking. It increased the penalty for weak product thinking.

When output is expensive, bad ideas die e

subject: The Vertical SaaS Org of the Future (And Why Yours Isn’t It) (Yet)
body:
# The Vertical SaaS Org of the Future (And Why Yours Isn’t It) (Yet)

[![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!2Dy_!,w_1100,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fc7709b7c-a697-475a-aeb0-dd30e0b897c0_1536x1024.png)](https://substack.com/redirect/b57e67c8-890f-4a2c-8b99-b6bd7a396f83?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ)

It’s not looking good, folks.

Organic search traffic is [declining.](https://substack.com/redirect/d5e50831-1cb0-4286-8c59-f049bd91b12e?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ)

Cost per click is [rising](https://substack.com/redirect/ef555d7b-a347-4f40-b6ef-e2581ff0e2d5?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ) while conversions are in free fall.

Your Google Search, LinkedIn Ads, and Meta CPAs are creeping up there. And don’t even ask about the CAC.

But those are just symptoms. The actual change lies in *how* buyers research and decide, and *where* that research is happening.

## The Buyer’s Journey Was Always a Lie

Doug’s [Zombie CMO hit piece](https://substack.com/redirect/ee44403d-95e0-47d9-818e-4881a81ce3b3?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ) from a few weeks back pointed us in this direction. Your entire go-to-market function was designed around a buyer journey that pretty much no longer exists (if it ever did). And if you’re a vertical SaaS company, you’ve had the luxury of not feeling the full pain of this yet, because your unit economics used to be good enough to hide it.

## How We Got Here: The Collapse of the Blue Links

In the olden times, buyers would begin their journey with a web search. A list of blue links, and they’d start clicking, researching their purchasing decisions, and hopefully, they’d make it to your site (or you bought an ad at the top to encourage that).

Then in 2024, [Google debuted AI Overviews](https://substack.com/redirect/2bf08ce0-c55b-4f8c-b471-c9ebecacbbae?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ) in search results. Now, buyers didn’t have a list of links to sort through to get an answer. Google’s AI Overview just gave them *the answer*. That’s why [organic click-through rates have dropped by 61%](https://substack.com/redirect/0a8b77b2-dcbf-4939-aada-03e3d2cb4469?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ), and paid click-through rates by 68%. Some sites have seen a [97% percent decline in traffic.](https://substack.com/redirect/80faaa5c-3a31-4885-b68e-3a3f1a1345ca?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ)

But that’s only half the story.

As AI mows through everything in its path, buyers are turning away from search engines and toward ChatGPT, Claude, and Google Gemini for research. (Shut up, Grok, nobody asked you.) Keep in mind, these chat-based tools are optimized to keep people *in the chat*, which means two things are happening simultaneously:

1. Any GenAI system reflects your prospect’s existing biases back at you.
2. It surfaces what’s publicly known about a brand (reviews, coverage, community sentiment), which means your brand reputation, or lack of one, is part of the answer your prospect gets.

Your targeted buyer is in ChatGPT, essentially pre-validating vendor choices.

So, the assembly-line org you built to serve the old buyer journey, Product Marketing to MarComm to Content to Digital to SDRs, each team handing off to the next, is optimized for a world that no longer exists. It was always 1920s production-line thinking applied to an emotional, nonlinear buying process. AI just made that undeniable. The Black Belts can’t save us now.

**Quick gut check:** Go ask your GenAI of choice to rank the top five vendors in your category. It’ll rank based on a combination of the data it can access and the brand’s reputation. That’s the new search result. That’s what your buyers are seeing.

Congrats to [Pete Steinberger on joining OpenAI](https://substack.com/redirect/13aae0fb-9c8a-489a-8f02-18fcf82c766e?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ), as we [predicted](https://substack.com/redirect/a499c34b-2dd1-443a-a523-de09a8c6d970?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ). Not much else to add there so we won’t.

Today’s headliner is Qwen 3.5, which followed the other Chinese model labs like [Z.ai](https://substack.com/redirect/6b05904b-6157-4b90-8a24-f2521e16a771?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ) and [Minimax](https://substack.com/redirect/fb93518f-01c5-4e27-b6f2-f035d5f23c93?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ) and [Kimi](https://substack.com/redirect/76685c6a-8ac9-44d0-964a-aaee763047a3?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ) in refreshing their leading models, but unlike the first two, Qwen 3.5 is in the same weight class as Kimi, 400B with about a 4.3% sparsity ratio instead of Kimi’s more agressive 3.25%. They do not claim SOTA across the board, and most notably not across coding benchmarks, but make solid improvements compared to [Qwen3-Max](https://substack.com/redirect/8d553ef4-08a7-4fda-b0aa-ed191e3387e3?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ) and [Qwen3-VL](https://substack.com/redirect/1c8f6267-3520-411d-8da1-840c9a0eb5b7?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ).

Native Multimodality and [Spatial Intelligence](https://substack.com/redirect/2113e524-ff77-4e1e-9491-91647ef10eff?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ) are headline features of the model and we encourage clicking over to the blog to check out the examples, as there isn’t much else to say - this is a very welcome headline model refresh from China’s most prolific open model lab, and probably the last before DeepSeek v4.

subject: The Great AI Power Shortage
body:
# The Great AI Power Shortage

Compute-hours are not governed by a single supply curve. They are the output of a tightly constrained system with many interdependent variables. We analyzed public commentary from leading AI operators and hyperscalers and mapped the bottlenecks they consistently cite across the stack.

[![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!PK5x!,w_432,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Ffc08cd77-7ef3-492f-af09-85b483658a74_432x700.png)](https://substack.com/redirect/d4b31636-475e-44a8-94d1-7dc03ad0e0d5?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ)

These constraints arise from a tightly coupled stack:

[![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!sREe!,w_349,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F0de31da9-2ab1-4c0a-bad9-ba6d64fc7330_349x274.png)](https://substack.com/redirect/bef9e754-409d-4a3b-9213-596306b978e6?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ)

Each layer has independent lead times and independent bottlenecks. When constraints stack, supply elasticity collapses. Even if GPU output doubles, effective compute-hours can remain scarce.

And that scarcity is not evenly distributed.

---

## **The Fiber Analogy Is Incomplete**

There are clear parallels to the late-1990s fiber buildout:

* ~$500B in telecom infrastructure investment
* 39 million miles of fiber laid
* <5% utilization at the 2001 peak
* A decade to absorb excess capacity

But there are two critical differences:

1. Fiber could sit idle cheaply.
2. The AI buildout is funded by hyperscaler balance sheets, not junk debt.

[![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!FFXO!,w_468,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F404ac768-5e13-4df2-b631-c3f24dad882c_468x211.png)](https://substack.com/redirect/86aba526-30ad-4831-a95b-2222da060464?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ)

**Source**: [Coatue chart of the day](https://substack.com/redirect/ea59c969-fa7b-4753-8058-85126baa2dd3?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ)

Fiber could sit idle at near-zero marginal cost.

AI infrastructure burns cash every day it sits unused.

* Power contracts
* Cooling costs
* Staffing
* Depreciating GPUs

Compute depreciates in ~5-8 years. Fiber depreciated over decades.

Which brings us to the most important constraint in the stack:

---

## **Power is the binding constraint in AI**

[![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!8YO5!,w_1100,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Ff4987ed9-a75a-421f-9784-d5c557ea768c_1206x928.png)](https://substack.com/redirect/5991717b-d79f-479e-84bd-056c89d8d673?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ)

Unlike GPUs:

* Power is location-bound.
* Interconnection queues take years.
* Transmission upgrades take longer.
* Generation requires long-term offtake.
* Permitting is political and regional.

You cannot spin up gigawatts the way you spin up GPU clusters. A GPU order cycle is measured in quarters. A transmission upgrade is measured in years.

In many U.S. regions, **power availability is already the binding constraint on new AI campuses**. Each major data center operator is rushing to lock up as much cheap power as they can.

[![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!hrOI!,w_352,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fe14438e7-0fd1-4191-965b-61ddfed505ae_352x262.png)](https://substack.com/redirect/47260fcf-6167-4e85-acbd-b20fbe167c3d?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ)

**Source**: Public estimates

From pioneering software-defined networking to backing many of the most aggressive AI model companies of this cycle, **Martin Casado** and **Sarah Wang** sit at the center of the capital, compute, and talent arms race reshaping the tech industry. As partners at a16z investing across infrastructure and growth, they’ve watched venture and growth blur, **model labs** turn dollars into capability at unprecedented speed, and startups raise nine-figure rounds before monetization.  
  
Martin and Sarah join us to unpack the **new financing playbook for AI**: why today’s rounds are really compute contracts in disguise, how the **“raise → train → ship → raise bigger” flywheel** works, and whether foundation model companies can outspend the entire app ecosystem built on top of them. #### About Our Contributing Expert

### John Hughes | Director, Data & AI, Public Sector

[![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!VjVJ!,w_1100,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Ff86b646a-8271-43f5-9ed0-dfbb89f3c46c_1600x900.png)](https://substack.com/redirect/a179120b-9137-4150-8545-f1367a9f483f?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ)

[John Hughes](https://substack.com/redirect/5c90bf31-23a4-489e-b534-485979afbba9?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ) is a **Director of Data & AI for Public Sector at KPMG US** and an AI and data analytics transformation leader focused on public sector and financial services modernization. John has over 15 years of experience spanning public sector institutions, international governments, and financial services.

Prior to this, John built his foundation in financial crime, regulatory technology, and analytics through roles at **Bloomberg LP** and **Société Générale Corporate and Investment Banking**, where he worked on KYC/AML data platforms, entity resolution, and financial planning & analysis transformation. He played a key role in developing AI-enabled regulatory solutions, improving transparency, and supporting global compliance initiatives in high-stakes banking environments. His early career also includes experience with **UK Trade & Investment**, where he worked at the intersection of international policy, regulatory risk, and cross-border investment.

At KPMG, John has led AI Centers of Excellence, driven large-scale KYC/AML and financial transformation programs, and delivered data modernization initiatives for state and local governments. Known for translating complex regulatory and operational challenges into scalable AI, analytics, and governance frameworks, he focuses on building intelligent systems that enhance decision-making while maintaining strong human oversight in mission-critical environments.

\**The thoughts and opinions expressed by John Hughes are his own and do not represent the views, positions, or official thought leadership of any current or former employer, client, or affiliated organization.*

> *We actively collaborate with data experts to bring the best resources to a [20,000+ strong community](https://substack.com/redirect/bc5c31f5-7d0c-4285-aed9-8574820b5d2b?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ) of data leaders and practitioners. ### Let’s Dive In

Throughout my career in international affairs, finance, and public sector managed services consulting, I have always found ways to apply data analytics, automation, and now AI to improve processes for my team and clients.

In the 2010s, applications of data science and automation were heralded as Herculean achievements, with one senior manager from a prior fintech company even stressing that we could “*grow [our] careers by automating [our] jobs.*”

subject: Compatibility and Fragmentation in the AI Era
body:
# Compatibility and Fragmentation in the AI Era

If you go far back enough in time, every new computer design had a new instruction set.

Which, of course, was a pain!

[![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!IpyB!,w_1100,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F02b7d6be-d42d-4393-9ccc-ab5352e6c813_800x1067.jpeg)](https://substack.com/redirect/49bf906f-4edd-44be-b846-d675f049d923?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ)

IBM 709 Front Panel - By ArnoldReinhold - Own work, CC BY-SA 3.0, https://commons.wikimedia.org/w/index.php?curid=18267293

When IBM introduced the 709 mainframe in 1958 as the successor to the popular (with a grand total of 123 systems sold in total!) 704 the new computer’s architecture was incompatible with its predecessor. Fortunately, by then high level languages - and FORTRAN created by John Backus in 1957 in particular - were available to enable software to run on machines with multiple architectures. For example, CERN was one important 709 installation that [adopted](https://substack.com/redirect/b607ec9b-055c-4f4a-83c7-c218488a8940?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ) FORTRAN early:

> With *Mercury* [a computer from the UK’s Ferranti] and the 709 operating together, CERN had its first experience of compatibility problems. This was a continuing source of difficulty as various different computers came into operation at CERN. Many of CERN’s programs were also used on a range of computers in its 13 member states.
>
> A high-level computer-programming language called “FORTRAN” (short for “FORmula TRANSlating”)that made its CERN debut with the 709, and this language quickly became the only programming language in general use at the laboratory. A new generation of programs, written in FORTRAN to exploit the greater speed of the IBM 709, were brought in to analyse measurements from bubble-chamber photographs.

IBM also provided an optional emulation system - the first of its kind - so that the 709 could run 704 machine code.

The 709 was laughably [simple and slow](https://substack.com/redirect/fc66e8f3-512d-4ec0-834f-55b0573d8816?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ) when compared to today’s machines:

> The 709 had 32,768 words of 36-bit magnetic-core memory and could execute 42,000 add or subtract instructions per second. It could multiply two 36-bit integers at a rate of 5000 per second.

There was a good reason for new computers having new architectures: the technology was advancing so quickly that it made sense to abandon old designs in order to cast off their limitations.

High level languages like FORTRAN helped deal with this architectural ‘tower of Babel’. Soon, though, the number of languages (and different implementations of those languages) the [costs of supporting](https://substack.com/redirect/9d37b794-7c0d-42df-a4d2-57f93ef878eb?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ) those languages across architectures also grew:

> Every time a new architecture or high-level language was developed then a number of new or revised compilers were needed. For every new language, compilers for each architecture were needed and for a new architecture compilers for each language were necessary.
>
> This led to what became known as the **‘n \* m problem’**. With n architectures and m machines, n \* m compilers were needed to implement all the languages on all the architectures. Writing a new compiler was a significant undertaking.

> Users wanted a better approach.

# Is follower growth harder now?

[![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!UIaB!,w_1100,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F97396d83-7270-4164-b75e-4854c2171655_1268x684.jpeg)](https://substack.com/redirect/5ab50e1b-d0ea-453c-8253-5c93fec8d690?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ)

Early 2026, there’s still a big sentiment floating around that you can’t grow followers quickly anymore (especially on LinkedIn). That it’s become harder than it’s ever been.

And honestly, there’s some truth to that.

It does feel like the days of “post any educational carousel, go viral, gain thousands overnight” have largely gone. Between 2022 and 2024, you could publish a broadly useful infographic, hit the right trend at the right time, and wake up to a follower spike that felt unfair.

That can still happen, but it’s less common, and in a weird way, that’s a good thing.

Because when the platform rewards cheap virality, everyone chases cheap virality. Your feed fills up with the same recycled “10 tips” posts, and creators start optimising for hacks instead of trust.

But none of this means you shouldn’t want to grow.

Growing your audience still matters, because audience is leverage. It gives you options.

If you don’t want to do client work forever, an audience gives you a way out. If you want to change direction later, an audience makes that possible. If you want to educate at scale, build trust faster, and increase visibility without having to do everything manually, audience is how you do that.

So the question isn’t “can you grow?” It’s “what do you optimise for now?”

And in my experience, the answer is simple.

You optimise for **saves**.

---

## The growth metric most people ignore

A “save” is when someone bookmarks your post so they can come back to it later.

Almost every major platform has some version of this, and the reason it matters is because it tells the algorithm something very specific: *this content is valuable enough that someone doesn’t want to lose it.*

* Likes can mean “nice.”
* Comments can mean “I want to be seen.”
* Saves mean “I need this.”

If a platform sees that a post is being saved at an unusually high rate, that’s a strong signal that the content is creating a good user experience. That’s the kind of content platforms want to push into more feeds.

So if you want faster follower growth, you want to create content that makes people think:

“I’m going to need this later.”

That’s what drives saves.

---

## Why people save posts

People save things because they’re afraid they’ll lose them.

They save because the content feels practically useful, or because it contains an insight they want to revisit, or because it gives them something they can apply later. Sometimes they save it as inspiration, like I do when I’m collecting examples of good writing.

But the most common reason is education.

And not just “education” in the broad sense of sharing a thought.

I mean education that is structured in a way that is easy to use.

Over the years, from growing from 0 to 188,000 followers, the biggest follower spikes I’ve ever had almost always come from posts that are highly educational.

However, there’s an important nuance here: educational content alone isn’t enough.

Because anyone can post “educational content.”

What matters is the format.

---

## The 3 educational formats that consistently drive saves (and follower spikes)

[![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!0vaO!,w_1100,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fbe5de698-f42e-45a0-a04d-d58275d1d496_1268x684.jpeg)](https://substack.com/redirect/a5b4d373-d3fa-4496-9b72-1f8d2054f063?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ)

# An Applied Crop Genetics BBN

Today’s piece is a guest post by [Karen Sarkisyan](https://substack.com/redirect/9caf5cce-f067-4754-8a34-6df2bb8eb172?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ).¹ Karen is the founder of Syntato, an applied crop genetics BBN. BBNs pursue ambitious North Star technical visions with a mix of contracts and grants. As Karen puts it, Syntato’s North Star technical vision is “computer chip design and manufacturing — but for plants.”

Karen is the perfect founder to present the first example of a modern BBN in this series. Syntato has both an extremely ambitious technical goal *and* a great customer — one that has enabled the org to be a break-even operation from day one. Beyond those attributes, Karen is an exceptionally effective writer.

While Karen’s name may be new to readers, his work might be more familiar; Karen previously co-founded Light Bio. Light Bio inserts genes from fungi into petunias to make them glow *(see below)*. Syntato’s work builds on methods developed at Light Bio and ideas from Karen’s research group at London’s MRC Laboratory of Medical Sciences.

In today’s piece, Karen will paint a picture of where Syntato hopes to go. In reading it, I hope readers develop confidence that BBNs can swing big in the modern era while covering their own costs.

subject: Simple algos have intrinsic motivations — AI isn’t “just linear algebra"
body:
# Simple algos have intrinsic motivations — AI isn’t “just linear algebra"

Hello fellow humans! Sharing [the latest interview](https://substack.com/redirect/97201e64-f69b-4cc0-bc52-fedd5d883dfa?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ) I had with famous biologist and co-author of xenobots (computer-designed “living robots”), **Michael Levin, on AI consciousness**.

**Key moments:**

* Intelligent systems are not equal to consciousness. We can’t rule out consciousness in AI. Consciousness shouldn’t be attached to hardware (silicon vs. biological origin).
* Humanity might be on the path to Neanderthals (depending on how AI development progresses).
* The barrier to creating bioweapons has never been high. AI can make it easier, but the barrier was never high to begin with.
* Even very simple algorithms can show intrinsic motivations that resemble free will. We need tools to recognize them, suppress unwanted behaviors, and encourage the ones we want. We should stay humble and not dismiss AI as “just linear algebra,” because even simple deterministic code can have motivations we don’t fully understand.
* It’s a continuous process from the blob of chemicals of an unfertilized egg to forming a human mind — there is no magic lightning flash at which you were a bunch of chemicals and now you are a formed mind.
* Where is that fine line at which some creatures are considered to be sentient and others are not? It doesn’t exist, but the crazy thing is that we have to divide.
* The cognitive light cone captures the scale of goals humans can pursue and the largest things we can truly comprehend. It’s not just about intelligence — it also includes compassion. That combination is what makes us human.

**[Watch the full episode on my new YouTube channel on AI sentience](https://substack.com/redirect/97201e64-f69b-4cc0-bc52-fedd5d883dfa?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ)**

Check out previous talks by our guests on the [BuzzRobot YouTube channel](https://substack.com/redirect/4585bb4d-c96a-404c-8c4f-a56b2031b027?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ).  
  
[Join our Slack community](https://substack.com/redirect/0ba75245-1509-4bb9-9a5b-80aa500441fd?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ) to connect with fellow developers, AI engineers, researchers, and practitioners.  
  
[Join me on X](https://substack.com/redirect/5960837e-2428-4469-91a6-22471bc62ebf?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ).

## Developer marketing insights

### 1. How to get your engineers to blog (new podcast episode)

This time I had an awesome chat with [Ivan Brezak Brkan (IBB)](https://link.mail.beehiiv.com/v1/c/83g6t%2BM%2FpwvLiQn9Do%2F1h%2FdnU05Zsw4RQ0SJvwNbETNWVKXTNxwRqPqV%2BrrO%0AHn7MgAH7MbBXvcFGJSCaI7HW5QezSKCB71DWyPfY%2B4Qp5NhCZoe2h4vSJA39%0Abyu%2BeLsFp7QnopMRHUMGBPRMngZkaF3oInDamEtmTxawSiXQgnJ4eLzi0TxE%0ANhjrfthTOorD%0A/7f8729e36b4015f1) about building programs that get engineers to write at scale. He build that with [shiftmag.dev](https://link.mail.beehiiv.com/v1/c/7S9TyoG39QFB1ZnZRuwBq9yWmgCP5KfJ7IpZ%2BRY4RX77qMv%2BBp5lGtyCQlFx%0AzgOOu50SuZ8aiAc1Q2atoIK00ui5JmwCy9Q%2FUrvXCdWBpe8JRU2eSsP5He7h%0AzqEu9f6Dn0XPDU6OGYeGz4%2FAL28Oe0rWfXJXYSYfSrMGC8d1WmLc6cXQ0V0j%0AuAP%2FRxYyumGZ%0A/6b23b15b0ebb8e3c) at Infobip.

[[![YouTube video by developer markepear](https://i.ytimg.com/vi/h51qg7RL2y8/maxresdefault.jpg)](https://link.mail.beehiiv.com/v1/c/zL2Y9AyhogH%2Bh6J1%2BcTAhq14hldizsAiMBzos05tFe4uoQ5iB0IuSzPzjMFQ%0AWhA9QVtYOArOCqXYWBBRfjOeQD9K0hUGa0jI%2FPX46iyorYCF9RGju7YQ4FPp%0A%2FdV0TOdTYBBflbJnOYfWOLfkJv6uD1RpR%2FDaOlOKpmDXBFumK7MXBEULV3Qp%0AKkI1n4d%2BNQPE%0A/02a4dc6d95d29f3f)

#13 [Interview] How To Get Your Engineers To Blog (In 2026)](https://link.mail.beehiiv.com/v1/c/5ilwBcoF2hQvIcB1nawtwzD0vQj0BI%2FmFCjXsVEKiw1HGLMKwMrxJJpEI0FW%0A1FaB4lFlZbfsuNuo2gyilKRW%2F0yAQ0nvx57izjQeXPQxwwpgI7roWR2NkTpo%0A98S%2B0EGLAUhT7RkUQmcyTWr1Q6DY91MQ02UzUAO8g7juVc5ioQpBO16hmRAF%0AArAUG%2FAxiIC3%0A/cc20b47b4db0e771)

Takeaways/themes:

* **“Begging” + bonuses don’t get engineers to write:** Most engineers won’t write for money. They write when you give them **time + permission + support** (peer feedback + real editorial help).
* **Run writing like a sprint, not a side quest:** Timebox it. 2-day workshops produce ~80%

# The Efficiency Moat: Why China Is Beating the U.S. on AI… And Everything Else

Today, Donald Trump is in China negotiating with Xi Jinping, with the possibility of reordering the global economy. As with most of these kinds of summits, the symbolism and pomp is rich. Trump understands imagery, and he brought with him a group of CEOs. In this picture, where Trump is greeted by Chinese Vice President Han Zheng, you can see Elon Musk and Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang in the background.

[![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!WMlb!,w_1100,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F450d4c0e-b605-44d8-b91e-a4f9a12ce95c_985x647.png "")](https://substack.com/redirect/f149ae8c-bfb0-455a-9ed1-90a98d46c23b?j=eyJ1IjoiZnZlciJ9.8N73-dqQlrWLx3o5gPfyirClhk7-cxP_NqOwOQYAApk)

These men are both worth over $100 billion, and they project Trump’s view that dominant American firms represent the strength of the nation.

What has happened so far? Rush Doshi, a savvy China analyst, noted there were few promises here and there, but ultimately not very much has yet occurred.

[X avatar for @RushDoshi Rush Doshi @RushDoshi Day 1 of the Trump-Xi summit is over. Here are my key takeaways from the readouts, interviews, and the banquet. (1) New Chinese Formulation: Most interesting takeaway for me is that China is out with a new frame for the relationship: “I have agreed with President Trump on a 1:22 PM · May 14, 2026 · 56.5K Views 9 Replies · 105 Reposts · 277 Likes](https://substack.com/redirect/f6e78e35-9b62-44a0-a621-2c70e0411b14?j=eyJ1IjoiZnZlciJ9.8N73-dqQlrWLx3o5gPfyirClhk7-cxP_NqOwOQYAApk)

The reason for that is simple - Chinese leaders are happy with the status quo, and they don’t feel there’s any reason to change what they perceive as a winning hand against the U.S. And when I say winning, I mean something specific - they are in the process of monopolizing the industrial base and high tech industries of the entire world. Increasingly everyone depends on China for vital goods, while China systematically removes their need to import anything from anyone else. We saw this most obviously when China cut off rare earth magnets to the U.S. and the rest of the world last year, but the vulnerability exists across many sectors.

For a long time, I’ve been labeled a China “hawk” in D.C. parlance. Hawk is often seen as a proxy for war, and that conflation is intentional, because it confuses the left around the world. My concern is not about the need to mobilize for war, China is a nuclear power and there is simply no winning in any conflict. The concern is economic; there are certain important predatory practices that China is using to monopolize industrial production and technological development. I do not want to live in a world where China controls all commerce, because it means very bad things for everyone else.

There’s a lot that China does well, and I’m going to talk about that. But first I want to start with why China is a toxic actor in the global economy. If you look at consumer spending in a country, in most countries that share is between 55-65%. The U.S. is at 67% or so. Most of what we produce goes back to the people themselves. China is different; Chinese consumption rates are at [roughly 40% of GDP](https://substack.com/redirect/2f170548-e6ea-4b7e-8dec-f7f027cbd39a?j=eyJ1IjoiZnZlciJ9.8N73-dqQlrWLx3o5gPfyirClhk7-cxP_NqOwOQYAApk), with about that same amount going to investment. Those are insane levels.

[![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!8ih9!,w_1100,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F832e01e3-b424-43cd-b00b-99a5d6954895_1283x307.png)](https://substack.com/redirect/8a6bddaf-3480-4bda-bda2-a1dd20861fc3?j=eyJ1IjoiZnZlciJ9.8N73-dqQlrWLx3o5gPfyirClhk7-cxP_NqOwOQYAApk)

# The gentle obsolescence

[![Up In The Air](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!nqmO!,w_1100,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fb4632642-c304-4889-816c-78af5a1182a7_1296x730.jpeg "Up In The Air")](https://substack.com/redirect/30733c29-a3ae-4665-ac89-c254a9c676f8?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ)

When ChatGPT first came out, a smart thing you could say was that “ChatGPT is like an intern.” So, many people said this. [ChatGPT is your new intern.](https://substack.com/redirect/a8c39a65-c362-4ddc-8a70-69e05d15bc75?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ) It is a [well-read intern.](https://substack.com/redirect/db35bb7c-fe62-4db1-899b-9dd4c4885c01?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ) It [lacks common sense](https://substack.com/redirect/1a8128ee-485a-410f-9b26-74d3ea0a6459?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ). It is very smart, [but a little drunk](https://substack.com/redirect/ee50310f-072c-4e90-bf0d-382eaaab9423?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ). It [lies a little bit](https://substack.com/redirect/d7fec0b0-4113-41b5-99de-c628a786d8eb?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ). It can do practical tasks for you, but “in the end, [you are the one](https://substack.com/redirect/c432d484-ad62-438f-ab15-3d509edc07e3?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ) behind the steering wheel!”¹

Eventually, this became the rough conventional wisdom about AI. It became the sober take that every serious person was supposed to have. Yes, it is capable, but it hallucinates. Yes, it can do many things, but it also makes dumb mistakes.² It is best thought of as an eager undergrad; a junior developer; a *helpful assistant*, just as every system prompt tells it that it is.

And so, a lot of AI products adopted these same ambitions. They exist, it seems, to do our chores.³ What does OpenClaw,⁴ the [hottest AI project on the internet](https://substack.com/redirect/ecf8c6f8-270d-451e-a0c2-b4e082df2c29?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ), do? It “[clears your inbox](https://substack.com/redirect/7c05ad4d-2f4a-45cd-aa61-11256bb97238?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ), sends emails, manages your calendar, and checks you in for flights.” What is the “extremely bull case” for why it is a real breakthrough? That it can [remind you to respond to text messages](https://substack.com/redirect/bcbeb6a0-4d1a-435d-b15d-230449049f0f?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ), book reservations, maintain a grocery list, and fill out forms on the internet. AI has access to the entire internet and [we use it as an egg timer](https://substack.com/redirect/fa9f38b3-46a1-4796-ba72-161ad2de9556?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ).

Of course, we’ve started to stack a lot of interns and egg timers on top of each other. We create [teams of them](https://substack.com/redirect/b8796a25-35e3-4089-8375-326ea9c58c19?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ). We create a whole town for them, and [run it as their mayor](https://substack.com/redirect/04ac9771-7405-4543-b534-b7c558832d47?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ). We orchestrate them, and plan with them, in the now-ubiquitous [planning mode](https://substack.com/redirect/19855b70-d9a6-461d-a374-facc26c635da?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ). There are many of them, the AIs, but they are still our [minions](https://substack.com/redirect/c8616bf1-961f-4d61-b09f-fe363908721e?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ).

Except—what *is* planning mode, exactly?

# Linear #172.5: The Best Vertical AI Founders Will Build Systems Of Love W/ Alex Niehenke (Partner @ Scale)

---

There’s a specific kind of startup worth paying attention to right now: the one that goes straight at a category everyone else assumes is locked up.

Not glamorous markets. Not greenfield software. Markets with incumbents. Markets with procurement. Markets with ancient systems of record. Markets where customers have been overpaying for mediocre software for years.

[![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!wBhM!,w_1100,h_618,c_fill,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/l_play_button_usfui2,w_144,e_colorize:0/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-video.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fvideo_upload%2Fpost%2F194288812%2F7b0db792-b0dd-4651-b7f8-a2d1c4df1740%2Ftranscoded-1776255582.png)](https://substack.com/redirect/776334a2-d765-42a5-a87a-b46edfa51138?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ)

That’s the backdrop for this episode’s conversation with Alex Niehenke of Scale Venture Partners. The core idea is simple: vertical AI is having its moment not because incumbents are small, but because many of them are slow, bloated, and structurally unable to reinvent themselves fast enough. When the dominant players have low customer love, rising prices, and little appetite to disrupt their own revenue streams, the opening for startups gets real very quickly…

[Watch The Episode](https://substack.com/redirect/7c9b5ddc-2b45-4a30-9cbd-ed342183f1ac?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ)

[Listen To Episode Here](https://substack.com/redirect/ac77add3-f0d8-45fe-8974-279afac787ae?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ)

[![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!rRHa!,w_1100,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F6826d5f2-8464-4cb5-9486-9066631ebaa8_1875x625.jpeg)](https://substack.com/redirect/d70669b7-e808-4886-8ac2-d4b9ff48b9e9?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ)

Alex Niehenke is a Partner at Scale Venture Partners, where he focuses on early investments in vertical markets where incumbents have failed to invest in advanced technology. He has been at Scale since 2012 and has backed companies including Motive, Root Insurance, Scout RFP, Range, Proscia, and Archipelago. His investing lens was shaped early by watching his father’s transportation businesses intersect with the rest of the economy, which gave him a long-running curiosity about how real industries actually work.

That background matters because Alex has spent years leaning into sectors many investors historically dismissed as “boring”: insurance, logistics, construction, procurement, financial services, and other operationally dense industries. In the episode, he makes the case that these are exactly the kinds of markets where startups can win big, because the software is often deeply entrenched but poorly loved. The old venture knock on vertical software was always that TAMs were too small and buyers were too hard. Alex’s view is almost the inverse: those markets often only look unattractive until someone finally builds something customers actually want.

Scale’s own positioning maps cleanly to that worldview. The firm describes itself as backing early-stage AI companies on the journey from founder-led growth to a go-to-market machine. In other words, Scale is not just underwriting raw technical novelty; it is looking for companies that can turn product advantage into durable commercial momentum. That framing shows up all over Alex’s comments in the episode, especially in his emphasis on growth velocity, category timing, and whether a startup can become indispensable before the incumbent fully wakes up.
