body:
# The GTM Barbell at $11B ElevenLabs

ElevenLabs [just raised at an $11B valuation](https://link.mail.beehiiv.com/ss/c/u001.jGY3i_l4dDwQlqT7xK9Awow5hCfkWIjgDT9fAUTEiSideG0UKA56VoypV0t3Z0DG510ytQPb60e8O08Qc75rPfG62EABt80fG1o0UCg4DLrHIqGhCIPw-goC4EoVnNxlSdmrYJ6LH5H7_dxgf_wK8aFoosxLgSZIwFQ1F9qZ0gH9w8v6teY3q89be2N4lr_if0H4AeOfgrc03Y8qfTlTJDH1wGyvclYoKEG41NpEyq-nbbji6BauteXV_upYeZWw1DAvVPxx2SawIUNV1AF3SbPd6rmkkp_3-4f_0A0BvssH6DSD9lwkap6OqUqBbwMMuR_KYDTtXQrj_JnD73dDatq2Ro5DgQ7hyW54UAU2kBQ/4oa/-SKMX5e7TOefkcA6o1ygFg/h5/h001.LaDzynzHIWIY4yIoEUTeDOikvfsEYZVvDWlWRZy4qiE). Poetic number, right?

They have the dream GTM “barbell” model. I think you’re going to see this shape in a lot of the hot AI companies. Many of them have the PLG side (Lovable, Gamma, Cursor) and we’re seeing them [build the Enterprise side](https://link.mail.beehiiv.com/ss/c/u001.jGY3i_l4dDwQlqT7xK9Awow5hCfkWIjgDT9fAUTEiSideG0UKA56VoypV0t3Z0DGo9s_2tagnXtDtRa2MWJ8X01Z9BcKZB5ZDt9F4yb7Fuus-2HXJH9CVDDIkrAyflVvjpKKP36-p45glclD-XksWrzZ3TGv8Dh1hQ6_dmmLbiNdJSN4BRR4YgVd6IYDDmHqkh-yNg6cn3pawC3_l51K_NcK9lXWbx_ZemP5dDR3tELvrqFr1G1oHx9vy4ekqlTdG5LURX32ANsNfq6iwaDaJr2PS64RKd41Gm3ngQQWKDjCauMznOIcXC_LfTeHb9mLWCNzyUgIHKqdFEuP38eQDEJK57-Qt-qqWAyhDtEXGXY/4oa/-SKMX5e7TOefkcA6o1ygFg/h6/h001.GS6wfm7b4TQ3J9nIyJHU_S_8D1nCfVjUfjjKmrsr1-Y) very quickly now.

![](https://media.beehiiv.com/cdn-cgi/image/fit=scale-down,format=auto,onerror=redirect,quality=80/uploads/asset/file/0b40f156-1330-4576-9087-ebdb44065618/ElevenLabs_Barbell_Flywheel_Graphic.png?t=1770846955)

And with the brand and community momentum, it becomes a flywheel.

Two core motions — PLG and Enterprise. On one side, mass market adoption and touchless revenue. On the other, 6-7 figure deals, enterprise AEs, Forward Deployed Engineers.

Minimal investment in the middle. No gated eBooks. No MQL factory. No mid-ACV sellers.

**The hollow middle is a feature, not a bug.**

ElevenLabs went from $0 to $330M ARR in 3 years. They're profitable. They just raised $500M from Sequoia at $11B. And they're eyeing an IPO in 2027-2028.

Here's the revenue trajectory:

| **When** | **ARR** | **What Happened** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| End 2023 | ~$5M | Early traction, mostly self-serve |
| Jan 2024 | ~$25M | Series B, hit unicorn status |
| Oct 2024 | ~$90M | Enterprise kicking in |
| End 2024 | ~$120M |  |
| Apr 2025 | $100M | Hit $100M in 20 months from launch |
| Aug 2025 | $200M | $100M to $200M in 10 months |
| End 2025 | $330M+ | CEO confirmed to TechCrunch |

Revenue per employee is somewhere between $570K and $1.65M depending on whose headcount number you use.

The barbell GTM is one of the ingredients to this success.

# The PLG Motion

The left side of the barbell is pure product-led growth.

| **PLG Proof Point** | **Detail** |
| --- | --- |
| Website traffic | 16M monthly visitors |
| App downloads | 2.7M (ElevenReader, iOS + Android) |
| Pricing ladder | Free → $5/mo → $11/mo → $99/mo → usage-based |
| Users at launch | [1M+ registered in first 6 months](https://link.mail.beehiiv.com/ss/c/u001.mE3ZG6TkHu555uoidRdSqrwPmis91znuwJS1chobDrPjU5niqRqsEeCM9TbJ_DwIBtVMfA4PqFlGXUYoZfMYMsAPlbVA74SI5wv1mYlAgb4t_pdXc05SDVrmeBdzX0J4A8zshhNCBu0ICkc6y7FAPyjIugvo2oAmKUBkCJdwXfo_-xOypt3AJhDdF6Bs4BIjLcyimkpl5e67a7bjqn9n75xLnLWavB0DioMOTQ7nMbfpHBHB93HecUX_smjfgXE4OEJS8mfRC75YUGMIcXn5LQ/4oa/-SKMX5e7TOefkcA6o1ygFg/h7/h001.TxIguLPCZUvugftNbcDaSnYj_ibimUwqV4AWe9aNkXY) |
| Audio generated | 1,000+ years of AI audio |

The product surface area is massive: text-to-speech, voice cloning, AI dubbing in 30+ languages, podcast generation, sound effects, music, a free mobile reader app. Every surface is a top-of-funnel entry point.

![](https://media.beehiiv.com/cdn-cgi/image/fit=scale-down,format=auto,onerror=redirect,quality=80/uploads/asset/file/99aaf086-8e77-4953-8468-02068ec7cf0c/CleanShot_2026-02-11_at_13.57.30_2x.png?t=1770847085)

### The Creator Flywheel

ElevenLabs didn't just build a product — they built a creator economy around it.

subject: How to Kill the Code Review
body:
# How to Kill the Code Review

*Second wave [speakers for AIE Europe](https://substack.com/redirect/f8d06564-fae7-409e-8b0d-a7496766b94d?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ) and [CFP for AIE World’s Fair](https://substack.com/redirect/5931f5d1-fc97-4182-80fd-5b8c16ad04ca?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ) are announced today, and [OpenCode is confirmed for Miami](https://substack.com/redirect/f4bbdeb6-8566-46aa-b65a-05e6f4f6ccf9?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ)! We’ll also be in [Melbourne](https://substack.com/redirect/714a115a-4c1b-49a9-95bf-e42d07d26817?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ) & [Singapore](https://substack.com/redirect/82180e09-8222-425e-89fb-8392763423c7?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ).*

*Editor: This is the latest in [our guest post program](https://substack.com/redirect/d0a02e26-450a-4682-af46-a599dca4dc2e?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ), where we will publish AI Engineering essays worth considering, even if we don’t personally agree with them — having just shipped an [AI review tool](https://substack.com/redirect/00ecdcc1-a129-4267-bb65-52a19bdb908b?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ), this is one of those cases where I am not there yet, but is clearly on the horizon, and am happy for [Ankit](https://substack.com/redirect/0ab15c5c-ab75-422e-8afa-b494a688efa4?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ) to argue the case!*

---

Humans already couldn’t keep up with code review when humans wrote code at human speed. Every engineering org [I’ve talked to](https://substack.com/redirect/b72d5f37-1c4d-4e1f-8590-fe63392fda3f?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ) has the same dirty secret: PRs sitting for days, rubber-stamp approvals, and reviewers skimming 500-line diffs because they have their own work to do.

We tell ourselves it is a quality gate, but teams have shipped without line-by-line review for decades. Code review wasn’t even ubiquitous until around 2012-2014, one veteran engineer told me, there just aren’t enough of us around to remember.

And even with reviews, things break. We have learned to build systems that handle failure because we accepted that review alone wasn’t enough. This shows in terms of feature flags, rollouts, and instant rollbacks.

## **We have to give up on reading all the code**

Teams with high AI adoption complete 21% more tasks and merge 98% more pull requests, but PR review time increases 91%, based on [data](https://substack.com/redirect/e056df0a-4296-451a-bbba-ccead5648561?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ) from over 10,000 developers across 1,255 teams.

[![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!AC1C!,w_1100,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fc8dc3ebd-973c-4d94-bb3e-1a2b77615f28_1250x830.png)](https://substack.com/redirect/4fc42597-4df3-4ce5-88c4-adc7c9121b23?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ)

Two things are scaling exponentially: the **number** of changes and the **size** of changes. We cannot consume this much code. Period. On top of that, developers keep saying that reviewing AI-generated code requires more effort than reviewing code written by their colleagues. Teams produce more code, then spend more time reviewing it.

There is no way we win this fight with manual code reviews. Code review is a historical approval gate that no longer matches the shape of the work.

## **AI code review is still review**

AI code review tools are just buying us time. If AI writes the code and AI reviews it, why do we need a pretty review UI to display that? As much as AI code reviews can be valuable, these will shift left in the dev cycle. There’s no reason to waste CI resou

subject: Email Deliverability 101
body:
# Email Deliverability 101

[![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!MTOJ!,w_1100,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F99b877b1-9b3f-4e6a-a934-7c38a04756d9_1536x1024.png)](https://substack.com/redirect/209cade8-fd98-4658-bbc2-0f4f423fdf68?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ)

The Cannonball methodology is a true advancement in how companies think about and execute their go-to-market strategy. We’ve written at length about [finding hidden customers](https://substack.com/redirect/8ca57aed-00e8-4d29-bd43-1d52fd525ce4?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ), [pain-based segmentation](https://substack.com/redirect/0c45af18-a549-451b-b887-8bc814579ce8?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ), [using public data as a unique edge](https://substack.com/redirect/8f58f187-ef9c-404f-b74b-d39f6d4d6c56?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ) to get ahead, and [how to use Claude Code to do it all](https://substack.com/redirect/b1bdd0a3-df80-469c-9f01-6cd727602906?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ) faster and better than ever.

But, I then would say to myself:

*You still gotta send the damned email.*

And that’s the decidedly less glamorous part of the whole process. It is also the part where one wrong decision about your sending infrastructure can mean your own customers stop receiving your emails. Not the prospect you’re trying to reach. The customers you already have. Because, at the end of the day, someone is sending a cold outreach email or making a phone call to someone they don’t know.

But how can you tell if your messages are actually getting through? I’ve worked at companies where the sales team has been carpet bombing huge exports out of Apollo or ZoomInfo and nothing is getting through. (We call this TAM spam). The results were zero. Nothing. And I always suspected that was because of email delivery issues.

Email deliverability measures the likelihood of an email you send actually reaches the recipient’s inbox. Not if it was *sent*. Not if it was *accepted* by the mail server. Whether it landed in the inbox, the spam folder, or nowhere at all.

Every email you send is evaluated in transit. Inbox providers like Google and Microsoft run continuous scoring based on the sender’s domain reputation, past sending behavior, engagement history, and message content. A high deliverability rate means your emails arrive where you intended them to. A damaged one means they disappear silently, or worse, train recipients to treat you as spam.

Most teams do not know their deliverability is broken until the damage is already done.

I interviewed [Kellen Casebeer](https://substack.com/redirect/c2cb2d92-741a-4d2b-bbff-dd58fe0557ec?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ), founder of [The Deal Lab](https://substack.com/redirect/120460f4-8124-489b-b0fd-a0dca26675d0?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ), a go-to-market agency that has been doing this type of work for over three years. Kellen started as an SDR, worked full-cycle AE, and has been a GTM leader. He has been there, and he has seen some things! He now builds these systems from scratch.

“Think of it like clinical trials,” suggested Kellen. The greatest clinical researcher isn’t just saying, ‘Trust me, bro.’ They’re the best at coming up with a testing methodology that efficiently measures inputs and outputs.”

Here is what he knows.

When most people think about email deliverability, they think about one thing: their inbox. But that’s the wrong unit of analysis. Deliverability is a layered system with five distinct levels, and problems can originate at any of them.

Here are the five layers in this trifle:

**Layer 1: The domain.** Your brand’s domain name exists independently of whether anyone sends email from it. Eve

# The seam through the center of things

[![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!RPT5!,w_1100,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fb8e70e09-90f9-416c-a15c-692c1efe5a77_1181x1575.jpeg)](https://substack.com/redirect/6f045691-1dcd-4819-8056-73407ad2836f?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ)

*Illustration by [Alexander Naughton](https://substack.com/redirect/e32f72cb-3a29-4c0c-b3fc-0f2b2b98a12c?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ)*

> *The Lord will take control of you. You will dance and shout and become a different person.* 1 Samuel 10:6

In the weeks after Sasha and I sent the final manuscript for our book to the publisher, I found myself crying a lot. In some cases, it made sense: Reading [Aella’s writing](https://substack.com/redirect/f7e4c089-767d-4747-9a10-e76cbfdc43cd?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ) on her mother’s death, for instance, or [Bess Stillman](https://substack.com/redirect/70cfe2a6-010d-4363-bf22-e5819c207c7d?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ) on her husband’s, or [Tatiana Schlossberg](https://substack.com/redirect/4212ccfc-be5c-43f2-9b2b-23e718af3495?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ) on her own. But other cases were more perplexing: A great plate of risotto. A warm breeze on a late December evening. A competitor on Physical: Asia holding an uncomfortable position for a really long time.

It took a while for me to connect the weepiness to finishing the book. But once I did, something clicked into place and I knew it was true: Writing the book had fixed something inside of me that I’d stopped noticing was broken.

This requires some backstory.

I’ve mentioned the fact that I’m a recovering drug addict a couple of times on this blog. I’ve said a little more about it in my [TED talk](https://substack.com/redirect/e40099b7-0775-45c6-a753-0822a0956fc2?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ) and on various podcasts. The short version is that I spent more than 3 years, from 2017 to 2020, devastatingly addicted to nitrous oxide — an addiction that utterly wrecked my life, and that I’m lucky to have come back from.

What I’ve never said much about, even to many of the people who know me well, is: *Why?* Why did I get addicted, and why wasn’t I able to stop, despite being smart and agentic and all the other things people know me to be?

To the extent I do talk about it, I usually abbreviate the story to “I had a spiritual experience on drugs and chased it.” That’s not wrong, but by design it’s the least complete true thing I can say about it. It’s meant to move the conversation along.

To understand the *why*, you need to understand some of what the experience was like from the inside — so I’m going to try to explain it. I will preempt it by saying, I know what it looks like from the *outside*, though you are welcome to point it out to me anyway.

From the outside, I went insane, and thus encountered God. From the inside, I encountered God, and thus went insane.

---

For three months before it happened, I felt it coming, though I had no idea what “it” was. I’d already been experimenting heavily with psychedelics of all kinds when, in June 2017, I got really interested in nitrous oxide. The first time I sustained a nitrous high for a long time, with a friend feeding me balloons in the backyard of our Vegas rental after we busted out of some poker tournament, I felt myself shatter into multiple shards, like a mirror breaking. “I” dissolved and a swarm of simpler things appeared in my place.

Pretty neat trick! And an exciting new psychonautical vista for someone whose identity was already largely built around that sort of thing. I quickly started experimenting with it — on its own at first, then in combination with other drugs. I discovered nitrous did two th

# The Ceasefire That Wasn’t

A couple of weeks ago, I showed you what it looks like when [the world’s most important waterway shuts down](https://substack.com/redirect/25ed4426-64ab-4a5c-90f3-bc72d6b69dc1?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ). 130 ships a day dropping to single digits. Iran’s toll booth. Ships going dark. The data was alarming.

Then on April 7th, Trump gave Iran a deadline to reopen the Strait of Hormuz by 8 PM ET -- or else “a whole civilization will die tonight” -- and by that evening, Pakistan had brokered a two-week truce. Oil futures crashed 15% in minutes. The headlines said the crisis was over.

One week later, a US naval blockade is in effect, the ceasefire exists in name only, Israel has launched a ground assault into southern Lebanon, and Iran is calling the whole thing piracy.

So I loaded up God’s Eye -- swapped in the latest AIS maritime data, overlaid the strike coordinates, and started scrubbing the timeline to see what the data actually says.

**Watch the full video here:**

[![](https://substackcdn.com/image/youtube/w_728,c_limit/l_youtube_play_qyqt8q,w_120/7HEUCLc7aL8)](https://substack.com/redirect/d25d50c0-ee1c-488a-a2bf-c4e881e84429?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ)

---

## Is It Open?

Before the conflict, roughly 130 ships transited the Strait of Hormuz per day. On the first day of the ceasefire -- April 8th -- 15 got through. The day after: about 6. The oil futures that crashed on the ceasefire announcement? They bounced back above $120 within 24 hours. Traders figured it out faster than the headlines did.  
  
If you scrub through the AIS data in God’s Eye day by day, it’s stark. Where there used to be a constant stream of vessels, there’s just... nothing. A handful of dots where there used to be hundreds.

Trump called the strait “completely, immediately, and safely open.” Then a few days later said Iran was doing a “very poor job” of handling traffic and that “that is not the agreement we have!”

When I started clicking through vessels post-ceasefire, the picture was pretty clear. The ships that are getting through aren’t taking the normal shipping lanes at all. Iran published a map confirming mines in those lanes and is routing ships north, past [Iranian-controlled islands near Larak](https://substack.com/redirect/16821338-5bd7-47cc-97de-6759553bedae?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ) -- putting them within range of light artillery from Iranian shores.

The toll booth from the last video? Still operational. $1 to $2 per barrel. A fully loaded VLCC pays $2 to $3 million per transit. IRGC escort, one ship at a time. Insurance premiums have hit 2.5 to 5% of hull value -- we’re talking $600,000 to $1.2 million per trip for a $120 million tanker. Several major insurers pulled Gulf war risk cover entirely. The US doubled its reinsurance backstop to $40 billion to keep the market from freezing.

[![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!E8lP!,w_1100,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F0cd14572-662a-4fd1-9c34-a8830ae145c5_2861x1819.jpeg)](https://substack.com/redirect/12366f66-c92c-426d-a8cb-8bb547e06f1d?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ)

Two bottlenecks. Insurance and Iran. The strait was technically open the way a highway is technically open when every lane is closed except one, and there’s a toll collector with a rifle.

---

[![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!sbZu!,w_1100,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fd0a6cca4-feed-4f9b-8adf-cc74bfe3466f_3840x2160.jpeg)](https://substack.com/redirect/42dcb00c-5688-4236-89cf-0fd27531690e?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ)

# Listen: Most CROs are salespeople. Vanta’s CRO says that's changing

*Vanta CRO Stevie Case is on Executive Function this week to unpack how revenue leadership is evolving in the AI era.*

[![](https://review.firstround.com/content/images/size/w1600/2026/02/Stevie-5.png)](https://email2.firstround.com/c/eJxUj8Fu6yAQRb8GdraGGRhgweJJT_4PBnBtxQmRQ1L176tG3XR5r450dGoSMWx1S8Z74z0Tet2ueT-mvSaOUTCsJWSQsAKAaViDK3pLppVQq1jLxTEVlsLGSZQmdRUUr_eEgAyIaBgc8myzDxKJnC2IBpqysO7nY5z9eatz6Vd9pG2M-0PRP4WLwuVsr719zn-pn1_h4sjEbNkrWq6K_leyPodaJjIIk7XZTZEjTd4LuRVizmj0mWq-7e2Yy9bu7XbpysJX3np_20eS53GZ3vF6pI-tP8bveiX8DgAA__9rKVhs)

### Listen now: [YouTube](https://email2.firstround.com/c/eJxUj81q6zAQRp9G2tmMZmT9LLS4cPF7zEhyLeJEwVFS-valoZsuv48Dh1OSiHFW12S8N947Qq_rldsxtZJcjIJhy4FBwgYApmIJS9Z7cotBW0KgLJRj4c2akMFXIyhAgrolBHSAiMbBgm627INEosVmRANVWdja-Rhnf97KnPtVH2kf4_5Q9E_hqnA966vVz_kv9fMrXDl63iKLovWq6H8h6zmUPJFBmKzlZYou0uS90LJBZEajz1T41uox573e6-3SlYUv3nt_20eS53GZ3vF6pI-9P8bveiX8DgAA___eU1gv) | [Apple](https://email2.firstround.com/c/eJxUj8tq6zAURb9Gmtmch6wjDTS4cPF_6FmbOFFwlJT-fWnopMO9WbBYJaSE1ugaUARFLJPoeo37Me0lWO8TuZZdhOQaAGCl4past5DRMuHiS3LGFdOyw0YWCzUXpSTReyAgC0SEFhays4nikmdeTCZCqMpA28_HOPvzVubcr_oI2xj3h-J_ilZF61lfe_2c_1I_v6KVXUUDTRSvV8X_CxuJruSJkWAyJi6Tt54nkcRLAx8joT5Dibe9HnPe6r3eLl0Z-Ipb72_7COl5XKZ3vB7hY-uP8btegb4DAAD__7MDV7U) | [Spotify](https://email2.firstround.com/c/eJxUj81q6zAQRp9G2tmMRiONZqHFhYvfY_Tj2sSJg-Ok9O1LQzddfh8HDqflUlwk27NjdszRI9t-1XUb1pajSME016RQ0gwArmNLodolE6NSryKpMiAJtlZUI0MQDFTErhkBIyCiixAwjqScingfqCI66IZgXo_HeezPWxvrfrVbXs7z_jD-n8HJ4HT019o_x7_Uz29w0iDquaDx09X4_80Ta2p18A5hINIwSBQ_MBcfZhBVdPbITW9r38a69Hu_XXZD8KXLvr_tZy7P7TK84-2ZP5b9cf6uV8bvAAAA__96dFeD)

“In 2028, CROs will need to be systems-first instead of human capacity-first. That's not to say we won’t have large go-to-market teams, but we’re going to have to have CROs who know both sides of that equation. **And I think less than 10% of current CROs are capable of making that transition**.”

**Stevie Case** is no ordinary revenue exec. A former pro gamer, she found her way into sales when a mentor took a chance on her, climbing her way up as a sales leader at **Twilio** before joining **Vanta** as CRO.

She sat down with First Round Partner Brett Berson to dissect how she operates as CRO today, and how she thinks her role is going to change over the next few years.

She shares:

* **What founders get wrong about early sales hire**: Founders filter for pedigree when looking for the first sales hire, when they should be looking for hunger. “A lot of times founders are hiring for someone with shiny logos on their resume. But the right profile for a first sales hire in your company is probably not that big logo person. You need what we call a Renaissance rep, somebody who’s more creative, more entrepreneurial. They're not necessarily going to have the prettiest resume.”
* **Why “Midwest assassin” is such a powerful seller persona**: "We've got this Midwestern vibe of people at Vanta who feel like they're outsiders and have this hunger," she says. To find those people, Stevie asks candidates to describe a time they had to grind to get an outcome they wanted, personal or professional, playing close attention to how they tell that story. “When people tell you the story of something they had to really work hard to achieve, you either hear somebody who is ultra-confident and tells you how everything went right, or somebody who can own the things they did wrong."
* **Why the next generation of CROs will be technical**: Stevie says CROs in 2028 won’t necessarily have a profile like hers. “You're going to see people who have enough exposure to sales, but also are technical and get systems. It could be someone with a growth, RevOps or GTM engineering background, and it won’t necessarily be somebody who came up through 10-plus years of selling.”

[Listen to the episode](https://email2.firstround.com/c/eJxUj81q6zAQRp9G2tmMRj8jL7S4cPF7jKRRbeJEwVFS-valoZsuv48Dh1NTziY4LckQGaJgkbRceT-mvaawLBljK5Eh

subject: When Time Series Meet Transformers
body:
# When Time Series Meet Transformers

[![](https://gallery.mailchimp.com/4c1d0cf4959586b47ef210e9c/images/ae24e896-3de7-4a4e-a678-06035fe33714.jpg)](https://quantopian.us5.list-manage.com/track/click?u=4c1d0cf4959586b47ef210e9c&id=1e3804e0d1&e=7d796f23db)

[Join Professor Esfan Haghverdi on March 3 for a live conversation with Marco Peixeiro, author of *Time Series Forecasting in Python*.](https://quantopian.us5.list-manage.com/track/click?u=4c1d0cf4959586b47ef210e9c&id=99789bf636&e=7d796f23db)

Hello Daniil,

If you’ve ever had a credit card, you’ve probably lived this moment: you’re buying dinner in a new city, or making a purchase that’s slightly higher than your usual spending, and your card is suddenly declined for suspected fraud. Annoying, yes. But from your bank’s point of view, that swipe is not just a single event. It is the latest point in a sequence. Banks analyze spending as a living timeline: how often you buy things, what you normally spend, when you spend, and what kinds of merchants you use. That timeline is a time series, and it is messy, irregular, and full of context.

Fraud detection is fundamentally about modeling behavior over time. The challenge is that transaction time series are not neat or evenly spaced, and “normal” behavior can shift depending on the person, the day, or the situation. A useful model needs to understand both short-term context and long-term patterns, then decide whether a new transaction is genuinely suspicious or simply unusual.

This is one reason Transformers have drawn so much attention in time series research. Attention-based models offer a flexible way to learn from sequential data, and researchers have explored many adaptations to make Transformers work better for time series challenges like long sequences, seasonality, and non-stationary patterns. “Transformers in Time Series: A Survey” by Wen et al. provides a structured overview of this research, organizing the field around both how Transformer architectures are modified and where they are applied across forecasting, anomaly detection, and classification.

You can find more details about the paper in the section below. And if you’d like to hear more about the practical applications of time series in finance, join [our next Quantopian book series conversation](https://quantopian.us5.list-manage.com/track/click?u=4c1d0cf4959586b47ef210e9c&id=24fd984985&e=7d796f23db) with Marco Peixeiro, author of *Time Series Forecasting in Python*.

### Paper Summary

The paper, “Transformers in Time Series: A Survey” by Qingsong Wen, Tian Zhou, Chaoli Zhang, Weiqi Chen, Ziqing Ma, Junchi Yan, and Liang Sun, reviews how Transformer models have been adapted for time series analysis, motivated by their ability to capture long-range dependencies. The authors organize prior work using a taxonomy from two perspectives: network modifications (positional/timestamp encoding, attention changes, and architecture-level redesigns) and application domains, especially forecasting, anomaly detection, and classification. They summarize representative models and discuss the main design trends that make Transformers better suited for time series data.

The paper also includes experiments to understand how Transformers behave on time series benchmarks, showing that many variants still struggle to benefit from very long input sequences. The authors find that increasing model depth does not consistently improve results, unlike in NLP and vision. A major takeaway is that injecting time-series inductive biases—particularly seasonal-trend decomposition—can strongly boost forecasting performance. The survey ends by highlighting future directions such as improved inductive biases, Transformer+GNN hybrids for spatio-temporal data, and pretraining for time series Transformers.

[![](https://mcusercontent.com/4c1d0cf4959586b47ef210e9c/images/fa8aa542-0560-ce8c-89e2-583a28d6e406.png)](https://quantopian.us5.list-manage.com/track/click?u=4c1d0cf4959586b47ef210e9c&id=7f7d

subject: Fighting the Global Cost of Living Crisis
body:
# Fighting the Global Cost of Living Crisis

In the last four years, one word has come to dominate popular discourse in most developed economies: inflation. As prices surged following a perfect storm of the Covid-19 pandemic and a global energy price shock, governments across the G7 have made tackling the rising cost of living a top priority.

But inflation hasn’t been limited to major developed economies - in fact, it’s been even more pronounced in many emerging markets. These economies are often more dependent on imports for key products like energy, more prone to foreign exchange instability, and have weaker monetary policy institutions to manage these risks. The result: emerging markets consumers are more exposed to rising prices.

[![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!GpAS!,w_1100,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F027b814f-6e4a-4aa4-a0c4-e68322021161_1600x989.png "Chart")](https://substack.com/redirect/843d03e2-f5a8-453f-bc85-8ff730ae798f?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ)

Whilst the rising cost of living in emerging markets is a macroeconomic phenomenon, shaped by global factors like energy prices and monetary policy, it also reflects market inefficiency. Fragmented supply chains, limited access to affordable financing options, and anti-competitive behaviour by large, monopoly players.

Take food delivery, for example. In Pakistan, a McDonald’s Big Mac Meal on [Foodpanda](https://substack.com/redirect/780d3730-146e-425c-9125-1dd3244bb65c?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ) is priced at 1,173 Pakistani rupees, or around US$4.2. Compare that against an in-store price of 995 rupees, or $3.55, and we can see that consumers face an 18% mark-up.

[![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!xpz6!,w_378,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F7de848f0-68a2-4101-baf4-1fbc50b1cdbf_768x1198.png)](https://substack.com/redirect/200e7f15-5660-4955-9923-e3cdeafabd4b?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ)

Take another example - logistics. A [recent study](https://substack.com/redirect/0c53f996-832f-44e9-acd9-9b5d9983fde5?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ) by United Nations Trade and Development found that median transport costs for maritime trade in developing countries were twice that in developed economies. This doesn’t just mean that vital imports cost more - it also makes it harder for these economies to develop by exporting to global markets.

The human impact is accentuated by the fact that people in emerging markets generally spend a greater share of their income on essential goods like food and transport. For example, food represents up to 51% of household spending in Nigeria and 38% in Mexico, versus only 11% in the US.

[![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!K1np!,w_1100,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fe1f15607-ede8-4eaa-839e-ebabf89eb5c1_1200x742.png "Chart")](https://substack.com/redirect/8a7fa851-8e20-4b0b-978f-301880f5523d?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ)

However, inefficiency begets opportunity. That’s why at inDrive, we see the rising cost of living as a chance to disrupt the status quo by simplifying supply chains, cutting out the middle-men and taking on monopolists. The problem is both ethical and financial, but the solution is also an economic opportunity that can enhance the spending power of hundreds of millions of people across the world’s most dynamic emerging markets.

At inDrive, we serve a fast growing audience of more than 60 million monthly active users in 48 countries. Our core mission is simple: give these consumers a fair choice in ride-hailing by allowing them to negotiate directly with drive

body:
# OpenClaw Emperors

*JingYu is a designer, architect, and the author of the [Old North Whale Review](https://substack.com/redirect/10429f84-15b3-4a66-8668-86721ea02c24?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ) (老北鲸). Driven by a love for exploring the crossroads of rationality and creativity, his work traces the tangled roots of modern China’s ‘Chineseness’ across history, culture, and art.*

To capture the chaotic zeitgeist of China in spring 2026, look at just two photographs. They are separated by exactly thirty years. Yet, placed side-by-side, they echo the exact same frequency of desperation and hope.

On the left, captured in the hazy 1990s, hundreds of laid-off factory workers and ordinary citizens sit in tight rows, aluminum cooking pots balanced precariously on their heads. They are participants in the great “Qigong Fever” (气功热), attempting to channel invisible cosmic energy to cure their ailments and secure their uncertain futures.

On the right, a modern crowd packs an auditorium in March of 2026. Instead of aluminum pots, they wear plush red “lobster claw” headbands. A glowing screen displays a stark warning: *“2026: Humanity is no longer divided by gender, but by creators and bystanders. Mastering OpenClaw is your ticket to Web 4.0.”*

[![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!vy90!,w_1100,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F6ed6a986-9f39-4eca-b154-786177bd0124_1456x387.jpeg)](https://substack.com/redirect/fbe740c0-c001-410f-aabe-30606a49c796?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ)

(Left) “Qigong Fever”: people gather with [aluminum cooking pots (信息锅)](https://substack.com/redirect/4dc0e783-d47f-43fc-a798-7fc9909ddcbe?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ) on their heads, 1990s | (Right) OpenClaw rush: people gather wearing red “lobster claw” headbands, 2026 (Image from a Web 4.0 sharing session in Shenzhen, by Kong Jianping 孔剑平, founder of Nano Labs)

Three decades ago, people wore ‘antennas’ to grasp at the mythical salvation of supernatural powers during a period of massive economic restructuring. Today, they wear red claws, queuing up to embrace the cyber-deity known as the AI Agent.

This fever reached its zenith earlier this month in Shenzhen. Just days after black-market scalpers were charging 1,000 RMB a pop to install OpenClaw instances for desperate tech workers, internet giant Tencent took to a public square for a “charity installation” event. They transformed into the ‘Goddess of Mercy,’ granting the eager masses not just the fun of tech deployment, but actual, whimsical “Birth Certificates” for their “digital lobsters” 小龙虾.

[![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!BS3m!,w_1100,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fdb578bf9-5f83-4762-bd40-0969859e247d_1456x798.jpeg)](https://substack.com/redirect/b8232fe1-3102-47b0-bf7d-178721de2f91?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ)

(Left) People line up at Tencent Headquarters to install OpenClaw | (Right) “Birth certificate” issued after getting OpenClaw installed

### **From Monolithic Skyscrapers to Master-Planned Cities**

For the past few years, interacting with LLMs required managing the fragile context window, employing “Prompt Engineering” to coax out brilliance without triggering a break. Ask an LLM to manage a complex, multi-step software deployment, and it would hallucinate imaginary code libraries, contradict its own logic, or simply forget.

The fundamental issue is of structural design. Relying on a single, monolithic LLM to execute complex, real-world workflows is like trying to build a city by stacking a single skyscraper infinitely high. Without proper foundational engineering, zoning laws, or internal load-bearing structures, it eventually collapses under its own immense

subject: Time’s Up for SaaS (Grow Faster or Vanish)
body:
# Time’s Up for SaaS (Grow Faster or Vanish)

The public software (SaaS) index is down 37% since the end of Q3’25, and the median company trades at a paltry 3.5x NTM (next-twelve-months) revenue. We have had 2 consecutive quarters of negative share price returns; the only other time this has occurred in the last 10 years was in 2022. The public markets want high growth, yet growth rates for public SaaS have been lackluster for years.

Put simply, time is up for public SaaS to grow revenue (through AI) or vanish. Investors have seen AI companies such as [Anthropic grow from $0 to nearly $10B](https://substack.com/redirect/7e4e8147-d803-4fcf-ad20-2f91b9d5b2ec?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ) in annualized revenue, and [Cursor grow from $0 to $1B in annualized revenue](https://substack.com/redirect/b84adc0f-99c5-4d29-87e5-bb5280163422?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ), both in very short periods. Public markets are demanding high growth, and unfortunately, SaaS isn’t delivering; share prices are paying the price.

While the recent releases of [Anthropic’s plug-in](https://substack.com/redirect/4cb320a7-12b8-4a89-a716-8c40108dbdb6?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ) and [Cowork](https://substack.com/redirect/7c1b0ee4-a6f0-4fbe-89f2-0ba349b34482?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ), and [OpenAI’s Frontier](https://substack.com/redirect/8bd8621c-c6ab-428e-9d98-340f85a08381?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ) signal a deeper push into business applications, which could be to blame, continued slow revenue growth may be the primary issue. IT budgets are also realigning toward consumption-based models, and seat-based pricing is under pressure, adding further uncertainty. The markets seem to be realizing that the widely expected AI growth re-acceleration in public software is not materializing.

The following chart shows the average LTM (last-twelve-months) revenue growth rate across all public software over the past 10 years. Average growth has slowed to 16% year-over-year last year, its lowest level in a decade.

[![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!k8MO!,w_1100,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F6916b78e-72ea-41c1-8233-52b8ae911e9f_1250x700.png)](https://substack.com/redirect/e4437283-8495-4241-81f5-84c687f62ced?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ)

For many years, the most reliable assumption about public SaaS was that it would continue to grow durably even with a larger revenue scale. Quarter after quarter, companies would ‘beat and raise’, and the average company grew at 30-40% for almost 10 years, culminating in a growth pull-forward and high multiples during 2021, the ZIRP (zero-interest-rate policy) period. Post-ZIRP, rates rose, demand slowed, and revenue growth rates fell. AI was supposed to come to the rescue and reinvigorate growth rates. That has not yet happened, and the market appears to be betting that it won’t.

#### ServiceNow: The Barometer of Success in SaaS

ServiceNow ($NOW) is easy to highlight, as it is arguably one of the most (if not the most) successful SaaS/Cloud 1.0 companies. They went public in 2012 at a $2.7B market cap and reached a peak market cap of over $240B in January, up ~65x on a per-share basis from their IPO price. Just last week, ServiceNow r[eported their Q4 and full-year 2025 results](https://substack.com/redirect/7b779ddb-2501-44dd-8b59-9ab55221f30a?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ); the company exceeded top and bottom-line targets and did $3.6B of revenue in Q4, growing 21% year-over-year with $2B of free cash flow. ServiceNow is a Rule of 56 company that consistently grows by 20%+ each year and generates billions in free cash flow. By any comparison, the company is performing exceptionall

subject: Emergency Pod: PLA Purges Continue!
body:
# Emergency Pod: PLA Purges Continue!

Zhang Youxia 张又侠 has fallen. We thought he would be the last man standing, but instead, he is a “tiger blocking the road” who “seriously fueled threats to the Party’s absolute leadership.” Xi had already purged more CMC members than Mao ever did, but this round of expulsions is distinct from mere anti-corruption housekeeping.

To discuss what makes this purge unique, ChinaTalk sat down with [Jon Czin](https://substack.com/redirect/b2fc2d8c-7c05-4bae-b70f-9957f83202b3?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ), a former China analyst at the CIA who served as China Director on Biden’s NSC and now works at the Brookings Institution. You can check out Jon’s previous ChinaTalk appearances [here](https://substack.com/redirect/735676ab-9111-4d6a-a5dc-0d79cdae682c?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ) and [here](https://substack.com/redirect/745dd0ec-c6e1-4e44-a235-df4a574a0a73?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ).

**We discuss…**

* **Zhang Youxia’s long personal relationship with Xi, and how it could have soured,**
* **The WSJ’s bombshell report claiming that Zhang leaked information about China’s nuclear weapons to the USA,**
* **Why corruption alone can’t explain Zhang’s fate and the uniquely harsh methods of discipline Xi chose to use,**
* **Why Xi could be getting paranoid, and what this means for succession plans,**
* **Whether Zhang was purged because he stood up against Xi’s Taiwan invasion plans**

Listen now on [your favorite podcast app](https://substack.com/redirect/4a90e621-cef8-433a-b003-9e8f7b5954d0?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ).

**Jordan Schneider:** Zhang Youxia had a rough week. Jon, where do we begin?

**Jon Czin:** A lot of people in the China-watching community were frankly astonished that the rumors accumulating last week were real this time around — that Zhang Youxia was actually in trouble. And not just Zhang Youxia. His takedown has somewhat overshadowed the demise of Liu Zhenli 刘振立, who was running the Joint Staff Department. That’s another CMC member leaving the Central Military Commission, which now has just two members: Xi Jinping, of course, and Zhang Shengmin 張升民, who ironically runs the Discipline Inspection Commission — the chief internal investigator for all these anti-corruption campaigns.

**Jordan Schneider:** “Ironically” might not be the right word here, Jon.

**Jon Czin:** That’s fair. Maybe “tellingly” is better. This is a pretty remarkable moment in Chinese politics — it’s not an overstatement to call it Shakespearean. The few facts we do know are quite dramatic, even without the embroidery of speculation and rumors from the last few days.

We know their fathers served together in China’s civil war. We know there was some kind of nexus between Xi and Zhang Youxia — and that’s not just historic. **Xi kept Zhang around at the last Party Congress even though he had exceeded the retirement age.** That alone was quite telling.

[![2022年10月25日習近平出席軍委會議（右二張又俠）。](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!Vdms!,w_1100,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F80918d17-be6c-4cfb-8529-56bb26ca2802_830x553.jpeg "2022年10月25日習近平出席軍委會議（右二張又俠）。")](https://substack.com/redirect/5e3fb982-4617-4ec5-be01-1478c52ce1f1?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ)

Xi Jinping and Zhang Youxia (middle) during a meeting of the Central Military Commission in 2022. [Source](https://substack.com/redirect/4295f026-4b89-4e87-a9ff-9ed1d2a9130b?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ).

To my mind, this represents a qualitative leap. Xi started his term by going after his enemies. In his third term, he started going after associates — kind of like a mafia boss, seeing these guys as disposable. He made them, he could break them. But now he’s going afte

# MCP and other features

Hi Daniel,

Software is moving toward A2A (agent-to-agent). Your AI assistant calls another agent, which calls another, and the chain executes work you used to click through yourself.

LinkedIn content sits inside that shift. The trigger ("post about X"), the research, the draft, the scheduling - increasingly, that happens outside a UI - in a chat with Claude, Cursor, or whatever agent you live in.

Chatbots still aren’t the ideal surface for social media, but that’s where users are going - and we want to be there first  

**So we shipped MCP.**

2pr.io is now an MCP server. Any agent that speaks MCP can:

1. search post ideas
2. drafts (including deeplinks),
3. refine,
4. schedule & publish,
5. reply to comments,
6. read your analytics on your behalf.

![](http://cdn.mcauto-images-production.sendgrid.net/2cf06fe5f3e52e6e/d77e207d-fd28-4d71-a3d9-c1623734230f/2396x1798.png) ![](http://cdn.mcauto-images-production.sendgrid.net/2cf06fe5f3e52e6e/5fbaf33c-379e-4e28-93e5-a37b2cbe9096/960x720.gif)

The agent calls into all of that with one tool call.

Setup: settings → MCP tokens.

- Native video + multi-image on LinkedIn posts  
- Full UI in 4 more languages (German, Spanish, Portuguese, French)

subject: Context Graphs and the Future of AI Autonomy
body:
# Context Graphs and the Future of AI Autonomy

For most of the data era, systems existed to *observe*. They collected, aggregated, and explained the past.

AI changes that contract. AI systems don’t just analyse data, but are required to **act on it**. They recommend, approve, escalate, and commit changes to the world. And the moment a system acts, analysis is no longer enough.

Action demands **judgment**. Jaya Gupta and Ashu Garg brilliantly [summarise this premise](https://substack.com/redirect/f8cbd6d7-d72a-4702-8f8f-2088fae3881d?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ) in their groundbreaking piece on context graphs, which has, by itself, started a domino effect of clearer understanding in terms of true AI requirements.

Judgment is not a function of more rows or cleaner schemas. It emerges from context: what was known at the time, which rules applied, where exceptions were allowed, and which precedents mattered in *this* situation.

Without access to decision-time context, intelligence stalls at insight and never translates into autonomy.

---

### Where existing data systems are breaking bad

[![Breaking Bad Run GIFs | Tenor](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!15mb!,w_728,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_lossy/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F12fe1a30-b543-4378-8732-f86ab1ccddaa_220x100.gif "Breaking Bad Run GIFs | Tenor")](https://substack.com/redirect/a0f483f8-8686-40d5-b6b0-9c84945845f0?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ)

The current data stack was never designed to carry judgment. Systems of record preserve **state** (what the world looks like now), but they overwrite the reasoning that led there.

Warehouses preserve **history** (how metrics changed over time), but not the intent or tradeoffs behind those changes. Knowledge graphs model **relationships** (how entities connect), but not how conflicts were resolved or why one path was chosen over another.

The result is a familiar gap: we can see *what* happened, but not *why it was allowed to happen*. The reasoning that turned data into action dissolves into chats, calls, and memory.

---

## What is a Context Graph?

### The anatomy of a decision

Every meaningful decision, whether made by a human or an agent, follows the same structure.

1. Something is evaluated: data points, signals, historical snapshots, versions of truth that existed *at that moment*.
2. Rules come into play. Policies are checked and constraints surface. Often, those rules collide, leading to conflicts and edge cases.
3. Exceptions are invoked, explicitly or implicitly, and authority is exercised. *Someone* approves and *something* is allowed.

Only then does an action commit, and the world changes state.

**Most systems record the last step.** A context graph is concerned with everything that came before it.

### Defining the context graph

A context graph is not a model of entities. It is a **record of decisions**. Each node represents a decision made at a specific point in time. Not an object, not a metric, but a moment of judgment.

The edges carry the meaning:

* the context that was evaluated
* the constraints that were applied
* the precedents that influenced the outcome
* the authority that sanctioned the decision
* the action that was ultimately committed

Over time, these decisions stitch together into a structure that shows not just *what* changed, but *why it was permissible to change*.

### Relevance of context graphs in an AI-first world

Agents do not operate inside a single system. They move across boundaries, synthesising signals from many sources before acting. As they do, they must be able to explain themselves: to justify why a path was taken, why an exception was granted, why one precedent outweighed another.

They must learn not just from outcomes, but from prior judgments. And they must be governed (audited, constrained, and trusted) as their autonomy increases. None of this

# To Trillion(s) and Beyond: A SpaceX IPO Odyssey!

In *2001, A Space Odyssey*, a movie that was well ahead of its time when it was released in 1968, Hal (the computer) famously responded to questions about his reliability with “it (mstakes) can only be attributable to human error”. I was reminded of my fallibility repeatedly as I tried to value SpaceX ahead of its initial public offering, a market debut that is shaping up as a barn-burner for three reasons. The first is that in a market where there are many young companies all trying to claim to be futuristic in their offerings, SpaceX clearly stands out as the real thing, with rockets, satellites and AI all residing under its corporate umbrella. The second is that its founder (Elon Musk) is the richest person in the world, has upended one legacy business (autos), bought a social media company as a soapbox and made his presence felt on the the political stage. Love him or hate him, Musk is definitely not boring, and his capacity to spin business narratives that seem outlandish at first hearing. but become conventional wisdom later, clearly adds to the allure of SpaceX. Third, if the private market pricing feeds into the public offering, SpaceX could very well become the most valuable IPO of all time, joining the rarefied list of trillion-dollar companies, on listing. That said, I may be getting a little ahead of the game here, because SpaceX has not filed a public prospectus yet, and little is known about its financials other that drabs of information that have been leaked to the press. I will forge on, nevertheless, with the stipulation that this is a first iteration, and that I will revisit it, as more information comes out about the firm’s financial standing and its IPO plans.

**The History of SpaceX**

You may be surprised to hear that SpaceX is older than Tesla, at least in terms of chronological age, founded on March 14, 2002, in El Segundo, California. At its founding, Musk stated its goals as reducing the costs of space transportation and travel to Mars, but was viewed as having little chance of success by the space establishment, composed then of government agencies (NASA) and a few defense firms (Boeing and Northrop Grumman). SpaceX applied the lessons of modular engineering from the software business and it launched Falcon 1, its first space launch vehicle in September 2008; that successful launch led to a NASA contract for $1.6 billion, and rescued the company from near bankruptcy. In subsequent years, SpaceX developed Falcon 9, a reusable and heavier vehicle, with the Dragon Spacecraft unit, and became the first commercial entity to deliver cargo to the International Space Station. In 2013, SpaceX launched its first mission for a private customer, and quickly secured a dominant market share of commercial launch contract market. In recent years, SpaceX has invested in an even more ambitious version (in terms of size and power) of reusable spacecraft with Starship, and while its first launch in 2023 exploded in space, the company is clearly moving towards making it functional.

Along the way, the company added to its business mix, first with The Boring Company, a company that specialized in building tunnels that could be used to transport people, in 2017, before spinning it off as a separate entity. More significantly, in 2019, the company launched sixty Starlink satellites, with the end game of offering satellite-based internet services to customers, especially in areas where conventional internet service was limited. That endeavor has now grown to include thousands of satellites and had more than ten million active subscribers spread across the world, at the end of 2025. In February 2026, the company created its third business arm, with its acquisition of xAI, the parent to Grok, the Musk-developed competitor in the LLM space.

# Forecasting in a usage based world

---

> [![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!PkdP!,w_510,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F31d163c9-6cda-4078-a4f5-34c646d6b4fd_3840x2160.jpeg)](https://substack.com/redirect/79cc8db6-0fe0-45f0-b8c4-d6012a9b8151?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ)
>
> Disparate tools, expensive value-selling consultants, and manual CRM updates make your sales process hard to follow. For sellers and buyers. **[Accord](https://substack.com/redirect/0c9b42be-2e58-46d1-9ca4-55399aacdf2d?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ)** turns what your top reps do naturally (multi-threading, business cases, mutual action plans, and more) into playbooks that become the deal workspace. Consolidate your RevOps stack, eliminate busywork, and make excellence unavoidable for every rep. **[Learn more.](https://substack.com/redirect/0c9b42be-2e58-46d1-9ca4-55399aacdf2d?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ)**
>
> [![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!GfXq!,w_300,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F548b9c9d-a5e3-48de-8f05-2ee6d6a4c3b5_300x300.webp)](https://substack.com/redirect/0f68c07a-02ef-40f6-b648-b53d53a8c46e?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ)
>
> I personally use [Zapier Agents](https://substack.com/redirect/e28ce755-44d1-4e1d-a80f-68e86c5790bf?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ) to configure my own Executive Assistant which reads my emails, transcripts to identity prospects to reach out to, identity tasks to be completed, and followups across my personal and professional life. [Build yours today with Zapier](https://substack.com/redirect/e28ce755-44d1-4e1d-a80f-68e86c5790bf?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ).
>
> **Thanks to our sponsors who keep this email free. Interested in sponsoring these emails? See our [partnership options here](https://substack.com/redirect/c49c1b98-cef2-4b30-acb8-00d5f934bc21?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ)**

---

Most finance teams are still running forecasting processes designed for a world where revenue = contracts × time. That math doesn’t work anymore.

Usage based pricing turns forecasting from a deterministic exercise into a probabilistic one. You’re predicting how customers will behave after they sign, which is a fundamentally different problem than predicting when deals will close.

## Why your current forecast model is lying to you

Traditional SaaS forecasting follows a simple logic:

Pipeline value × Win rate = Expected bookings

Bookings × Recognition schedule = Revenue

It’s clean. It’s predictable. CFOs love it because they can answer “are we on plan?” with confidence.

Usage based pricing breaks this at every step.

> [![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!lOas!,w_1100,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fdaa70dbf-235e-4648-b214-29765dfdfac3_2084x894.png)](https://substack.com/redirect/718bf2c2-7c9f-4371-92a9-d3946201dc34?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ)

First, the deal value itself is uncertain. When a customer signs a $100K annual commitment with overage pricing, you don’t actually know if that’s a $100K deal or a $180K deal. It depends on what they do after they sign.

Second, the recognition schedule is no longer fixed. Revenue happens when usage happens. A customer might front-load their usage in Q1 and go quiet in Q4. Or the reverse. Or something entirely unpredictable.

# 🎯 Why Startups Stall — And How to Fix It

## **The Orbit Brief**

## **The Growth Flywheel: Why Startups Stall (and How to Fix It)**

Most startup founders think growth is a moment — that one “magic launch” will make numbers skyrocket. But TR Harrington, Partner & Director of Growth at Orbit Ventures points out: real growth isn’t a moment, it’s a system. It's a structured, repeatable process that turns experiments into insights, insights into improvements, and improvements into compounding impact.  
  
This system — the Growth Flywheel — powers startups by turning every feature, onboarding session, and user interaction into actionable feedback. It’s not about hacks or luck; it’s about building learning loops that drive sustainable momentum.  
  
Want to see how the flywheel works in practice, including the four stages TR uses with portfolio companies to accelerate growth?

subject: InferenceX v2: NVIDIA Blackwell Vs AMD vs Hopper - Formerly InferenceMAX
body:
# InferenceX v2: NVIDIA Blackwell Vs AMD vs Hopper - Formerly InferenceMAX

InferenceXv2 (formerly InferenceMAX) builds on the foundation established by InferenceMAXv1, [our open-source, continuously updated inference benchmark](https://substack.com/redirect/63dc0f8e-81a7-4f50-a79c-1c8b2dc307f6?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ) that has set a new standard for AI inference performance and economics. InferenceMAXv1 moved beyond static, point-in-time benchmarks by running continuous tests across hundreds of chips and popular open-source frameworks. [Free dashboard available here.](https://substack.com/redirect/5b91e6b8-7ed5-4ac0-b7fb-0d836c7f4b25?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ)

[Our benchmark has been widely reproduced, validated and/or supported by almost every major buyer](https://substack.com/redirect/b5ea1ae9-f5fc-469b-92db-9617c91dd020?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ) of compute from [Google Cloud](https://substack.com/redirect/5ac6fed5-a265-4c1e-9f64-120417f7f69a?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ) to [Microsoft Azure](https://substack.com/redirect/4119a774-25b4-4570-b42f-7a93e80d9c39?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ) to [Oracle, OpenAI](https://substack.com/redirect/b5ea1ae9-f5fc-469b-92db-9617c91dd020?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ), and many more.

InferenceXv2 builds on this foundation. It expands coverage to include large scale DeepSeek MoE disaggregated inference (disagg prefill, or simply “disagg”) with wide expert parallelism (wideEP) optimization to **all 6 NVIDIA western GPU SKUs from the past 4 years** as well as to every single AMD western GPU SKU released in the past 3 years – in total InferenceXv2 utilizes close to 1000 frontier GPUs for a full benchmark run across all SKUs.

With today’s release, InferenceXv2 is now the first suite to benchmark the Blackwell Ultra GB300 NVL72 and B300 across the whole pareto frontier curve, and it is the first third party benchmark to test disagg+wideEP multi-node FP4 and FP8 MI355X performance. In future iterations of InferenceX, we will continue to focus heavily on disaggregated serving with wide expert parallelism as that is what is deployed in production at Frontier AI Labs like OpenAI, Anthropic, xAI, Google Deepmind, DeepSeek as well as advanced API providers like TogetherAI, Baseten, and Fireworks. In this article, we will also break down the system engineering principles and economics in play around the [latest Claude Code Fast mode feature](https://substack.com/redirect/32e1888d-e126-48e1-a108-2f432ccdd655?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ).

Our benchmark is completely open-source under Apache 2.0 – this means that we are able to move at the same rapid speed at which the AI software ecosystem is advancing. If you like our work and would like to show us some support, [please drop a star on our GitHub](https://substack.com/redirect/63dc0f8e-81a7-4f50-a79c-1c8b2dc307f6?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ)! We also provide a free data visualizer at [https://inferencex.com](https://substack.com/redirect/d3f6ef56-840a-4618-878e-f967f8b15904?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ) for everyone in the ML community to explore the complete dataset themselves.

We will add DeepSeekv4 and other popular Chinese frontier models with day 0 support as over the past 6 months, we now have cleaned up a lot of tech debt and are able to [move fast with stable infrastructure](https://substack.com/redirect/54752a70-5da0-49d7-8613-62a792dd33c6?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ). We will also be adding TPUv7 Ironwood and Trainium3 to InferenceX later this year! # 🍐#143 Closing chapters, acquisitions, and sabbaticals. 

Hey,

Big things happened to your favorite markepear🍐. And because of that I’ve decided to go on a sabbatical for a few months. I’ll still write this newsletter and blog during the break but I am just not sure how frequently.

Took me a while to write this. Needed a minute to put what I feel in words. But the **[neptune.ai](https://link.mail.beehiiv.com/v1/c/AiOKXOZcstHcsk9M8H6qKQXzU0WTPjUxD3jWmTzrKVyrqQ3yCFZZ%2BW197n4B%0AO8sxg%2BC07sH4WqlRMpVgxDGytAj3VPNfeonGGUNAfmeAe6hyd1TvhfqAq%2Bd1%0APyHLSfbGonuKuGDgBPia3aUaxE9TSss2iT4p309KucqvhL0lY6j4zsj%2FOrM8%0A4BWfMWIKjkQV%0A/bb5b4d1e1b808b1a)** **chapter of my career is really officially over**. Happy, proud, nostalgic, sad. Tired (though this one could be because of our new 2month old addition to the family;)).

In December we’ve been [acquired by OpenAI](https://link.mail.beehiiv.com/v1/c/0e8%2B4%2Br%2FjhsZV%2B9XFTFqCl1JdUvY7RY8WJ2NsN5QbUuVkjm2GKV%2FBUMS%2BCUy%0ATLjDLeDBuammL%2FosX34thZpNAdIEBSKo%2FrtbWVGcmXoEYCm91DrCDXEXJXCS%0AtIZinKydk39As2armX%2BVC1OY9HeL7HLs1Hlgk45RwMBjjrSPs0Zk%2F5RPOQd6%0ASP15N9SZ%2Bbp7%0A/8ea4d8de2078ae4f) and a moonshot goal that I put on one of our internal presentations, that “the training run that gets us to AGI will be logged to Neptune” may actually turn out to be true. Time will tell.

And **Neptune is winding down it’s operations completely** (so you may want to screenshot some of those cool things we’ve done on the website if you haven’t already ;)).

**Thanks to Neptune I found my true passion** -> developer marketing. I was a chess pro, poker player, theoretical physicist, stock trader, and a data scientist. And yet marketing to devs gave me so much joy that I’ve decided to create [Developer Markepear](https://link.mail.beehiiv.com/v1/c/alEkPXCmMyJEQiAEgIid%2BInOEFk%2BEXjX53xHoRBfccPOjPZSY%2F2%2BhdonDFWX%0A6c%2Bdccy9jfz5SFmZFtDDk8uFXl04ci9C%2FOyIdGINTbG8Hs9fQ4LnmibV4Pi1%0AY7SzUuqUEZjWmngIZ7g4PR686TPVJyoWIpEydF%2BYj5SO3CjoPEY8y2XDafKy%0AXr%2F6wqp17fAn%0A/0c906fc073bf45f9) and to share my learnings with others.

Extremely happy that cards aligned this way and a moment of “somebody needs to learn marketing” hit us at Neptune. And with my love for learning messy things I decided to take a leap.

**Huge thank you** to:

* all the amazing people who worked on our **marketing/GTM** **team** (do let me know **if you are hiring, some folks are still exploring**),
* **advisors** who helped me learn along the way,
* **leadership and founders** as we worked through thick and thin,
* **investors** for their wisdom and poise when we thought we were smart (and probably were just smartasses),
* and **all the amazing neptune people** I met along the way that made this journey so much more fun.
* my business partner **Piotr, CEO**, the driver of change who pushed me to where I’d never push myself. I wouldn't be where I am now if it wasn’t for him.
* and finally **my wife Magda** (I know you are reading this for the pear puns but still ;)) for supporting me throughout this whole time. You are my rock. Thank you.

And while many Neptuners went to OpenAI and other exciting places **I am taking a sabbatical**. Neptune's acquisition coincided with my second kiddo being born. And while in startups there never seems to be a good time to take rest, it is hard to find a better spot than this.

So for the next few months the only role that I have lined up is CDO (Chief Dad Officer). And after that back to marketing cool stuff ;)

![](https://media.beehiiv.com/cdn-cgi/image/fit=scale-down,format=auto,onerror=redirect,quality=80/uploads/asset/file/8f8f16c4-4146-4104-8508-609855f991d5/PHOTO-2026-02-28-16-51-16.jpg?t=1772307824)

body:
# A note from the Softwars

Another day, another software sell off caused by something Claude did. We’re on the other side of the weekend now, and at this point I’m not really sure what it even was.

Or if you believe [some](https://substack.com/redirect/41bc1db9-f9e2-47d5-9469-fb7bb255f671?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ) on Twitter, software crashed because of [me](https://substack.com/redirect/89509b22-e2e7-41b1-ae22-99bc210d1286?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ)… which I find unlikely. *(BTW, semi-anon? Come on, I’m a real person. My username is first\_last. What more do you want!)*

Whatever the cause, this time it led to the 2nd worst day [on record](https://substack.com/redirect/b7224775-9583-4046-bff6-dae71c537302?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ) for software vs semis. The market has pretty much left software for dead. Due to some combination of labs eating their lunch, free cash flow falling precipitously, or terminal value being literally zero.

And look, I can’t for a minute claim that software is doing itself many favors. Neither with their results, nor with their messaging. Calling agents parasites and freeloaders, threatening to tax access to agents, does not inspire confidence that the leaders of these companies understand the world that’s coming.

Claude has shown us a future in which software is far more capable than ever before. No amount of marketing will change that and you can’t bury your head in the sand. The more you fight it, the more that the world will build around you. Which is the worst possible outcome!

Existing software vendors play a critical role for businesses. They’re the hub that organizes and manages how work gets done. The challenge for software is that this entire system was built with the idea that workers were exclusively human.

We know of course that’s no longer the case, and as workloads shift from humans to agents, these systems *must* not just play nice, but actively support the work of agents.

Because this is what’s coming for the ratio of agent to human work.

[![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!X1dm!,w_519,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fe59a5f4c-d0b9-423c-965d-05a5557e0137_1200x618.png)](https://substack.com/redirect/ddf365f2-a55a-478b-bd3d-5e48f4fa64d4?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ)

The market has come to a conclusion that software will not succeed. Whether because of a lack of [capability](https://substack.com/redirect/4f8026bb-aa63-4baf-86df-126d53a9ecea?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ), a lack of will, or ironically, a lack of agency.

I’ve been working on a much longer essay that paints a picture of the future of software in an age of abundant intelligence, but this [tweet](https://substack.com/redirect/6f97ad37-9daa-4337-99c0-72c10bd65fb8?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ) inspired me to post a bit ahead of that.

[![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!Fiyh!,w_1100,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Ff56dbb60-628d-4fa1-bd35-01d5833b85a7_960x276.png)](https://substack.com/redirect/1154673d-3d13-4d12-aa95-6f912a020cbb?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ)

This is a startlingly negative view on the state of software, and specifically on two businesses whose software provides the backbone of a huge percentage of the world’s businesses (and those not running on these are running on even *more legacy* vendors, for the most part.)

So how is it that while the TAM of software has grown 10x, and almost everything that will serve that explosive demand has yet to be built, that the market has decided the companies at the center of these ecosystems are terminal zeroes?

How do y

subject: Dead Companies Walking
body:
# Dead Companies Walking

Tomasz Tunguz

Venture Capitalist at [Theory Ventures](https://6a50e11d.click.convertkit-mail2.com/wvulv0l734sghkmqn82i7hnq2okxxs8hq36k2/3ohphkh3xo3x73fr/aHR0cHM6Ly90aGVvcnkudmVudHVyZXM=)

“[Silicon Valley] is the biggest, most volatile petri dish of raw capitalism on the planet.” So what lessons does a successful short-seller living here have? As founder of Crown Capital Management, Scott Fearon has [shorted the stocks of over 200 companies](https://6a50e11d.click.convertkit-mail2.com/wvulv0l734sghkmqn82i7hnq2okxxs8hq36k2/reh8hohmk2mk0kt2/aHR0cHM6Ly93d3cuYW1hem9uLmNvbS9EZWFkLUNvbXBhbmllcy1XYWxraW5nLU9wcG9ydHVuaXR5LVVuZXhwZWN0ZWQvZHAvMTEzNzI3OTY0OA==).

In his book *[Dead Companies Walking](https://6a50e11d.click.convertkit-mail2.com/wvulv0l734sghkmqn82i7hnq2okxxs8hq36k2/reh8hohmk2mk0kt2/aHR0cHM6Ly93d3cuYW1hem9uLmNvbS9EZWFkLUNvbXBhbmllcy1XYWxraW5nLU9wcG9ydHVuaXR5LVVuZXhwZWN0ZWQvZHAvMTEzNzI3OTY0OA==)*, Fearon distills three decades of meetings with executives into six failure modes :

> Despite their differences, they all failed because their leaders made one or more of six common mistakes that I look for :
>
> 1. They learned from only the recent past.
> 2. They relied too heavily on a formula for success.
> 3. They misread or alienated their customers.
> 4. They fell victim to a mania.
> 5. They failed to adapt to tectonic shifts in their industries.
> 6. They were physically or emotionally removed from their companies’ operations.

The hairpin turn from SaaS to AI amplifies each.

**Learning only from the recent past.** Software moves in 20-year waves. Mainframe, then client/server, then SaaS. When these waves come, they create bull markets. As they wane, growth flattens & multiples collapse. [SaaS multiples have been flat for three years](https://6a50e11d.click.convertkit-mail2.com/wvulv0l734sghkmqn82i7hnq2okxxs8hq36k2/08hwh9h2no2ndvcl/aHR0cHM6Ly90b210dW5ndXouY29tLzIwMjUtMTAtMjctZ3Jvd3RoLXByZW1pdW0tbXVsdGlwbGVzLw==).

**Relying too heavily on a formula for success.** Sales motions have changed because of dramatic growth rates in product-led growth & multi-million dollar lands. Many of the rules around efficiencies & quotas no longer apply.

**Misreading or alienating customers.** Customers want to be AI native. They are willing to pay huge sums for education & solutions. Budgets have exploded with [41% of AI spend net new](https://6a50e11d.click.convertkit-mail2.com/wvulv0l734sghkmqn82i7hnq2okxxs8hq36k2/8ghqhohow0owldsk/aHR0cHM6Ly90b210dW5ndXouY29tL2J1ZGdldC1mb3ItYWkv). Selling the same software application that no longer solves the customer’s pain point is a path to churn.

**Falling victim to a mania.** The AI hype cycle creates pressure to ship half-baked features. Announcing an AI roadmap isn’t the same as delivering value. This distinction will become increasingly stark as long-running agents enter the workforce in 2026.

**Failing to adapt to tectonic shifts.** If ever this were true, it’s true today.

**Being physically or emotionally removed.** Teams who don’t use AI daily miss the pace of change. The technology moves too fast for quarterly strategy reviews. If leadership isn’t prompting Claude or GPT every day, they’re already behind.

Cognitive biases are always hard to see in ourselves. A short seller’s mirror is a useful one at this moment in AI.

subject: The Most Expensive Dysfunction in B2B Product Companies
body:
# The Most Expensive Dysfunction in B2B Product Companies

Someone recently said something to me that I haven’t been able to shake. We were talking about a product team (a good one, by most measures) that had been heads-down building for months. They were shipping features, clearing the backlog, hitting their sprint goals. And yet the business wasn’t moving. Worse, the team didn’t realize that without that connection, the business would eventually stop scaling.

The phrase they used was:

> # **“We have to force the work back into connection with reality.”**

I love this phrase because of the word “force.” Not “nudge.” Not “align.” Force. It implies that the natural state of product work is *disconnected* from reality, that the drift happens on its own, and reconnecting requires deliberate, sometimes uncomfortable effort. And honestly? That tracks with everything I’ve seen over ~25 years of building software.

I’ve been writing about this problem, from different angles, for years now. So I want to use this post to pull those threads together into a single argument, because the phrase captures a pattern I keep coming back to: the gap between what product teams do and what the business needs is the single most expensive dysfunction in B2B product companies. If you’re new here, this is a crash course. If you’ve been around a while, it’s a reminder of why this stuff matters so much.

---

### What Disconnection Looks Like

Let’s start at the top. During my job search last year, I had a conversation with a CEO who described their last head of product as “the worst kind of nothing, an expensive nothing.” That phrase hit hard, and it wasn’t an isolated sentiment. I kept hearing variations of it across multiple CEO conversations: an impatience with how long it takes product leaders to create impact, a growing belief that the function hasn’t delivered ROI.

I wrote about this in [The Unimpactful PM](https://substack.com/redirect/66dc8cc3-6b95-4025-9b8b-512a30ff4c99?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ), and the pattern I kept seeing was structural: there are fundamentally 3 assets within a product company:

* product vision
* R&D resources
* the P&L statement

And you need to control at least one to have any shot at impact. Most product leaders who are deemed unimpactful never got the ability to pull any of these levers. The work was disconnected from reality not because the people were bad, but because the scaffolding for impact didn’t exist.

But even when the structural conditions are right, the drift still happens. It usually starts with teams losing their sense of direction.

---

### Why Teams Drift

I picked up a piece of trivia from a podcast a while back: the word “orientation” comes from The Orient (the East). In olden times, when a traveler was lost, they situated themselves by confirming they knew which way east was. To be “oriented” means to know where you are relative to your ultimate goal. I wrote a short post about this called [Disoriented Teams](https://substack.com/redirect/1bd39777-b216-4490-b9a2-dd171ff19b77?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ), and the core observation was this: as leaders, we spend enormous energy trying to make oriented teams more effective (better metrics reviews, tighter execution, faster cycles). But we underinvest in the lower-hanging fruit: getting *disoriented* teams re-oriented. A disoriented team isn’t just underperforming - it’s creating drag on the entire org.

So what keeps teams oriented? Strategy. But not just any strategy. A *coherent* one. After the Disoriented Teams post, a reader asked me: “are there systematic practices to prevent disoriented teams in the first place?” That question led to [Staying Synced on Strategy](https://substack.com/redirect/a6ff5efa-1ad2-4283-9f78-559467fd256c?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ), where I laid out 4 dimensions of strategic coherence:

* **legibility** -
