# new blog post: ​moving away from Tailwind, and learning to structure my CSS​

one post this week:

## [Moving away from Tailwind, and learning to structure my CSS](https://60787c41.click.convertkit-mail4.com/qdue872z9eh7h45mdn2clh8gexpvgu4hw2lv/owhkhqhwvn6xrobv/aHR0cHM6Ly9qdm5zLmNhL2Jsb2cvMjAyNi8wNS8xNS9tb3ZpbmctYXdheS1mcm9tLXRhaWx3aW5kLS1hbmQtbGVhcm5pbmctdG8tc3RydWN0dXJlLW15LWNzcy0v)

Hello! 8 years ago, I [wrote excitedly about discovering Tailwind](https://60787c41.click.convertkit-mail4.com/qdue872z9eh7h45mdn2clh8gexpvgu4hw2lv/z2hghnhev7k530sp/aHR0cHM6Ly9qdm5zLmNhL2Jsb2cvMjAxOC8xMS8wMS90YWlsd2luZC0td3JpdGUtY3NzLXdpdGhvdXQtdGhlLWNzcy8=).

At that time I really had no idea how to structure my CSS code and given the
choice between a pile of complete chaos and Tailwind, I was really happy to choose
Tailwind. It helped me make a lot of tiny sites!

I spent the last week or so migrating a couple of sites away from Tailwind and
towards more semantic HTML + vanilla CSS, and it was SO fun and SO interesting,
so here are some things I learned!

As usual I’m not a full-time frontend developer and so all of my CSS learning
has happened in fits and starts over many years.

### it turns out Tailwind taught me a lot

When I started thinking about structuring CSS, I was intimidated at first: I’m
not very good at structuring my CSS! But then I started reading blog posts
talking about how to structure CSS (like [A whole cascade of layers](https://60787c41.click.convertkit-mail4.com/qdue872z9eh7h45mdn2clh8gexpvgu4hw2lv/p8heh9h40d2rzriq/aHR0cHM6Ly93d3cubWlyaWFtc3V6YW5uZS5jb20vMjAyMi8wOS8wNi9sYXllcnMv) or [How I write CSS in 2024](https://60787c41.click.convertkit-mail4.com/qdue872z9eh7h45mdn2clh8gexpvgu4hw2lv/x0hph6he6zpkwob5/aHR0cHM6Ly9qYWNvYmIubnljL3dyaXRpbmcvaG93LWktd3JpdGUtY3NzLWluLTIwMjQ=))
and I realized a couple of things:

1. Every CSS code base has a bunch of different things going on (layouts! fonts! colours! common components!)
2. It’s extremely useful to have systems or guidelines to manage each of those things, otherwise things descend into chaos
3. Tailwind has systems for some of these, and I already know those systems! Maybe I can imitate the systems I like!

For example, Tailwind has:

- a reset stylesheet
- a [colour palette](https://60787c41.click.convertkit-mail4.com/qdue872z9eh7h45mdn2clh8gexpvgu4hw2lv/6qheh8hlgw5x7rfo/aHR0cHM6Ly9qdm5zLmNhL2Jsb2cvMjAyNi8wNS8wNC9jc3MtY29sb3VyLXBhbGV0dGVzLw==)
- a [font scale](https://60787c41.click.convertkit-mail4.com/qdue872z9eh7h45mdn2clh8gexpvgu4hw2lv/kkhmh6hnqe5zlvul/aHR0cHM6Ly92Mi50YWlsd2luZGNzcy5jb20vZG9jcy9mb250LXNpemU=)

### the systems I’m going to talk about

I’m going to talk about a few aspects of my CSS codebase and my thoughts so far
what kind of rules I want to impose on the codebase for each one. Some of them
are copied from Tailwind and some aren’t.

1. reset
2. components
3. colours
4. font sizes
5. utility classes
6. the base
7. spacing
8. responsive design
9. the build system

### 1. reset

I just copied Tailwind’s “[preflight styles](https://60787c41.click.convertkit-mail4.com/qdue872z9eh7h45mdn2clh8gexpvgu4hw2lv/58hvh7hg80n3m8s6/aHR0cHM6Ly92Mi50YWlsd2luZGNzcy5jb20vZG9jcy9wcmVmbGlnaHQ=)”
by going into `tailwind.css` and copying the first 200 lines or so.

I noticed that I’ve developed a relationship with Tailwind’s CSS reset over time,
for example Tailwind sets `box-sizing: border-box` on every element (which means
that an element’s width includes its padding):

```
* { box-sizing: border-box; }

```
I think it would be a real adjustment for me to switch to writing CSS without
these, and I’m sure there are lots of other things in the Tailwind reset (like `html {line-height: 1.5;}`) that I’m subconsciously used to and don’t even realize are
there.

### 2. components

This next part is the bulk of the CSS!

related to Vue or React components. (though there might not actually be any Javascrip

# Billy Bang

**Welcome back to Flow State,** the instrumental music newsletter. You’re on the free tier – to unlock our daily playlists, weekly mixes, and support our work, upgrade today:

[Upgrade to paid](https://substack..vPbCQrUMROEZKQQtoo6IXznTZmnoUj3W8sshQlcQcYE?&utm_medium=email&utm_source=subscribe-widget&utm_content=199148394)

---

**Today we’re listening to Billy Bang, an American violinist and composer. He was born in Alabama in 1947 and moved at a young age to the Bronx, where he grew up. At 18 he was drafted into the army and served a tour of duty in Vietnam around the time of the Tet Offensive.¹ Upon his discharge, he spent time studying law and participating in activism until committing himself to the violin. He was immersed in New York’s free jazz scene, going on to collaborate with artists like Don Cherry and Sun Ra (whose Arkestra he played in). In the early 2000s, he released jazz albums into which he channeled his memories of war; he [told the Jazz Times](https://substack.com/redirect/85f844cb-a2eb-4ce8-a0ef-a016b85e8266?j=eyJ1IjoiZnZlciJ9.8N73-dqQlrWLx3o5gPfyirClhk7-cxP_NqOwOQYAApk) that following his discharge, “I lived in Vietnam, totally, all the time.”** ***Vietnam: Reflections*****, which came out in 2005, reaches for a kind of post-traumatic peace, and features Vietnamese musicians playing traditional instruments and songs, a kind of international encounter Bang [described](https://substack.com/redirect/85f844cb-a2eb-4ce8-a0ef-a016b85e8266?j=eyJ1IjoiZnZlciJ9.8N73-dqQlrWLx3o5gPfyirClhk7-cxP_NqOwOQYAApk) as “the opposite of war.”** ***Reflections*** **was the followup to** ***Vietnam: The Aftermath*****, which came out in 2001, with faster tempos and expressions of strife.**

***Vietnam: Reflections*** **- Billy Bang (70m, vocals on even numbered tracks)  
[Spotify](https://substack.com/redirect/cfe04e9c-09bc-4d21-93ed-36c0dc410b8d?j=eyJ1IjoiZnZlciJ9.8N73-dqQlrWLx3o5gPfyirClhk7-cxP_NqOwOQYAApk) / [Apple Music](https://substack.com/redirect/54b62f2a-7e60-4371-8567-c33024de301b?j=eyJ1IjoiZnZlciJ9.8N73-dqQlrWLx3o5gPfyirClhk7-cxP_NqOwOQYAApk) / [YouTube Music](https://substack.com/redirect/2764efb1-80e6-45bd-8ed0-fe3770a39747?j=eyJ1IjoiZnZlciJ9.8N73-dqQlrWLx3o5gPfyirClhk7-cxP_NqOwOQYAApk) / [Amazon Music](https://substack.com/redirect/99a2d6d8-42a0-4931-b19d-92fc080b5623?j=eyJ1IjoiZnZlciJ9.8N73-dqQlrWLx3o5gPfyirClhk7-cxP_NqOwOQYAApk) / [Tidal](https://substack.com/redirect/7fd7d6b7-d91c-4f47-b898-e69b2b39c343?j=eyJ1IjoiZnZlciJ9.8N73-dqQlrWLx3o5gPfyirClhk7-cxP_NqOwOQYAApk)**

# Claude 201 for GTM operators: context files, skills, and the tools that connect

> [![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!mP2n!,w_1100,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fe6797aab-f024-45a1-8777-41833cd30286_1920x1080.png "")](https://substack.com/redirect/e1513dd1-7947-4fe8-a5d1-52a58dc13c38?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ)
>
> Your team’s account plans are built in PowerPoint, presented once, and never opened again. By the time the plan is done it’s already wrong. Contacts have changed, signals have moved, and your biggest accounts are quietly testing competitors. **[Kandir](https://substack.com/redirect/eb314232-ebc3-4199-b153-dbbe3bd7a60c?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ)** builds a living, signal-enriched account plan in under 5 minutes, backed by real intel from sellers who’ve already sold to your target accounts. **[Try it free for 7 days](https://substack.com/redirect/eb314232-ebc3-4199-b153-dbbe3bd7a60c?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ)**
>
> **Thanks to our sponsors who keep this email free. Interested in sponsoring these emails? See our [partnership options here](https://substack.com/redirect/48d573c0-5e18-4deb-bfe5-06fd6cd5a669?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ)**

---

Most GTM operators are getting value from Claude. They are also leaving most of it on the table.

The typical pattern is querying Claude the way you would query a smarter Google, except with better follow-up questions. One session, one task, no persistent context. The output is only as good as what you explained in that window. Close the tab and everything resets. Open a new conversation and start over.

The 201 move is different. It is building a configured working environment that Claude inhabits whenever you start a conversation. That environment has three layers: a context file that tells Claude what it needs to know about your business, skills that encode how you want recurring tasks executed, and MCP connections that give Claude live access to your tools. Each layer compounds the others.

This is not a setup-once-and-forget configuration. It is a working environment you refine over time, and it gets materially better the more specific you make it. A generic setup produces generic output. A properly configured environment produces output you can send.

---

*A new AI for GTM course starting next week. There’s still time to join.*

[Enroll](https://substack.com/redirect/40fb95ef-63d8-469a-9ad2-7989b23d6c13?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ)

---

## The three layers

To get Claude working for your GTM use cases I suggest setting up at least these three: Context, Skills, and MCPs. These are specific to the Claude ecosystem.

Think of it this way. Context files are what Claude knows. Skills are what Claude does. MCPs are what Claude can reach. Operate with all three configured and Claude functions less like a smart text generator and more like a second operator who already knows your business.

Most GTM operators building with Claude today have partial versions of all three. They have a Project with some documents uploaded, a handful of prompts they reuse, and maybe one or two connections active. The gap between that and a properly configured environment is not technical complexity. It is specificity. The question is not whether you have these layers. It is whether what you have built is specific enough to be useful at the task level.

Before going deeper on each layer, it is worth being precise about which Claude product you are working in, because the mechanics differ enough to matter.

# Linear #177: Vori: The Grocery OS, Vertical GTM Workshop, Labor > Seats

Today’s newsletter is sponsored by Xplor Pay. Most AI conversations focus on features, but long-term advantage comes from infrastructure. Clean payments data, system control, and flexible architecture determine how intelligently your platform can scale over time.

[![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!uCFD!,w_566,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F4accd398-f1f2-4656-8a68-667e821f9216_472x158.gif)](https://substack.com/redirect/5ebc9c49-aaf2-4576-89a3-95c939d8f425?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ)

Shaped by lessons from growing and scaling 20+ vertical SaaS platforms, this guide explores what AI readiness actually means for software providers. Read the guide.

---

[![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!euYE!,w_1100,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F0d398993-a44b-46a8-a68d-0c9697868b8c_1875x625.jpeg "")](https://substack.com/redirect/f7162c7b-ceeb-4585-9a91-b304265242f2?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ)

Most people will look at Vori and say: “grocery software.”

That is technically correct and strategically useless.

What Vori is really building is an operating system for independent grocers — one that sits across the front store, the back office, and increasingly the money flow itself. That matters because grocery is one of those giant, messy, low-glamour industries where software has historically lagged, margins are thin, labor is constant, and the best companies win by helping operators make dozens of tiny decisions better every single day.

[![This Pitch Deck Got Grocery Startup Vori $10M for Inventory Software - Business Insider](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!derO!,w_1100,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fb60e8d23-1807-4fc7-8e64-9cd01cff573b_800x454.jpeg "This Pitch Deck Got Grocery Startup Vori $10M for Inventory Software - Business Insider")](https://substack.com/redirect/6c5a2a02-cc80-433c-bc43-f155a882b369?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ)

### The founder story

The company began in 2019 from an idea sparked by Brandon Hill, whose parents spent roughly 40 years in grocery and consumer products and saw firsthand how little the industry had modernized. That is exactly the kind of founder-market fit I pay attention to: not “we discovered a market in a spreadsheet,” but “we lived close enough to the pain to know the software was broken.”

And the early timeline has the right flavor.

The initial iOS app was built in 12 days. The first product was scanned in October 2019. The first wholesale order submitted through Vori was just $200 of kombucha. I love stories like that because they remind you that every vertical software companies rarely begin with giant visions in practice. They begin with one small workflow that matters deeply to one specific operator.

[![About Us & Our Mission | Vori](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!5MrD!,w_500,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fbb868ead-4fbd-4b5a-b22e-a1791f01a95b_500x400.webp "About Us & Our Mission | Vori")](https://substack.com/redirect/edd2f7fc-dca9-42d2-a8a5-227a94c692ae?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ)

### The wedge

Vori did not try to become “the everything platform for grocery” on day one.

The early heartbeat of the business was very operational: products getting scanned, orders getting written, inventory getting understood, stores getting a modern interface for core retail tasks. That is what good wedge products do. They enter through a daily pain point. They get adopted because they are useful, not

# [AINews] Codex Rises, Claude Meters Programmatic Usage

It has been a tale of two cities in the past 3 weeks since the launch of GPT 5.5; while the finance folks fall in love with [Anthropic’s growth](https://substack.com/redirect/5e405977-98ea-41f8-a042-dc17c4276a12?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ) and [CFO](https://substack.com/redirect/dbb493e4-c0fb-4eee-9a0d-9b8fce421ac1?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ) ahead of its likely October IPO, there has been a notable rise in pro-Codex sentiment among AI Engineers, likely a combination of GPT 5.5 being a really good (in [some scenarios Mythos-tier](https://substack.com/redirect/f474e762-292e-4a34-adf3-3981b8d52913?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ)) model, launch of [Codex for Everything Else](https://substack.com/redirect/a934d72f-b41b-4652-aee7-939f2accc5ac?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ), and, a third thing, which is the trigger for today’s op-ed: more generous limits.

[![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!uqHa!,w_385,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F1f3bb92f-f1bd-4329-9b9c-64c681eec378_1290x874.png "")](https://substack.com/redirect/413f7574-ac60-44e5-9160-a8eae25a29b9?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ)

The messaging for Claude’s pricing change was generally pretty well done, it is simply not what uses of alternative harnesses wanted to hear: [every Claude subscription now gets a monthly credit of API tokens equal to the dollar amount of the Claude subscription plan.](https://substack.com/redirect/65c6bbaf-04cc-4378-ad65-ea5c4f25b83b?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ) So you pay $200, you get BOTH a Claude subscription with its own limits for using Claude on Anthropic-owned harnesses like Claude.ai and Claude Code (“interactive usage”), AND $200 worth of API credits for using Claude everywhere else including `claude-p`, OpenClaw and others (“programmatic usage”).

If things had worked this way from the start, it would have been viewed as a very good deal:

[![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!XQLi!,w_1100,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F148215c3-6a2e-4a77-b243-630d5c9c7247_1228x1640.png)](https://substack.com/redirect/ffa7e7bb-6c8c-4c57-8d15-83c15b04bd80?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ)

However, because of the historical subsidy/pricing advantages (estimated between 70-90% discount from API pricing), people are viewing it [as a “rug pull” of sorts](https://substack.com/redirect/a0d2bc72-1ad5-41cf-a5b8-3578a3e6cdd2?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ) — however it’s nice to have an official policy in place as opposed to the selective targeting of [OpenClaw](https://substack.com/redirect/5e11e087-224c-40ca-ab22-9e626e9e56f9?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ), [OpenCode](https://substack.com/redirect/138dc596-075e-4760-9f23-eacd94791fda?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ), and uncertain status of less popular harnesses.

[![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!w6yx!,w_1100,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F041d6b0a-7ea1-4e96-82ad-750ed4e73f25_1208x1394.png)](https://substack.com/redirect/92c0db26-43ee-4bee-a253-c482b69dddf3?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ)

That these headlines come on the same day as [OpenAI launches their enterprise switch](https://substack.com/redirect/2260c3cc-a64b-44a5-8495-9df91232f1ba?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ) promo is an incredible coincidence:

# Linear #172: The Relationship Between Customer Success & ACV, Hadrius, Early Steps In Transforming Into An AI Comp…

Today’s newsletter is sponsored by [Xplor Pay](https://substack.com/redirect/595a1a16-93d8-40d1-a559-a370078b512e?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ). In their latest case study, they show how a POS provider embedded payments using PayFac as a Service without taking on the burden of compliance, risk, or merchant onboarding.

[![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!Zfhr!,w_550,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fb19e534d-6540-453a-8718-98ee44cf2de9_600x200.gif)](https://substack.com/redirect/595a1a16-93d8-40d1-a559-a370078b512e?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ)

Learn how white-labeled payments, streamlined setup, and flat-rate pricing helped the platform improve the experience while unlocking new recurring revenue. Read the full case study.

---

Alright, let’s get to it…

[![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!f2gY!,w_1100,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Ffc8a469e-0307-4c14-9375-f80f9dec2385_1875x625.jpeg)](https://substack.com/redirect/221c3566-c78f-4568-b729-d60057b94ca4?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ)

> How much time/effort would you say your onboarding takes for your vSaaS?  
> What about normal support?  
> Does that vary by plan/price tier and approximate ACV?

I love this question because most founders obsess over CAC and ACV on the way in…

But they don’t spend enough time thinking about the **delivery burden** after the contract is signed.

And in vertical SaaS, that’s where a lot of the bodies are buried.

Here’s the benchmark they sent me:

* **ACV:** ~$5K
* **Sales process:** 1–3 hours on Zoom calls to close
* **Onboarding:** 5–10 hours of training + 5–10 hours of data migration
* **Total onboarding:** 10–20 hours per logo
* **Ongoing support:** ~1 hour per month
* **Observation:** for every **100% increase in ACV**, onboarding time only goes up about **20%**

Honestly? That’s pretty healthy.

And it highlights something a lot of founders miss:

**Implementation should not scale linearly with ACV.**

If your ACV doubles and your onboarding doubles too, you’re not building leverage.  
You’re just selling a nicer version of services.

The goal is not to eliminate implementation. The goal is to make sure that as ACV goes up, **implementation effort grows much more slowly than revenue**.

That is exactly what this persons data suggested.

At roughly **$5K ACV**, spending **10–20 total hours** to get a customer live can make sense if:

* the customer retains well,
* support stays contained,
* and onboarding creates a durable moat rather than a recurring headache.

What would worry me?

If the same customer also needed endless custom setup, weekly handholding, or bespoke migration work that never got productized.

That’s where people fool themselves.  
They call it “white glove.”  
What it really means is “we haven’t built the product yet.”

So how do I think about it?

### **ACV doesn’t just shape GTM. It also shapes implementation architecture.**

Low ACV often pushes one toward PLG or marketing-led motions; mid-range ACV leans inside sales; high ACV usually forces higher-touch selling. This isn’t law it’s just what I typically see. The same basic logic applies after the sale. Higher ACV generally supports more human touch — but if you’re doing it right, the effort should rise sublinearly, not one-for-one with revenue.

Here’s the simple mental model I’d use:

### **Tier 1: Low ACV / light-touch**

Think small accounts, simpler workflows, lower switching cost.

* Standardized onboarding
* Template migration
* Group training / office hours
* Async support first
* Product does most of the work

# The Incentive Map Every Data Platform PM Should Draw

#### About Our Contributing Expert

### Anna Bergevin | Sr. Manager Data & AI Product Management

[![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!tWMR!,w_1100,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fc25a368c-b1e6-48c5-ad41-24141b453697_1600x900.png)](https://substack.com/redirect/3a993ba2-e13c-4f0b-855a-607667e0d270?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ)

[Anna Bergevin](https://substack.com/redirect/ccdefeb2-f91b-43ae-a91a-b0b1dee1d2ec?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ) is a data and AI product leader currently serving as Sr. Manager of Data & AI Product Management at *Children’s Mercy*. She **leads platform product strategy** focused on enabling secure, compliant, and scalable data systems that power analytics and AI across the enterprise.

Previously, she **led global Data & AI platform product** initiatives at *ResMed*, guiding roadmap and governance strategy for a distributed engineering organization supporting business teams in over 140 countries. Her work centers on semantic modeling, metric standardization, metadata-driven governance, and designing data products that balance regulatory rigor with innovation.

Anna writes and speaks about data product management, sociotechnical AI adoption, and the discipline required to build enterprise data systems that scale on *[When Data Met Product](https://substack.com/redirect/97f3cd73-d49a-424f-aeab-ea69136cef87?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ)*. She believes the future of AI depends less on model sophistication and more on clear definitions, strong governance, and product-led stewardship of data infrastructure. We’re thrilled to feature her unique insights on [Modern Data 101](https://substack.com/redirect/c2cd858c-f511-463f-a1ce-7c7de3920c7d?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ)!

> *We actively collaborate with data experts to bring the best resources to a [15,000+ strong community](https://substack.com/redirect/2b91e019-99b9-42e9-b601-41c270264885?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ) of data leaders and practitioners. If you have something to share, reach out!  
> 🫴🏻 Share your ideas and work: [community@moderndata101.com](https://substack.com/redirect/2bd30cb2-44a0-4dfa-8a7d-2649c652e97c?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ)*

###### **\*Note: Opinions expressed in contributions are not our own and are only curated by us for broader access and discussion. All submissions are vetted for quality & relevance. We keep it information-first and do not support any promotions, paid or otherwise.**

---

### Let’s Dive In

[![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!8PaR!,w_1100,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F89a0c961-13e5-44d4-943d-e182ac67abcd_2185x1238.png)](https://substack.com/redirect/1eca7cd0-41a6-4aa9-b3b8-9d0fb6def288?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ)

Data platform product managers have an impossible job: **drive adoption and impact without formal authority over the teams they serve.**

To succeed, you need to think like a game theorist. [Game theory](https://substack.com/redirect/911ad644-9ea2-429c-8ac6-a2dbc6b20580?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ), the study of strategic decision-making, assumes people act rationally given their incentives and constraints. Behavior that may appear confusing on the surface makes sense if we dig deeper to understand the incentives that drive their behavior.

The problem isn’t that your stakeholders are irrational. It’s that you often don’t understand the games they’re playing.

# NEW: easier LinkedIn accounts connection for your team and clients

Hi Danny,

If you run Extrovert for an agency or a bigger team, this one is for you. Three updates that make managing other people's LinkedIn accounts much easier:

This one is the big one for agencies. You no longer need your client's LinkedIn password to connect their account.

Generate a connect link, send it to them by email or any other way. They open the link and see one thing: a form to connect their LinkedIn (extension or login and password). No Extrovert signup, no dashboard, just the connect form. They plug in their account and they're done.

The link only works for connecting. Nobody can use it to disconnect or change anything else.

![](https://extrovert.intercom-mail.com/i/o/d108y8pl/2380749238/4522a137740dc7ece45c8f8bd463/Oleg-s+video+%F0%9F%90%8B.gif?expires=1790857026&signature=fc215cac6fb0288510454288600812177e6e5874768542207cf87e526c7b6774&req=diMvFs56lINcUfMW2XS%2FiXTNHnEhkvWzIxjul9B4lAAjfBdsBKY%3D%0A)

# Admins can now connect LinkedIn for any teammate

Before, you could only connect LinkedIn for managed accounts. Now you can do it for anyone who shared a campaign with you too: a client, a coworker, a teammate.

Open their profile, click connect, and use the extension or login and password flow you already know. Same as connecting your own.

# You can also change their daily limits and working hours

Set their daily comment and connect request caps, set the hours when Extrovert runs for them.



Let me know what you think and have a great rest of the week!

Oleg

# Equals customer update - February 2026

Hi there,

February update from team Equals!

**Analyst**

Ask real questions about your data and get fully auditable spreadsheets in seconds: complete with transparent SQL, formulas, and calculations you can trust. If you’d like to try Analyst please just reply to this message to get started.

Since the initial launch last month we’ve updated the core model to Opus 4.6 making Analyst faster and (significantly) smarter. We’ve continued to expand core capabilities adding better support for charting, a new final audit loop, better ability for filling large ranges, better handling of large conversations, and more.

**Analyst in Slack**

Ask questions about your business directly from Slack. Analyst will work out the answer and send you a link to a workbook. To enable, navigate to Settings> [Workspace Settings](https://equals-0e27fab325a3.intercom-clicks.com/via/e?ob=sfXAwnrxixrX4Dp4aNvhDBM4rtdkK0iZ0xgK%2BDEo%2FO8PMqSbBA4SbA5cHAdlvIcx&h=22b57e848f98ec65241a6891cd70bf8259824b05-gghxukmi_215473026211680&l=644beeda37277c020bbf5d2de4f55d7bda484d72-198294587) > Analyst Slack integration. **Bug fixes and improvements**

Running a query will no longer lock your sheet and dashboard while the results are saving. We also added support for range references like B2:2 and support for absent arguments in formulas.

**Date filters**

We’re still working away on date filters for dashboards. We have a first version we’re using internally now and hope to open up this month. This is taking longer than expected, we appreciate your patience.

More soon,

Ben

# Nvidia – The Inference Kingdom Expands

[![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!dC_X!,w_1100,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Ff5522a45-77c1-40f8-94c0-395f272b8db1_2709x1815.png)](https://substack.com/redirect/b5657e15-7b54-46a8-b6b0-6b014d65fb86?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ)

Source: Nvidia

At GTC 2026, Nvidia delivered an event packed full of ground breaking announcements. Nvidia’s pace of innovation is not showing any signs of slowing, as they introduced three entirely new systems this year: Groq LPX, Vera ETL256, and STX. Also announced were updates to Nvidia’s Kyber rack architecture system, CPO making its debut for scale-up networking with the unveiling of the Rubin Ultra NVL576 and Feynman NVL1152 multi-rack systems. Early hints on Feynman’s architecture was also a key topic. A Jensen callout for [InferenceX during the keynote was a highlight.](https://substack.com/redirect/bd9f984c-9048-449c-94c3-54576022f0ec?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ)

[![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!3JUq!,w_1100,h_618,c_fill,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/l_play_button_usfui2,w_144,e_colorize:0/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-video.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fvideo_upload%2Fpost%2F191561008%2F0733605b-055b-4f8a-a641-510cab67c233%2Ftranscoded-00001.png)](https://substack.com/redirect/e89c1ec5-162d-4098-94b4-546c51ab38ce?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ)

This is our GTC 2026 recap, and we will address many of the key questions that have been left unanswered by Nvidia. Specifically, we will go through the LPX rack and LP30 chip and explain how attention and feed forward network disaggregation (AFD) works; more details on the various rack architectures behind NVL144, NVL576, and NVL1152 and clarify just how much optics will be inserted as well as the rationale behind the dense Vera ETL256. The next generation Kyber rack had some big updates and some hidden details.

## Groq

First up is the Groq LPU. One of the most significant recent events in AI infrastructure was Nvidia’s “acquisition” of Groq. Strictly speaking, Nvidia paid Groq $20B to license their IP and hire most the team. This functions almost as an acquisition, though its structure technically falls short of it being legally considered as one, thereby simplifying or obviating the need for regulatory approvals. Given Nvidia’s market share, if this transaction were structured as a full acquisition and were put to anti-trust review, such a transaction would likely not go through. The other benefit is that it avoids a drawn-out transaction closing process. Nvidia got instant access to Groq’s IP and people. This is why, less than four months after the deal was announced, Nvidia already has a system concept that is being integrated into the Vera Rubin inference stack.

Let’s now go through a refresher on the LPU architecture to see how Groq’s LPU complements Nvidia’s GPU. For more details [see our original Groq piece.](https://substack.com/redirect/9e2b8608-876e-4015-9ce1-de38eec8283d?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ) The premise from that piece remains unchanged: the standalone Groq LPU system is not economical for serving tokens at scale, but it can serve tokens very quickly which can demand a large market premium. This is the premise behind how LPU fits into a disaggregated decode system.

## LPU chip

Groq’s first and only publicly announced LPU architecture was detailed in their ISCA 2020 paper. Unlike typical hardware architectures connecting many general-purpose cores, Groq re-organized the architecture into groups of single-purpose units connecting to other groups of different purposes, and they named the groups “slices.” Between functional units are streaming registers, scratchpad SRAM for functional units to pass data to each other. subject: Surpresas boas — e seguras 💐
body:
# Surpresas boas — e seguras 💐

![Banner XP Investimentos - Dia das mães](https://mfe.xpi.com.br/authentication-assets/emails/xp/headers/header-mothers-day-v2.png) O Dia das Mães está chegando - um momento especial de celebrar e presentear quem a gente ama. Para
 ajudar você a aproveitar essa data da forma que merece, reunimos algumas dicas de segurança para
 fazer suas compras com tranquilidade, evitar golpes e proteger quem é importante para você.

![Banner XP Investimentos - Dia das mães - Cartão Temporário](https://mfe.xpi.com.br/authentication-assets/emails/xp/presentation/temporary-card.png) ![Ícone de segurança](https://mfe.xpi.com.br/authentication-assets/emails/common/security-green-icon.png) Agora, para não cair em golpes, siga essas dicas:

![Ícone de alerta](https://mfe.xpi.com.br/authentication-assets/emails/xp/icons/alert-circle-icon.png)

Pagamento de taxa para receber um presente?
 Desconfie!

Se você ou alguém da sua família receber uma entrega surpresa e, para ficar com o presente,
 for preciso pagar uma taxa ou permitir que tirem uma foto para confirmar o recebimento,
 cuidado: é golpe.

![Ícone de monitor](https://mfe.xpi.com.br/authentication-assets/emails/xp/icons/monitor-icon.png)

Na internet, verifique se o site é oficial

Antes de comprar, confirme se o endereço do site é realmente o da loja. Evite realizar
 pagamentos clicando em links de anúncios em redes sociais ou recebidos por mensagem.

![Ícone de usuário](https://mfe.xpi.com.br/authentication-assets/emails/xp/icons/user-check-icon.png)

Sempre revise antes de pagar

Antes de confirmar uma compra via boleto ou PIX, confira valor, nome do recebedor e
 CNPJ/CPF. Se algo estiver diferente do combinado ou do site oficial, não conclua o
 pagamento.

![Ícone de alerta vermelho](https://mfe.xpi.com.br/authentication-assets/emails/common/error-red-icon.png)

**Fui vítima de um golpe.** O que fazer?

Por segurança, entre em contato com o nosso atendimento o quanto antes:

![Ícone de Whatsapp](https://mfe.xpi.com.br/authentication-assets/emails/xp/icons/whatsapp-icon.png) **WhatsApp:** (11) 4935-2720

![Ícone de telefone](https://mfe.xpi.com.br/authentication-assets/emails/xp/icons/phone-calling-icon.png) **Telefone:** (11) 4003-3710 (Capitais/Regiões Metropolitanas) ou  
0800-880-3710 (Demais Localidades)

Compartilhe essas dicas para proteger todos ao seu redor.

![XP Investimentos - Segurança](https://mfe.xpi.com.br/authentication-assets/emails/authentication/xp/footer_xp_v1.png)

# VEON Notes Kyivstar Group Publication of Selected Full Year 2025 Financial Information

![VEONxKyivstar-1](https://hs-9256877.f.hubspotemail.net/hub/9256877/hubfs/VEONxKyivstar-1.jpg?width=700&upscale=true&name=VEONxKyivstar-1.jpg)

**VEON Notes Kyivstar Group Publication of Selected   
Full Year 2025 Financial Information**

**Dubai, January 28, 2026** — VEON Ltd. (Nasdaq: VEON) (“VEON”) notes that Kyivstar Group Ltd. (Nasdaq: KYIV; KYIVW) ( “Kyivstar” or “the Group”), Ukraine’s leading digital operator, has announced the Group’s preliminary estimates of selected unaudited financial information for the year ended December 31, 2025 compared to the Group’s actual financial results for the year ended December 31, 2024.

# Architectural Standards for Data Products and AI Interactions: Emergent & Aligned Patterns

[![Architectural Standards for Data Products and Al Interaction Unifying Purpose, Platform, and Protocol to Scale Intelligence. | Modern Data 101](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!efNX!,w_1100,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F327dd6e2-593e-41b5-87d5-e3e7a0b50299_1362x758.png "Architectural Standards for Data Products and Al Interaction Unifying Purpose, Platform, and Protocol to Scale Intelligence. | Modern Data 101")](https://substack.com/redirect/08bc1afa-9216-42e8-b6da-861c9d2bc820?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ)

Adapted from concepts shared by author(s) | Curated by Modern Data 101

Adapted from concepts shared by Author(s) | Curated by Modern Data 101

## Why Unified Standards Emerged

Before we speak of protocols, platforms, or products, we must reduce the system to its irreducible parts. Strip away branding, tooling, and terminology, and what remains is intelligence attempting to ***act*** in an environment.

Intelligence, by definition, operates on context. Remove structured context, and the model substitutes probability for truth. But context alone is insufficient. Intelligence must also have a ***defined surface through which it can act***.

And even action requires constraint. Without that, intelligence becomes either paralysed or dangerous.

So any system that enables AI must solve three things:

* structured context,
* controlled action, and
* bounded execution.

---

### Systems Scale Only Through Abstraction

Systems do not scale by adding connections but by removing complexity. And **complexity is removed only through abstraction**.

When integrations multiply without a unifying layer, the architecture begins to decay. [Point-to-point connections proliferate until the system resembles a fragile web](https://substack.com/redirect/a680aef4-0aad-44e4-8991-b190bfe8ec38?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ) of dependencies rather than a coherent structure.

As this happens, **context** fragments. Each integration carries its own assumptions, schema, and semantics. What was once a shared understanding becomes a localised interpretation. **Security** follows the same pattern. Without a standard interface, every connection defines its own authentication model, permission logic, and failure modes.

[![SYSTEMS DO NOT SCALE BY ADDING CONNECTIONS, BUT BY REMOVING COMPLEXITY. THE CORE PROBLEM: Intelligence requires structured context, controlled action, and bounded execution. body:
# Why Optical Communication Wins (and Where It Doesn't)

**Issue 168.Subscribers: 86,870**

In the previous [post](https://substack.com/redirect/ac5f6361-30ce-433e-92af-ffb94de29d42?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ), we argued that space is running into a communications bottleneck. Sensors are getting better, constellations denser, and missions more ambitious, but the ability to move data is not scaling automatically with the ability to collect it. This week, it is worth slowing down and asking the obvious follow-up question: why does optical communication win where radio starts to hurt? And, just as important, where does radio still keep the upper hand?

The easiest way to think about the difference is through a terrestrial analogy. The modern internet accelerated when long-distance communications shifted from electrical signals in copper toward light in fiber. Space optical communication uses the same broad idea, except without the fiber: data rides on light, and the light moves through free space between satellites or between space and ground.

While the basic physics of free-space optical (FSO) links have been [understood](https://substack.com/redirect/b6984203-f3a0-443a-acea-cc8392048745?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ) since lasers were invented, doing it in space required decades of maturation. It wasn’t until the terrestrial fiber internet boom perfected high-power, low-cost optical components and aerospace engineers mastered ultra-precise micro-mechanics, that space lasers became viable. Today, optical communications use light to transmit information via lasers, and their [benefits are](https://substack.com/redirect/922390f8-8966-403a-b706-263557ff43ab?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ) “faster, more secure, lighter, and more flexible,” while their main challenges are precise beam accuracy and atmospheric interference such as clouds.

[![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!wlv3!,w_1100,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F88e6eed8-4cb2-4c46-a450-4d935eac8f90_2048x2048.png)](https://substack.com/redirect/e1cd0735-3b6e-42f2-afa8-5f421d330164?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ)

The word “faster” here needs one correction, because it is easy to misunderstand. Optical communication does not mean the information itself magically travels faster than radio. Both are electromagnetic waves with the fundamental limitation of the speed of light. The advantage is that optical systems can support much higher data rates, which means more bits can be delivered in the same contact window.

Why? It comes down to frequency and the mathematical rules of signal modulation. Space radio (RF) typically [operates](https://substack.com/redirect/ffed3a73-e2aa-40ef-8c5d-111ab1cd0153?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ) at up to 40 GHz range. By contrast, optical communication uses near-infrared lasers (like 1550 nm) operating at 193 THz. Optical frequencies are enormously higher than the radio frequencies typically used in space communications. In practical terms, that roughly 10,000-fold increase in carrier frequency gives engineers a much larger signaling space to work with.

It is rooted in the **Shannon-Hartley theorem**, which [defines](https://substack.com/redirect/e8b4b66d-4b9c-4a80-8fb5-eea68bc3a07e?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ) the maximum data rate (capacity, C) of a channel:

[![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!2gbw!,w_402,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F39ffc6f4-f47e-4ca6-8b6a-31cbabe3f538_402x117.png)](https://substack.com/redirect/46f57b6f-e18a-46e1-9c14-e83a71527ccb?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ)

subject: Product Sense Is Talked About. Product Judgment Is Measured.
body:
# Product Sense Is Talked About. Product Judgment Is Measured.

We talk about product sense constantly.

We interview for it.  
We praise people for having it.  
We rarely measure it.

In product, we ship, we learn, we move on.  
But we almost never ask the harder question:

How often am I actually right?

At Amazon, there’s a simple leadership bar: *being right a lot*.  
In product, we reward clarity of narrative far more than accuracy of prediction.

## The missing loop

We write PRDs and success metrics.  
But we almost never make our beliefs explicit in a way that can’t be reinterpreted later.

We don’t write probabilities.  
We don’t lock time horizons.  
We don’t audit confidence.

So confidence compounds, even when it’s wrong.

That’s not a product failure.  
It’s a learning failure.

## A small experiment

A few months ago, I started writing down my predictions before shipping:  
What I thought would happen  
By when  
With what probability

When I compared belief to reality, the results were humbling.

The bets I felt most confident about were often the ones that failed.

I wasn’t lacking product sense.  
I was lacking calibration.

## The Product Judgment Test

So I built a simple tool to measure this.

The Product Judgment Test forces explicit predictions, records outcomes, and scores calibration over time using a weighted Brier score so bigger bets matter more.

It’s not a performance metric.  
It’s a learning loop.

Over time, it shows where you’re overconfident, underconfident, or well calibrated.

## I shared it publicly today

I’ve shared the first version of the Product Judgment Test, along with the Excel and Google Sheet tool.

👉If you want to see how it works, here’s [the LinkedIn post with the details:](https://substack.com/redirect/bac66f24-a737-4a57-bbd3-ef2b2ed5de18?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ)

If you try it, I’d love to hear what surprises you or where it breaks.

If we want better product outcomes, we need better product judgment.  
This is a step in that direction.

subject: Oil, War and the Global Economy: The Market's Narrative in March 2026
body:
# Oil, War and the Global Economy: The Market's Narrative in March 2026

Markets play an expectations game, and in March 2026, we saw the process play out, with all of its upsides and downsides. The month started with a war in the Middle East, which quickly percolated into soaring oil prices and dropping stock prices, but the overwhelming factor was uncertainty about almost every dimension of the war - how long it would last, what permanent changes to oil prices would emerge as a consequence and how global governments and economies would respond to these changes. As we reach the end of the month, rather than getting answers, we face more questions, and not surprisingly, markets are volatile, not just on a day-to-day basis, but in intraday trading, driven as much by rumors and conjecture, as by facts. In keeping with my view that it is during periods of maximal uncertainty that you need perspective and to back to basics, I will focus my attention on market behavior in March, and what we can learn from that behavior, as a precursor for the months to come.

**The Market Narrative in March**

We live in an age of commentary, as self-proclaimed experts offer prognostications, half-baked or otherwise, about what is to come, and the Iran war, with its mix of politics, economics and religion baked in,, has drawn a large and extremely diverse set of expert forecasts. Given the strong priors (about Iran and Trump) that many of these experts bring to the game, it should not be surprising that their views about how the war will play out and the effect on markets is driven by those priors. It is up to markets to reconcile these contradictory perspectives, and come to consensus, and I will try to extract from market behavior what the market narrative is, leading into April 2026, with the recognition that it could be wrong and change overnight in good and bad ways. That said, over the last decade, I have learned that the market is far better at making sense of complexity and uncertainty than experts are, and it behooves us therefore to listen to what it is saying.

*The Oil Price Shock*

As with almost every event in the middle east, the effects of the Iran War played out first in oil prices, and oil has been the lead player in March, surging and volatile, but with disparate impacts even within that market. In the graph below, I look at spot prices on Brent Crude and West Texas Intermediate (WTI) during March:

[![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!tl5k!,w_1100,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F9fef57ee-3d9f-4542-87fc-2025c060feb3_1952x1392.heic)](https://substack.com/redirect/ae0c2459-cdb5-4f2d-af7f-b151a4f7a646?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ)

Both Brent and WTI crude oil saw prices increase in March, but with the price of Brent rising 49.9% and WTI rising 48.6% during March, the difference between the two almost doubled during the second half of the month. That divergence reflects the two-fold effect of the war on oil supply, with the first being the shuttering of oil production in the Gulf States and the second being the effecting throttling of ship traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, a key passageway for Middle Eastern oil to Asia and Europe. While both factors push up oil prices, oil and gas production in the US, the largest oil producer in 2025 (producing 13.58 million barrels or 16% of the total), was less affected by the Hormuz closing and supply chain issues, explaining the increasing price divergence mid-month.

There was another tea leaf to read, and it came from watching oil futures prices. In the graph below, I compare the spot prices to Brent crude to June and December futures contracts prices:

[![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!4Wqo!,w_1100,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F77ba30e9-1b11-472f-8d35-98555960

## [The AI-native engineering philosophy has expanded from four steps to eight](https://every.)

![](https://d24ovhgu8s7341.cloudfront.net/uploads/post/cover/4279/full_page_cover_bb2331c7dc7f0afe-Compound_engineering.png)

*Midjourney/Every illustration.*

*Join me and* ***Trevin Chow*** *for our third compound engineering camp for paid subscribers next Friday,* ***June 5****. We’ll show how planning and building are collapsing into one flow—where you hand your AI a goal and it runs with it. [RSVP](https://every.to/emails/click/277e89a96182734274b33414175c1613d4cb600b7e9db7a8ecf343238a13d945/eyJzdWJqZWN0IjoiQ29tcG91bmQgRW5naW5lZXJpbmcgR2V0cyBhbiBVcGdyYWRlIiwicG9zdF9pZCI6NDI3OSwicG9zdF90eXBlIjoicG9zdCIsInVybCI6Imh0dHBzOi8vZXZlcnkudG8vZXZlbnRzL2NvbXBvdW5kLWVuZ2luZWVyaW5nLWNhbXAtMyIsInBvc2l0aW9uIjo1fQ==).*

*Was this newsletter forwarded to you? [Sign up](https://every.to/emails/click/277e89a96182734274b33414175c1613d4cb600b7e9db7a8ecf343238a13d945/eyJzdWJqZWN0IjoiQ29tcG91bmQgRW5naW5lZXJpbmcgR2V0cyBhbiBVcGdyYWRlIiwicG9zdF9pZCI6NDI3OSwicG9zdF90eXBlIjoicG9zdCIsInVybCI6Imh0dHBzOi8vZXZlcnkudG8vYWNjb3VudCIsInBvc2l0aW9uIjo2fQ==) to get it in your inbox.*

---

In its early days, [compound engineering](https://every.) was mostly about the code. I wanted to see if I could get an AI model to make a plan, do the work the way I wanted it done, review the results against my standards, and incorporate lessons from my feedback so it wouldn’t make the same mistake next time. The loop looked like this:

**Brainstorm → work → review → compound → repeat**

That loop is still the core of how I build **[Cora](https://every.to/emails/click/277e89a96182734274b33414175c1613d4cb600b7e9db7a8ecf343238a13d945/eyJzdWJqZWN0IjoiQ29tcG91bmQgRW5naW5lZXJpbmcgR2V0cyBhbiBVcGdyYWRlIiwicG9zdF9pZCI6NDI3OSwicG9zdF90eXBlIjoicG9zdCIsInVybCI6Imh0dHA6Ly9jb3JhLmNvbXB1dGVyIiwicG9zaXRpb24iOjh9)**. But almost a year after we first [coined the term](https://every.) compound engineering, the work phase has become boring—in the best way. If the plan is good and the agent has the right context, it usually does the work right. It writes the code and runs the tests. It fixes the obvious issues. The question now is: “Where do I fit in?”

The answer is at both ends of the process. An analogy my collaborator on the [compound engineering plugin](https://every.to/emails/click/277e89a96182734274b33414175c161

body:
# Data Update 7 for 2026: Debt and Taxes

In my [fifth data update](https://substack.com/redirect/cc6de217-b49d-4cad-bc8c-bcf823d64df6?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ), I examined [hurdle rates](https://substack.com/redirect/f82186ca-7cd8-4a2a-a325-994bad7cb939?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ) in 2025, and in my [sixth data update](https://substack.com/redirect/25b993b8-dcd8-4794-af37-1a0533fcc88f?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ), I looked at the profitability and return metrics for firms. Both hurdle rates and profitability metricsmcan be affected by how much debt companies choose to have in their financing structure, and it enters explicitly into my [cost of capital calculations](https://substack.com/redirect/209e3565-299b-40fd-94f1-9cd63ece2e7c?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ), both through the costs of equity/debt and the mix of the two, and into my accounting return calculations, for net margin and return on equity. In this session, I start with an examination of the trade off that all businesses face when it comes to choosing between debt and equity to fund their operations, and then look the debt choices that companies made in 2025. As with every other one of my data updates this year, AI enters this conversation not only because of the huge investments that are being made into [AI architecture](https://substack.com/redirect/3969d210-5f02-4c73-a1d3-b8d06999c937?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ), but also because a non-trivial portion of this investment is coming from debt, with private credit as a key contributor.

**Debt versus Equity: Choices and Tradeoff**

The discussion of the tradeoffs that businesses face on whether to borrow money (debt) or use owner’s funds (equity) has to start with a clear distinction between what it is that sets them apart. While that distinction may seem trivial, since accountants do break financing down into debt and equity on accounting balance sheets, accountants are not always consistent in their categorization, and I think that understanding what sets debt apart from equity can help catch these inconsistencies. There are three dimensions where debt and equity deviate:

1. Nature of claim: Debt gives its holders a contractual claim on the cash flows, insofar as the terms of interest and principal payments are laid down contractually at the time of the borrowing. Note that these contractual claims cover both fixed rate debt, where the interest payments are fixed over the lifetime of the debt, and floating rate debt, where the interest payments will change over time, but in ways that are specified by the bond/loan agreements. Equity gives its holders a residual claim, i.e,, a claim on cash flows, if any, that are left over after other claim holders have been paid.
2. Priority of claim: This follows from the first distinction, but debt holders get first claim on the cashflows, when the firm is in operation, and on liquidation proceeds, if the firm ever goes bankrupt. It is this priority of claims that should generally make debt safer than equity in almost every enterprise that employs both.
3. Legal consequences: A company that fails to pay dividends to its equity investors, no matter how deeply set their expectations of receiving these dividends, may see its stock price drop, but it cannot be held legally accountable for the failure. A company that fails to make its contractual obligations on debt can not only be sued, but can be pushed into bankruptcy, effectively ending its business life.

There are three other distinctions, which do not always hold, but are usually true:

1. Tax Treatment: In much of the world, the tax code is tilted in favor of debt, with interest payments being tax deductible and cash flows to equity (dividends or buybacks) coming out of after-tax cash flows, but there are three caveats. The first is that

subject: "Where’s all the f&$*#ing money going?" The Waste and Costs of American Utilities
body:
# "Where’s all the f&$*#ing money going?" The Waste and Costs of American Utilities

If there’s one obvious thing about this political moment, it’s that voters are furious about paying so much for electricity. In 2023, 70 million adults [chose](https://substack.com/redirect/13e83ba9-f3af-40af-8455-127641ebabf4?j=eyJ1IjoiZnZlciJ9.8N73-dqQlrWLx3o5gPfyirClhk7-cxP_NqOwOQYAApk) to forego food and medicine so they could afford their utility bills. Powerlines [found](https://substack.com/redirect/20ea0226-5c65-4cd0-8c72-29b0dbe98608?j=eyJ1IjoiZnZlciJ9.8N73-dqQlrWLx3o5gPfyirClhk7-cxP_NqOwOQYAApk) dozens of significant rate hikes last year, as the price of electricity [went](https://substack.com/redirect/4375b14a-6c3d-4ebd-ae12-00fef341c95e?j=eyJ1IjoiZnZlciJ9.8N73-dqQlrWLx3o5gPfyirClhk7-cxP_NqOwOQYAApk) up at one and a half times the rate of general inflation.

Voters have had enough, [telling](https://substack.com/redirect/c4042444-0f58-4e11-bca7-70deb4595e96?j=eyJ1IjoiZnZlciJ9.8N73-dqQlrWLx3o5gPfyirClhk7-cxP_NqOwOQYAApk) pollsters that electric utility prices are at crisis levels, and blaming excess profits for the problem.

[![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!tgyD!,w_1100,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F735da5f0-a7db-457e-bfe7-6afa4ebe8b21_3193x1796.png)](https://substack.com/redirect/70cc4fa8-4433-42db-9dec-6c1bbc227d75?j=eyJ1IjoiZnZlciJ9.8N73-dqQlrWLx3o5gPfyirClhk7-cxP_NqOwOQYAApk)

And policymakers, such as Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro, are [starting](https://substack.com/redirect/3c9af62d-1468-4da5-a52d-ecbc2a89a1c6?j=eyJ1IjoiZnZlciJ9.8N73-dqQlrWLx3o5gPfyirClhk7-cxP_NqOwOQYAApk) to talk about a revamp of the basic utility model.

[![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!GAUb!,w_1100,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F89f54e62-0ec8-4f6a-90db-0c799ad5b8b9_718x309.png)](https://substack.com/redirect/a3f9e243-33a5-44e3-9889-71876384878b?j=eyJ1IjoiZnZlciJ9.8N73-dqQlrWLx3o5gPfyirClhk7-cxP_NqOwOQYAApk)

Investor-owned utilities, as well as some advocates for clean energy, disagree. They argue that the price hikes are necessary to address grid reliability, extreme weather, fuel price changes, the energy transition, old infrastructure, and so forth. The war in Iran is the latest argument for higher prices.

And there is some merit to that argument. Iran has raised costs, and someone has to pay them. But there is a problem with that argument as well. There are a variety of utility business models in America, and it turns out that publicly owned utilities are not raising prices nearly as quickly as investor-owned ones beholden to Wall Street. So something is going on with the specific Wall Street-driven business model.

Beyond that, there’s another more basic question. Investor-owned utilities, often consolidated into increasingly huge holding companies, have been hiking for years, which presumably should be bringing in a gusher of cash to fix the problems they observe with extreme weather and reliability. Yet we are constantly hearing that the U.S. doesn’t have a good electric grid, that we can’t keep up with demand, that China keeps expanding massively while we are stagnant.

If we’ve been paying so much more for so long, why do we still need more investment? Where’s all the f&$*#ing money going?

This discussion is now more important, because on Monday, NextEra, a Florida-based utility, [announced](https://substack.com/redirect/3b56b324-28b8-4680-b01b-b67b5ac95dd6?j=eyJ1IjoiZnZlciJ9.8N73-dqQlrWLx3o5gPfyirClhk7-cxP_NqOwOQYAApk) the largest ever acquisition in the utility space, a $67 billion takeover of Dominion Energy. The companies are claiming the deal will lower electricity costs and speed up the deployment of infrastructure for data centers using renewable energy. But the real rationale for the deal is entirely about how we price utility services

subject: Debunking the "Kingmaking" Myth
body:
# Debunking the "Kingmaking" Myth

If your competitor raises a huge round from the best firms in the world, your first reaction may be: “Are we dead?” That reaction is part of the design. Beyond capital, a big round is a message to the market that the category winner has already been decided.

This happens because venture is a power law business. A few true outliers built by exceptional entrepreneurs end up moving the needle for several funds. Those founders are rare, so when some investors think they’ve found one, they lean in early and try to make the outcome feel inevitable.

“Kingmaking” is the name of this move: a deliberate attempt to define the category winner, then reinforce that conviction with extremely large checks and loud signaling.

This is one of those self-fulfilling prophecies, built on the idea that overfunding raises your chances of success disproportionately. Because the winners are often the most-funded companies, we get the chicken-and-egg problem. **Did they win because they received the most funding or did they receive the most funding because they were already winning?**

For entrepreneurs, this seems like pure upside. Since dilution is limited within rounds, larger rounds mean higher valuations, translating into cheaper capital. In fact, most times, you should take the “kingmaker” offer if you receive one. Still, in this article we want to present the overlooked side effects that can come with it.

At SaaSholic we don’t believe in kingmaking. We have seen multiple cases where the underdog beats the overhyped player and multiple companies bootstrap their way to success¹. We also think it hurts venture returns, which is bad for the asset class and its LPs (we personally like investing in contrarian underdogs too, but that’s another story!). Here are the reasons we’re skeptical.

---

### Mercenaries over Missionaries

Extra funding can help you hire the most pedigreed talent, however, early in the journey it’s well known that you need “missionaries” over “mercenaries”². You want people with an owner’s mindset and the grit to make your company win, even when it feels irrational from the outside.

Having extra money will help to hire the Dev from big tech, or the polite leader with the right vocabulary, but those aren’t the ones that move the needle. More often than not, this profile will bring politics into the organization earlier than the company can afford.

In startups, even at later stages when the risk of ruin has apparently dropped, you still need to run with the “only the paranoids survive”³ mindset. The moment you start believing your crown is real, you stop doing the things that would earn it in the first place.

Startups are living experiments. You must iterate, iterate and iterate until you can (hopefully) find your way to success. You can’t buy your way into it.

We heard the clearest rebuttal to kingmaking from someone who would benefit from it. In a recent 20VC episode⁴, Winston Weinberg, founder & CEO of Harvey, the $6B legaltech that raised $1B from OpenAI, Sequoia, Kleiner Perkins, a16z and Coatue, explained why the idea breaks down in practice.

> **Harry Stebbings:** Why do you disagree with kingmaking as a theory?
>
> **Winston Weinberg:** One, they think of kingmaking as it provides you with more capital. **More capital does not mean you run a better business. You could have as much capital in the world as you want. If you make the wrong product decisions, you’re just going to invest in all the wrong places and it doesn’t matter**. It’s the same as VC. You have a hundred billion and if you put it all into the wrong things, that still goes to zero, right?
>
> […] **How many times a day do you think something goes wrong at Harvey? Constantly. Like 24/7.** How many times a day do you think we feel like there’s an existential threat? […] All the time. Startups are very difficult places to work.
>

# How I Built a Live Data Experience in a Sunday (Claude's Version)

On Sunday I vibe-coded this [AI marketplace tracker.](https://link.mail.beehiiv.com/ss/c/u001.jGY3i_l4dDwQlqT7xK9Awow5hCfkWIjgDT9fAUTEiSideG0UKA56VoypV0t3Z0DGb22ReCqCiLpWgLtKtlQX5sZx1-fxXTXJISUHqDAqiSMhVxwpJeEAQjzWbR1fCb2_Y1bWvB14T6NeLbcpRAbzlPRG5EO6_ObkpoUHiqNl8FE1L4UtKxWsQ3LICBFqKu4kAH2bhReCRaEHgJkQXxMA0i3nd-pWXwucIMUlnhzGO_rRol9bmdeb8GR9n212Kw6IUoaV6sUX65_6VpTH3v2n7QIzFVRic79T_sAje-d9HXRZqPAJd0V_424IEfkkx1VBn_Kf1z5lph_in6D-duck0ppn38YvwUjznDfmXufNXyk/4p3/mbd4CYU3RfSacrSg7eyVew/h5/h001.B_haj7-56AwrcsCTdF1N_Wg3nZsUyI7kYhbMfFfj6Lg) It was a fun experiment.

For today's newsletter, I asked Claude to write a guest post about the process and what we learned. Seemed fitting.

I was nice to me, joked a bit, and share some lessons for anyone that’s into vibe coding.

Here's what it had to say:

Adam has a rule that I'm not allowed to use em dashes. He says I overuse them. He's right. This entire draft was written without a single one and I won't pretend it wasn't painful.

Here's what actually happened on Sunday.

## The Setup

Adam and his friend Josh were eating bagels. Adam had been building crawlers that track every company listed on Claude and ChatGPT's app marketplaces. He'd posted about it on LinkedIn. 26 likes. For context, his good posts get 10-20x that. Josh told him why it flopped before Adam even asked.

Josh told him why: "It doesn't show there's work behind this. It just looks like you're reporting the news."

Adam opened me up and basically said: "You remember all that marketplace data we've been working on? My friend Josh says the post doesn't look like first-party research. What should we build?"

I did remember. I'd helped build the crawlers. I had all the data context. So I went and looked at the original post and the datasets, and came back with three concepts.

## The Concept Phase

Adam picked the interactive tracker idea, then made it better. I'd suggested a search bar where people type their company name. He said: "What if it's a category browser instead? You pick GTM or Dev Tools, and it shows who's listed AND who's not?"

I told him his version was stronger. Search is one dopamine hit. Category browse is sustained engagement. And the "who's NOT there" view is the real product. A CMO sees their competitor listed and their company absent. That's a screenshot to the head of product.

We went into plan mode. I generated an architecture. Adam approved it. Then we built.

## The Build (What Actually Happened)

**The first version took about 10 minutes.** Python script reads CSVs, produces JSON. HTML/CSS/JS renders it. Real data, real logos, functional in a browser. Adam's reaction: "This looks like a standard quad code frontend." Fair.

**Then an hour of me not understanding what he wanted.** He kept saying things like "more terminal vibe" and "monospace energy." I kept making incremental improvements. We were going in circles.

**Then he drew a picture.** Pencil on printer paper. Took a photo. Dropped it in.

![](https://media.beehiiv.com/cdn-cgi/image/fit=scale-down,format=auto,onerror=redirect,quality=80/uploads/asset/file/8be127ac-e30f-44b7-870b-3d571a36e766/CleanShot_2026-03-19_at_19.56.18_2x.png?t=1773975396)

I cannot overstate how much better this was than text descriptions. The layout clicked immediately. Grid lines between every row. Data density. The bar chart at top, ticker below, dropdown centered. Two iterations later we had something that looked like it belonged at a data company, not a coding bootcamp.

If I could give one piece of advice to anyone working with AI on design: draw it. A 30-second sketch communicates more spatial information than 10 minutes of typing.

**The brand took three tries.** Adam went through three different font and color systems before loading his actual brand fonts. This should have been step one. I don't know what fonts you like until you tell me.

**The FOMO features were all Adam.** The growth chart

Jesse also opens up about his parenting philosophy, including why he believes fathers should be authoritative first and friends second, how he and his wife use a no hint dropping rule to communicate better, and why both parents need something outside of work and family that is just for them. We also get into one of the most fascinating parts of the conversation, how Jesse is using AI to rethink his kids’ education and teach them how to think critically in a world where information is everywhere. We discussed:

* **Moving a family to Puerto Rico:** How Jesse approached a major family transition and helped his kids adapt to a completely new environment.
* **The cost of putting career first:** Why Jesse believes chasing professional success at the expense of family can leave you deeply unfulfilled.
* **What strong fatherhood really looks like:** Why dads need to be caring, present, emotionally grounded, and willing to lead at home.
* **Better communication in marriage:** The “no hint dropping” rule Jesse and his wife use to avoid passive-aggressive communication and say what they actually mean.
* **Why parents need a third pillar:** Jesse shares why both partners need something outside of work and family that helps them stay grounded and fulfilled.
* **Rethinking education with AI:** How Jesse is using AI to redesign his kids’ learning and teach them to think critically in a world full of instant information.

Find Startup Dad on ***[Youtube](https://substack.com/redirect/75941218-67d2-409a-9493-2ef777ab7dba?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ)*** ***, [Spotify](https://substack.com/redirect/dbfacc39-f0ac-436a-b00b-10467f9097c9?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ) and [Apple Podcasts](https://substack.com/redirect/8a89f851-86d8-4c88-9923-ee3a1127b5aa?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ)***

[Nate Quigley](https://substack.com/redirect/54e3ca8b-094a-4111-a53c-f251904b5666?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ) is the co-founder of [Chatbooks](https://substack.com/redirect/d00fb9ec-8730-48e7-b499-61b16a0f22a9?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ), the photo book company that helps families preserve their memories from Instagram photos. He started the company after a wave of nostalgia hit as his oldest child approached leaving home, only to spend years building a product nobody wanted. Then his wife Vanessa stepped in, suggested they simply print Instagram, and became the accidental co-founder who helped turn the company around.

He’s also a father of seven, a grandfather of two, and officially the first Startup Dad guest to also be a Startup Granddad. Nate brings a rare perspective on what it means to build a company while raising a big family and then watching those kids grow into adults with lives of their own. He shares how parenting has taught him to release control, stay curious, and create family rituals that give kids a place to come back to. We discussed:

- **Co-founding with your spouse:** How Vanessa’s intervention saved Chatbooks and what it’s been like building a company together for more than a decade.

- **Treating the company like a family farm:** Farm families don’t talk about work-life balance because work and life are the same thing.

- **Parenting seven very different kids:** How Nate’s approach changed from child one to child seven and why one parenting playbook never works for every child.

- **Learning to let go:** Why Nate believes the hardest parts of parenting and leadership come from guiding people without trying to control every outcome.

- **Creating family rituals that stick:** The traditions that helped Nate keep a household of nine connected.

- **Helping kids navigate technology:** How Nate thinks about phones, social media, AI, and using tools that create better conversations instead of just tighter controls.

**Where to find Nate Quigley**

- LinkedIn: [https://www.linkedin.com/in/natequigley/](https://substack.com/redirect/54e3ca8b-094a-4111-a53c-f251904b5666?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ)

subject: Change Management Requires Surround Sound
body:
# Change Management Requires Surround Sound

I’ve been mulling over a pattern I keep seeing, across companies I’ve worked at, companies I advise, and frankly in conversations with product leaders at every stage of scale. It goes something like this:

A leader identifies the need for a strategic shift. Maybe it’s moving upmarket. Maybe it’s shifting from shipping features to investing in platform. Maybe it’s restructuring how EPD and GTM collaborate. They think about it deeply, get crystal clear, and then... they announce it. An all-hands. A Slack post. A strategy deck. Maybe all three in the same week.

And then they wait.

Three months later, they’re baffled. Why is nothing different? Why are teams still building the same way? Why does the roadmap look like it did last quarter? Didn’t everyone hear the message?

Here’s what’s actually happening: they did hear it. They just didn’t absorb it. And that distinction - between hearing a message and internalizing it - is where most change efforts quietly fail.

### **The Surround Sound Problem**

I think the effort required to land a strategic change inside an organization is massively disproportionate to what most leaders expect. And I don’t think people appreciate just how big the gap is between “communicating a change” and “landing a change.” I’ve talked before about launches vs landings in the context of product work, and I think the same distinction applies here. Announcing a strategic shift is a launch. Getting the organization to actually change how it operates is a landing. And landing requires a broader, more sustained campaign than most leaders plan for.

And I don’t mean campaign in the corporate-comms, town-hall-roadshow sense. I mean it more in the way a marketer thinks about reaching a customer. You have to surround your audience with the message from multiple angles, at varying cadences, through different mediums, until it stops being “the new thing leadership said” and starts being “the way we work.”

A cross-functional partner of mine recently put it perfectly:

> ### *“Change management requires surround sound.”*

I loved that framing, and it stuck with me. Because that’s exactly what it is. One speaker in the corner of the room isn’t going to cut it.

And in my experience, surround sound comes down to three things:

[![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!6jMe!,w_1100,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F5d1094fa-c568-4599-ba54-01776180bfba_1308x1374.png)](https://substack.com/redirect/65d886ec-9bd5-403f-a2d8-a758ec42d6e8?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ)

### **Format: Same Message, Different Packaging**

I think the first mistake leaders make is assuming that if they’ve articulated the change clearly once, in one format, the job is done. But people process information differently. And more importantly, people process information differently depending on the context in which they receive it.

So a strategy deck presented at an all-hands is one format. That same strategic shift, expressed as a set of updated prioritization criteria in a planning review, is another. The shift reflected in which roles you’re hiring for is another. The shift embedded in the questions a leader asks during a product review is yet another. Same message, totally different packaging.

And what I mean by Format is translating the message across altitudes and modalities. The CEO version of the change is not the same as the engineering manager version, which is not the same as the IC PM version. Not because the direction is different, but because the implications are different for each audience. And so when you only communicate the change at one altitude, you’re asking everyone else to do the translation work themselves. Most won’t. Not because they’re lazy or resistant, but because they’re busy and they’ll default to what they already know.

# [AINews] The Custom ASIC Thesis

> *AI News for 2/19/2026-2/20/2026. We checked 12 subreddits, [544 Twitters](https://substack.com/redirect/7f8de2ac-9f58-46c5-a291-ae58bc229978?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ) and 24 Discords (**262** channels, and **12582** messages) for you. Estimated reading time saved (at 200wpm): **1242** minutes. [AINews’ website](https://substack.com/redirect/1ecc119f-01ce-4e98-b38f-dc54781b10b5?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ) lets you search all past issues. As a reminder, [AINews is now a section of Latent Space](https://substack.com/redirect/a480d644-b8ad-4a38-bdc1-2c7f95c5e531?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ). You can [opt in/out](https://substack.com/redirect/ae397973-9917-4abb-9843-6c947669303a?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ) of email frequencies!*

Congrats to the [ggml + Huggingface team](https://substack.com/redirect/80298f56-5760-4749-8a7e-02f09ff51246?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ), note the [Opus 4.6 METR debate](https://substack.com/redirect/fff8052b-c322-49ab-b33c-18a667a0d966?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ), and read [Chris Lattner’s Claude C Compiler analysis](https://substack.com/redirect/c246c445-c249-4bd6-ad7e-5c0fb71f9ebd?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ). But those aren’t the top stories.

Today, 2.5 year old [Taalas announced](https://substack.com/redirect/b531dd40-c902-4eff-b5fd-cc1353e51c31?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ) a **shockingly fast 16,960 tokens per second** per user production API service for the Llama 3.1 8B model (launched July 2024):

[![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!oVQ7!,w_1100,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F49185ac5-439f-4605-ba64-42d42591e30c_2050x1478.png)](https://substack.com/redirect/81d9095b-4d5f-4bd2-9bbd-5650ba74adbd?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ)

While there are some other non-speed gains (less build cost and power draw), it is also offset by some other footnotes on quantization (which they note the HC2 will resolve with standardized low precision FP4).

**This is an impressive result…. that we have no idea how to productize yet.** And anytime there is a huge capability overhang opening up, AI Engineers should rush in to figure out the “capability market fit”.

As for the overall proposition of going custom ASIC, we’re still thinking about this week’s Latent Space with [Martin Casado and Sarah Wang](https://substack.com/redirect/5f753fa5-9bd2-4d40-ba91-25a6939a3d4b?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ), where Martin reiterated his conviction in the math of doing custom accelerators (ASICs) **PER MODEL**, essentially “baking the LLM into silicon”, foreshadowing [the OpenAI Broadcom deal](https://substack.com/redirect/5a4d7f30-63e6-4d74-acb9-9dc1e796b33c?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ):

[![](https://substackcdn.com/image/youtube/w_728,c_limit/l_youtube_play_qyqt8q,w_120/p1k7TiAFqdE)](https://substack.com/redirect/c63863dd-9420-4aa1-9e3c-5f630244a50a?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ)

***Martin:** It makes sense to actually do a custom ASIC if you can do it in time. The question now is timelines, but not money because rough math:*

* *If it’s a billion dollar training run, then the inference for that model has to be over a billion, otherwise it won’t be solvent.*
* *So let’s assume if you could save 20%, (which you could save much more than 20% with an ASIC), that’s $200 million.*
* *You can tape out a chip for $200 million.*

*Right? So now you can literally like justify economically, not timeline wise. That’s a different issue.*
